COURSE_NARRATIVE: (ANTH 2101, 2401*) Introduction to Biological Anthropology Laboratory. (0-3). Credit 1. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores fundamental evolutionary principles and the concepts of population genetics. Applies the scientific method to investigate evolutionary trends relevant to humans through hands-on exposure to fossils of non-human primates, human relatives and ancestors, and modern human evolution. Evaluates and synthesizes information regarding human ancestry and contemporary variation. Analyzes key trends related to human evolution, such as encephalization and bipedalism, by measuring and comparing real and modeled skeletal specimens. Lab exercises are designed to complement and reinforce topics covered in the lecture course ANTH 225. TOPICS AND THEMES. Discussions of basic genetic principles, evolutionary mechanisms and population genetics. Analyzes human and non-human primate anatomy, focusing on skeletal morphology. Applies qualitative and quantitative methods for bone identification, skeletal growth, dental variation and locomotor function. Studies extant and extinct primate specimens, including their taxonomy, behavior and fossil record. Examinations of the hominin fossil record including casts of specimens from the following taxa: Australopithecus, Paranthropus and the genus Homo, including H. habilis, H. erectus, Middle Pleistocene Homo, Neanderthals and H. sapiens. Prerequisites: Concurrent registration in ANTH 225 is recommended; also taught at Galveston campus.

Introduction to Folklore. (3-0). Credit 3. Study of folklore through selected examples of traditional cultures, their beliefs, customs and art forms such as: tales, folksongs, proverbs, riddles and material culture.

Introduction to Forensic Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examine the foundational role of forensic anthropology within the broader forensic sciences which involves analyzing human skeletal remains for medico-legal applications, covering the history of the field and its development. Build theoretical knowledge of the discipline including the history of how the discipline developed and its role in the broader forensic sciences and international, federal and state levels. Apply proper anatomical terminology, taphonomy and comparative morphological methods to discuss and describe skeletal trauma, pathologies and anomalies. Apply and practice methods used to create a "biological profile" for an individual by estimating sex, age, stature and ancestry. Explore scene recovery methods and how skeletal analysis is applied in a variety of contexts, including routine casework, large-scale natural disasters, war casualties and human rights investigations. Critically discuss and analyze forensic methods by addressing the practical and ethical issues facing practicing forensic anthropologists today. TOPICS AND THEMES. Consider the history and foundations of forensic anthropology; study the broader medicolegal system, professional ethics and error assessment; apply osteological methods and anatomical terminology to describing human skeletal material; describe scene recovery methods such as location, recovery and taphonomic processes; apply and critically examine methods for estimating sex, age, stature and ancestry; identify and classify infectious disease, congenital conditions and nutritional deficiencies on the skeleton and teeth; explore individual identification techniques such as facial reconstruction and genetic genealogy; critically assess how forensic anthropology is portrayed in popular culture and the media. Discuss current topics considered relevant to the field by the American Academy of Forensic Science including, but not limited to, research ethics, reassessment of biological profile estimation methods and demographic underrepresentation in comparative collections.

Directed Studies. Credit 0 to 3. For individual research in anthropology on subjects not included in established courses. May be taken two times for credit. Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor.
Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of anthropology. May be repeated for credit.

Research.  Credit 0 to 3. Research conducted under the direction of a faculty member in Anthropology. May be taken two times for credit. Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor.

COURSE_NARRATIVE: Cultural Change and Development. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Investigates the broad spectrum of cultural dynamics, providing an overview of how societies transform and adapt through cultural change. Examines diverse methodologies and theoretical approaches used to document and interpret these shifts. Draws on case studies and source materials from all areas of anthropology, integrating knowledge from allied fields. Develops a strong understanding of the complexities inherent in cultural change. Enhances the ability to employ theoretical concepts in novel and innovative ways. Clarifies the practical need to apply anthropological knowledge in programs of directed change. Encourages respectful critique and defense of diverse points of view regarding current social issues. TOPICS AND THEMES. Studies the fundamental concept of culture; analyzes definitions, overviews and data sources related to cultural change; investigates dynamic processes such as innovation, diffusion and acculturation; considers theoretical approaches including functionalism, cultural materialism and cultural evolution; examines maladaptive traits and Darwinian evolutionary principles applied to culture; explores the intersection of cultural change and health; and analyzes colonial legacies and the dynamics of directed change.

North American Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the archaeology of North America from the first arrival of humans on the continent through recent historical archaeology. Emphasis will be upon the geographic area of the continental United States and Canada, with a focus on past Indigenous lifeways and their variation in time and in space. Discusses individual sites and places them into their regional context. Develops critical analysis skills of the lines of evidence most common to North American archaeology, including archaeological site reports, academic papers, historical records and other primary sources. Compares sites across space and time to form ideas of changing lifeways, technologies and social and individual identities of past people of North America. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include the concept of culture areas and its evolution over time, environmental archaeology, migration; adaption and environment; domestication and agriculture; technological innovation and development; trade; social complexity, warfare, culture contact, archaeological laws, ethics and politics, including the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act and Indigenous archaeology in North America. The course will include historical archaeology but focuses upon pre-European archaeology. Special attention is given to the diverse lines of evidence archaeologists use to explore these themes—including paleoenvironmental proxies, material culture analysis, iconography, colonial-era documents and ethnographic accounts. This multidisciplinary approach fosters a more holistic understanding of North American societies and their rich, complex histories. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to North American archaeology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisite: ANTH 201, ANTH 202, ANTH 204, ANTH 205, or ANTH 210.

Fundamentals of Anthropological Writing. (1-0). Credit 1. Basic types of writing expected of anthropology students; emphasis on the subject matter of an upper-division anthropology course in which the student is currently enrolled. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and co-enrollment in another upper-division anthropology course (the "companion course").

Mesoamerican Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the peoples and civilizations of Mesoamerica—a cultural region encompassing the southern two-thirds of Mexico and the northern half of Central America, including present-day Belize, Guatemala, El Salvador and northwestern Honduras. Traces the full arc of human occupation in the region, from the earliest settlements over 14,000 years ago to the arrival of Europeans in the 15th century. Critically evaluates archaeological data and interpretations and situates Mesoamerican case studies within broader anthropological and theoretical frameworks. TOPICS AND THEMES. Emphasizing critical engagement with key debates in Mesoamerican archaeology, the course examines topics such as the origins of agriculture and urbanism, household and state economies, social stratification, ritual and religion, warfare, mobility and migration, and processes of collapse and resilience. Special attention is given to the diverse lines of evidence archaeologists use to explore these themes—including ancient DNA, material culture analysis, iconography, writing systems, linguistics, colonial-era documents and ethnographic accounts. This multidisciplinary approach fosters a more holistic understanding of Mesoamerican societies and their rich, complex histories. Prerequisites: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204, or approval of instructor.

Fossil Evidence of Human Evolution. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines human evolution from the time of divergence from the other African apes through the appearance of anatomically modern humans. Delves into the detailed study of the fossil antecedents of humans. Applies fundamental principles from evolutionary biology, geology, primatology and paleontology to interpret the human lineage. Integrates evidence from the human fossil record, archaeological material, ancient DNA and living human populations. Studies comparative osteology and paleoecology to interpret the evolutionary relationships, diet and behavior of extinct and living human and non-human Primate species. Analyzes the evolutionary mechanisms that have patterned life on Earth and the forces that have acted upon these processes. Develops a deeper awareness of how humans fit into the natural world. Develops a comprehensive understanding of the evolutionary mechanisms that position humans within the larger Primate clade and the genetic and environmental underpinnings of modern human variability and dispersal. Hands-on, discussion and writing-intensive assignments are designed to develop students’ critical reading/thinking skills and apply paleoanthropological methods to real and modeled skeletal materials. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers human evolutionary biology, including evolutionary processes, natural selection and macroevolutionary principles. Analyses geological and paleontological contexts, focusing on fossils, taphonomy and dating techniques. Examines living and extinct primate diversity and evolution, covering early primates and apes. Studies specific hominin species, including the earliest possible hominins, Australopithecus, Paranthropus, Homo species (such as H. erectus, H. naledi and H. neanderthalensis) and Homo sapiens. Investigates comparative morphology, osteology and diagnostic skeletal features of the human skeleton. Explores and describes paleoecology, anatomy, diet, human evolutionary trends and the genetic and environmental underpinnings that have shaped our species. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisite: ANTH 225 or approval of instructor.

Historical Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the material and documentary evidence of European colonization in North America and its impact on Indigenous populations, African enslaved peoples and the environment. Integrates historical records with archaeological findings to understand how European imperial powers such as the Spanish, the Basques, the French, the Dutch and the English shaped the Americas through settlement, trade and social structures. Includes case studies from contact-era settlements, plantations, forts, battlefields and maritime contexts, highlighting how artifacts, architecture and written documents complement and sometimes challenge one another. Emphasizes methods of historical archaeology, including document transcription, genealogical research, artifact analysis and field methods that provide students with tools to critically interpret North American history through a material lens. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in historical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. European exploration and colonial expansion led by European nations including Spain, Portugal, France, the Netherlands and England; Indigenous populations; forced migration and enslavement of Africans; trade, exchange and economic structures; archaeology of gender, identity, racialization, plantations, forts, battlefields, settlements, graves and shipwrecks; historical archaeological theory and methods including survey and excavation methods, absolute and relative dating methods and artifact analysis; archival and research skills including genealogical research, transcription and historical document analysis; also taught at Galveston campus.

Nautical Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines shipwrecks, sunken harbors and other submerged evidence of human activity from the Stone Age through early modern times. Explores the archaeology, technology and cultural significance of maritime societies, emphasizing the methods used to survey, map, excavate, conserve and interpret submerged sites. Reviews case examples from the Mediterranean and northern Europe, including Bronze Age, Classical, Byzantine, medieval and Viking vessels, while considering the relationship of seafaring to cultural geography and the broader human past. Ship construction, diving technology, site preservation and surveying techniques are addressed and explored through various case studies. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in nautical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Shipwrecks; submerged harbors; inundated archaeological sites; Bronze Age Mediterranean vessels; Egyptian Nile boats; Classical Greek and Phoenician ships; Greek warships (triremes, polyremes); Roman merchantmen; Byzantine ships; late medieval Mediterranean ships; late medieval warships; carracks; Scandinavian and Northern European ships; Viking ships; cogs; hulks; ship construction; rigging; armament; nautical technology; maritime trade; naval warfare; cultural geography; survey and mapping techniques; excavation and conservation methods; diving technology; artifact analysis; heritage management; iconography; relevance to modern maritime research. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

Introduction to Biblical Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces students to the archaeology and material culture of the Land of the Bible from the Epi-Paleolithic period through the first century A.D. The course examines the peoples, cities and societies of biblical times through material remains, integrating artifacts, iconography and texts to develop a holistic understanding of the ancient Near East. Students explore archaeological discoveries in relation to biblical narratives, including early agricultural communities, Canaanite city-states, Egyptian influence and Iron Age polities. The course also emphasizes the interpretation of archaeological evidence, historical context and the relationship of seafaring and trade to cultural development in the ancient biblical world. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in biblical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Epi-Paleolithic period; Neolithic period; first agriculturists; Chalcolithic period; Early Bronze Age; Early Bronze IV; Middle Bronze Age I-II; Late Bronze Age; Egyptian influence in Canaan; maritime trade and seafaring; Iron Age I; Sea Peoples; Philistines; United Monarchy (Saul, David, Solomon); Divided Monarchy; Persian period; archaeology of biblical texts; material culture; urbanism; Canaanite city-states; fortifications; religious architecture; iconography; ceramics; metallurgy; inscriptions; settlement patterns; excavation techniques; interpretation of artifacts; relationship between archaeology and biblical narrative; cultural geography and human-environment interaction. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with RELS 317.

Ships and Shipwrecks of the Americas. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how ships and seafaring shaped the history and culture of the Western Hemisphere from 1492 through the American Civil War. Draws on archaeological discoveries and historical records to examine exploration, colonization, trade, naval conflict and technological innovation through the lens of maritime material culture. Reviews case studies of shipwrecks and other maritime sites, revealing the vessels, technologies and practices that connected cultures, facilitated economic systems and transformed warfare. From Indigenous watercraft to colonial gunboats, steamboats and Civil War submarines, engages with the archaeological evidence that illuminates change and continuity in the maritime world of the Americas. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in nautical archaeology of the Americas. TOPICS AND THEMES. Ship construction; ship rigging; seafaring technologies; European and American shipwreck archaeological case studies; Iberian voyages of exploration; Basque whaling; Spain’s maritime empire; Northern European maritime exploration; colonization; technological developments; economics and history of the Western Hemisphere; European-Indigenous relationships; Indigenous watercraft; Anglo-French wars; piracy and privateering; Revolutionary War; War of 1812; Shipping in the Commercial Age; canal transport; horse-powered boats; steamboats; packet ships; clipper ships; whaling fleets; Arctic exploration; Civil War naval warfare. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

Nautical Archaeology of the Ancient Mediterranean. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys seafaring and maritime culture in the Mediterranean from the Stone Age through the Roman Republic, with an excursus on fluvial galleys of Imperial Rome. Examines the archaeological and historical evidence for ancient navigation, shipbuilding and maritime trade, with a focus on both land-based and underwater sites. Students explore Egyptian seafaring on the Nile and in the Red Sea, Bronze Age shipwrecks such as Uluburun and Cape Gelidonya, Phoenician and Greek colonization, Etruscan maritime activity and Roman naval and merchant vessels. The course integrates material culture, iconography and archaeological discoveries to illuminate the technological, economic and cultural aspects of ancient Mediterranean seafaring. TOPICS AND THEMES. Stone Age seafaring; earliest evidence for boats; Egyptian Nile boats; Funerary Barge of Khufu; Tomb of Ti; Middle Kingdom Egyptian ships; New Kingdom Egypt; Queen Hatshepsut; Punt expedition; obelisk barge; Ramses III naval battles; Syro-Canaanite ships; Cape Gelidonya shipwreck; Late Bronze Age ships; Uluburun shipwreck; cosmopolitan trade; Phoenicians; Greeks; Etruscans; Greek shipwrecks; Western and Eastern Mediterranean; Bronze Age warships; penteconter; Archaic warships; Classical warships; Athenian trireme; Hellenistic giant warships; galley rams; Roman trade and economy; Roman merchantmen; Battle of Actium; Roman Imperial warships and shipwrecks; ship construction; rigging; armament; nautical technology; maritime trade; naval warfare; artifact analysis; cultural geography; surveying; excavation; conservation; interpretation of seafaring evidence; integration of material culture and texts; economic and social history of the Mediterranean. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
