COURSE_NARRATIVE: Music in World Cultures. (3-0). Credit 3.  Examination of music from an ethnomusicological perspective focusing on musical performance and the complex interrelationship of music to culture, society and daily life; examination of music from a variety of cultures through a series of case studies. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with MUSC 324.

Field Research in Anthropology.  Credit 1 to 9. Training for students in formulating and solving anthropological problems through field research; problem oriented field research under supervision. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANTH 201, ANTH 202, ANTH 204, ANTH 205, ANTH 210, or ANTH 225; approval by instructor.

Cultures of Central Asia. (3-0). Credit 3. Study of anthropological research in Central Asia: ecological adaptations; colonialism and post-colonialism; ethnic politics and ethnic conflict; religion and identity; gender and family; globalization and modernization. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

South American Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Archaeological study of South America from initial human settlement through European colonial encounters, with emphasis on the Central Andes. This region encompasses striking environmental diversity where societies developed technological innovations, monumental architecture and complex political systems. The course examines how archaeologists reconstruct past lifeways through material evidence, considering interactions between environment, technology, social organization and cultural expression. Students explore long-term processes of change, including agricultural development, urbanization, political centralization and cultural transformation. Study includes major pre-Inca societies, the rise of the Inca Empire and Spanish colonization. Contemporary Andean communities and their maintenance of ancestral practices provide context for understanding long-term cultural continuity. TOPICS AND THEMES. Course topics may include: environmental diversity and human adaptation across ecological zones; early settlement patterns and cultural change; agricultural systems, technological innovations and monumental architecture; artistic traditions and material culture as expressions of identity and belief; pre-Inca political systems and the development of complex societies; Inca imperial strategies, administrative technologies and infrastructure; Spanish colonial encounters and Indigenous responses; ethical dimensions in archaeological practice, including repatriation and collaboration with descendant communities; connections between archaeological evidence and contemporary Andean societies. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

European Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of human prehistory and history on the European continent and surrounding islands through the remains of material culture such as artifacts, human and animal remains, structures, landscapes and environments. Investigates the wide time span from the earliest Paleolithic hunter-gatherer hominids (up to two million years ago), through the Neolithic agricultural “revolution”, the metal ages, the classical civilizations of Greece and Rome, the medieval period and up to the modern era. Develops critical analysis skills using different types of information including archaeological site reports, academic papers, historical records and other primary sources to understand individual sites. Compares sites across space and time to form ideas of changing lifeways, technologies, and social and individual identities of past Europeans. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include human origins and migration; adaption and environment; domestication and agriculture; technological innovation and development; trade; social complexity, urbanization and state formation including hunter-gatherers, small scale societies, cities and empires; conflict and warfare; religion and ritual; art, music and culture; social, cultural and individual identity. Methodologies discussed include archaeological excavations, surveys, GIS, spatial analysis, analysis of landscapes and buildings, dating methods, artifact analysis, examination of human and animal remains, environmental and geoarchaeology, lab methods including ancient DNA, proteins, lipids, and stable isotopes, ethnographies and experimental archaeology. Class discussions may be thought-provoking and introduce new perspectives and material that students may not have encountered before. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

Classical Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. Origins and spread of Western civilization through the material remains of Minoan, Mycenaen, Etruscan, and early Greek and Roman cultures. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; Galveston campus.

Archaeology of Ancient Greece. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology of ancient Greece from the Stone Age through the Hellenistic Period, concluding with the rise of Rome. Explores the material culture, art, architecture and social history of the Greek world across its major cultural phases, from the Bronze Age civilizations of Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece to the flourishing of Classical Athens and the cosmopolitan Hellenistic kingdoms. Emphasizes the integration of archaeological evidence, ancient texts and artistic traditions to illuminate Greek religion, civic life, domestic space and cultural interactions across the Mediterranean. By examining key sites, monuments, artifacts and artistic achievements, students gain a comprehensive understanding of Greek society and its enduring legacy in Western civilization. TOPICS AND THEMES. Stone Age and Neolithic Greece; Bronze Age civilizations; Minoan Crete; Mycenaean palaces and the Trojan War; the Greek Dark Ages; Geometric period art and society; Archaic architecture, sculpture and vase painting; Classical Athens and the Acropolis; sanctuaries such as Delphi; fourth-century Greece and the rise of Macedon; Hellenistic art, architecture and urbanism; Greek houses and domestic mosaics; shipwreck archaeology; coinage and economic history; Greek religion and votive practices; interactions with Magna Graecia and the wider Mediterranean; Greek artistic and cultural legacy in Rome and later neoclassicism. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with CLAS 353.

Archaeology of Ancient Italy. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology of ancient Italy from the Stone Age through the collapse of the Roman Empire in the fourth century CE. Students examine the material culture, art and architecture of the Etruscans and Romans, as well as the prehistoric and early Italic foundations that shaped them. Explores how Italy’s peoples expressed identity, religion and power through sculpture, painting, mosaics, inscriptions, temples, homes and civic monuments. Special emphasis is placed on the development of Rome from a small city-state into a vast imperial capital, the role of urbanism and daily life, and the ways in which material remains reveal both continuity and transformation across centuries of Italian history. TOPICS AND THEMES. Prehistoric Italy and the Stone Age; Villanovans and the emergence of the Etruscans; Etruscan cities and art; early Rome and urban foundations; Romanization and the Republic; Augustan classicism; imperial art and architecture under the Julio-Claudians, Flavians and Antonines; wall painting, mosaics and domestic life; Pompeii and Herculaneum; the lure of the games and public spectacles; baths, theaters and civic monuments; coinage and inscriptions as evidence of social and political life; Ostia and imperial urbanism; ships and shipwrecks of Roman Italy; Severan and Late Roman art; Constantine and the transformation of Roman identity; collapse of the Roman Empire in the fourth century CE. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with CLAS 354.

Ancient Civilizations of the World. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores archaeological studies that have contributed to our understanding of the emergence and decline of states and civilizations between 3500 BCE and 1500 CE. Examines the complex origins of anthropology and archaeology within the discourses on "civilization" and comparative models of human development. Explores the political organization, social structures, cultural practices and technological advancements of complex societies in regions such as the Near East, Africa, Europe, India, China, Mesoamerica and North America. Explores theoretical frameworks, methodological approaches and the interpretation of archaeological and related data to comprehend the nature of these complex societies in various parts of the world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Theories of civilization and socio-political organization of ancient societies, neo-evolutionary models of social complexity, agricultural societies and the rise of states, archaeological evidence of hierarchy, heterarchy, urbanism, and state formation in ancient societies, environmental factors in the rise and fall of complex societies; trade, warfare and cooperation in ancient societies; comparative studies of complex societies, states and empires in various regions of the world; the collapse of ancient states and lessons for modern states. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Cultural Diversity and Ethics. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of the cultural construction of ethical values and how cultural diversity, including beliefs, values and ways of doing business, impacts human technological innovation; focuses on developing a holistic, social-science mindset and application of critical thinking skills.

Conflict Archaeology and Military History. (3-0). Credit 3. Military history; conflict archaeology; human conflict; diplomacy, ethics, and leadership in conflicts; warfare; modern global issues; public service. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with HIST 382.

Ice Age Humans in the Americas. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines archaeological, environmental, geological and genetic evidence related to the timing of human entry into the Americas and megafaunal extinctions at the end of the Pleistocene. Engages students in the most recent findings from archaeological sites across the Americas. In this class students learn to evaluate evidence critically and synthesize the most up to date information on human dispersals in the western hemisphere at the end of the last Ice Age. TOPICS AND THEMES. Chronology and migration routes of early settlement; environmental and landscape change, important archeological sites in North, Central and South America, controversial claims and standards of evidence, theories of forager mobility and landscape learning and current methods accelerating the pace of discoveries. Prerequisite: ANTH 202 or equivalent.

Archaeological Artifact Conservation. (3-3). Credit 4. COURSE OVERVIEW. Provides an in-depth introduction to the theory and practice of conserving archaeological artifacts, emphasizing the stabilization and long-term preservation of materials recovered from terrestrial and underwater sites. Examines both theoretical grounding and extensive hands-on experience in the laboratory, learning to assess artifact condition, select appropriate treatment strategies and apply conservation techniques to a wide range of materials including organics, ceramics, glass and metals. Through lectures, readings and laboratory exercises, students explore the chemical and physical principles underlying conservation, the ethical considerations surrounding intervention and preservation and the role of conservation within archaeological research and curation. TOPICS AND THEMES. Principles of archaeological conservation and preservation; conservation ethics and documentation; health and safety in the conservation laboratory; adhesives and consolidants; conservation of organic materials including bone, ivory, wood, leather, textiles and rope; stabilization of siliceous materials such as ceramics, glass and stone; corrosion processes and treatment of archaeological metals including iron, copper alloys, lead, tin and precious metals; electrolytic and chemical cleaning methods; desalinization and drying processes; material identification and condition assessment; factors of decay in burial environments; field conservation practices; reconstruction techniques and aesthetic reintegration; and integration of conservation data into archaeological interpretation and collections management. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Anthropology of Religion. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Applies fundamental principles of cultural anthropology (the study of human variation and commonalities using a holistic mindset) to the analysis of religion. Examines the relationships connecting religion, culture, society and the individual through cross-cultural, theoretical analysis of religion as a cultural phenomenon. Investigates core questions regarding the existence and persistence of religion, analyzing how religious behavior manifests and connects with other cultural elements across diverse global settings. Develops skills to critically assess research findings, analyze differing viewpoints and perspectives and formulate hypothetical research agendas. Engages potentially charged topics in diverse settings, challenging students to explore their own assumptions and biases regarding their personal worldview. Fosters greater understanding of self-awareness and personal responsibility in society through exploration of the diversity of religious behaviors. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers theoretical approaches to the study of religion; analyzes religious features including symbolism, myth and ritual; studies religious specialists, magic, divination and witchcraft; explores altered states of consciousness; evaluates beliefs regarding gods, spirits, souls, ghosts and death; assesses religious change and searches for new meaning; examines religious violence and fundamentalism; and investigates vernacular religion, secularism, atheism and irreligion. Includes analysis of religious practices, beliefs and institutions from a variety of cultures. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus. Cross-listed with RELS 403.

Applied Archaeology - Methods and Practices. (3-0). Credit 3. Provides practical experience in both terrestrial and maritime archaeological field methods. Emphasizes the applied aspect of archaeology by introducing tools, techniques, software and hardware, and prepares participants to design, implement and lead field projects across diverse environments. Includes engagement with the full spectrum of field operations, from initial planning to data collection and team coordination to final report writing. Explores the foundational principles of applied archaeology, with a particular focus on its role in cultural resource management (CRM). Examines how consultant archaeologists conduct investigations in advance of land development or resource extraction, offering insight into the professional, ethical and regulatory frameworks that guide CRM practice. Students develop technical proficiency, problem-solving and leadership skills. Major themes include project design; terrestrial and underwater surveying and mapping techniques; the use of GPS, compasses and maps; GIS applications and Google Earth; introduction to remote sensing and geophysical tools including side-scan sonar, magnetometers, echo sounders, LiDAR and sub-bottom profilers; terrestrial and underwater excavation methods; stratigraphy, spatial control and in-situ recording; data management and post-excavation analysis; use of software for 2D/3D modeling and hydrostatics; documentation and reporting standards; regulations governing fieldwork; ethical principles and professional standards; current trends and employment opportunities in archaeology; and effective methods for presenting archaeological data. Prerequisites: ANTH 202 or approval of instructor.

Science, Pseudoscience and Critical Thinking in Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examination of extraordinary claims made across a wide spectrum of media in the fields of anthropology, biological anthropology and archaeology. Emphasis on distinguishing science from pseudoscience through application of the scientific method, logical reasoning and critical evaluation of empirical evidence. Writing-intensive assignments develop students’ critical thinking, analytical skills and ability to communicate effectively about complex and sometimes controversial issues in anthropology and in broader scientific inquiry. Attention to recognizing and refuting poor scientific reasoning, evaluation of media portrayal of science and clear dissemination of ideas within and beyond academic contexts. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of science, pseudoscience, pathological science, junk science and anti-science; scientific hoaxes, frauds and exaggeration of evidence; the scientific method and the use and misuse of statistics and illustrations; distortions of anthropological and scientific knowledge across a variety of media platforms, including social media and ‘fake news’; history of the discipline of anthropology; IQ testing, race, and racism; creation science, natural selection, and evolution; cryptozoology, bigfoot and aquatic apes; the use, misuse and abuse of the archaeological record in both scientific and popular discourse; the supernatural realm; and conspiracy theories, climate science and vaccine efficacy. Course discussions may also engage diverse and sometimes unfamiliar perspectives, reflecting a variety of contexts – scientific, professional, political, cultural – in which group communication occurs. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

Anthropological Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the history and foundations of anthropological theory, connecting these historical concepts to contemporary professional concerns. Critiques the core assumptions, preferred questions and specific methods associated with major theoretical schools. Engages diverse points of view to examine current social issues and applied problems, fostering respect for cultural and human biological diversity. Develops comprehensive expertise in articulating theoretical explanations for research questions, identifying the major theorist(s) credited for theory development and detailing how theory is currently used by anthropologists. Practices critical synthesis of theoretical knowledge within existing disciplinary frameworks. Evaluates arguments by questioning the type and sufficiency of evidence presented. Assesses the cultural position, background and historical context of authors conveying messages, including whether the argument is shaped by a particular historical moment or if the author has an agenda. Requires active application of theoretical models against individual student areas of interest. TOPICS AND THEMES. Explores foundational classics; analyzes epistemology, axiology and related conceptual frameworks; considers the Nature/Nurture Debate; investigation of functional thinking, processes, structures and pragmatics; transformation and evolution; symbols and coherence; cultural materialism and economies; and critical advocacy, feminisms, Post Modernism, post-structuralism and the ontological turn. Prerequisite: ANTH 210 or ANTH 205.

Archaeological Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. An advanced undergraduate course reviewing the history of scientific archaeological thought, major theoretical paradigms and current trends in archaeology, provides firm grounding in the development and current application of archaeological theory, a fundamental component of all students’ training in archaeology, no matter their specialty. Covers the major theoretical “movements” in the development of anthropological archaeology, as well as important intellectual developments in other disciplines which have influenced explanation in archaeology (e.g., cultural anthropology, geology, evolutionary biology and other social sciences). Historically oriented, reviews how archaeological theory has evolved in the past century and how contemporary archaeologists use theory to explain variability in the material-culture record of past humans. TOPICS AND THEMES. History of scientific archaeological exploration; major theoretical paradigms and movements in archaeological theory; current trends in archaeology; intellectual developments from other disciplines that influenced archaeological thought. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor.

Geoarchaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. An applied course on the contribution of earth sciences to the interpretation of archaeological contexts, this course consists of field, lab and lecture components. Reviews Quaternary geomorphology. Investigates site formation processes in different depositional environments and impacts on archaeological sites. Provides training in stratigraphic description and interpretation and archaeological dating methods and interpretations. Applies earth science fields and methodologies to archaeological problems. Field trips will be a required component of the course in order to complete field descriptions and sampling. TOPICS AND THEMES. The development of geoarchaeology; sediments and soils and their relevance to archaeological sites; stratigraphy; dating methods and archaeological applications; landscape reconstruction and geoarchaeological interpretations; depositional environments and site formation processes; remote sensing; geophysics. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to geoarchaeology. Prerequisites: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 and approval of instructor.

Anthropological Writing. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Practices critical reading and writing skills through the study and discussion of anthropologically relevant literature. Examines various styles and formats of anthropological writing, treating the discipline as an ongoing conversation and discourse community. Develops writing proficiency necessary for professional participation in anthropology and related career paths, including the interpretation, critique and evaluation of scientific papers. Emphasizes effective peer review and the capacity to accept constructive criticism. Cultivates clear communication strategies for discussing complex anthropological topics with both academic and broader audiences. Organizes written work using careful and critical thought. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers common citation styles, including the appropriate inclusion of primary sources. Analyzes the scientific publication process and Reference Management Software (RMS) usage. Studies professional writing, including personal statements, cover letters, CVs and resumes, prepared as part of an application packet for jobs, internships or graduate school. Explores writing clearly and concisely for diverse audiences, including rewriting scholarly work for non-academic audiences and developing an original research paper on a topic of the student’s choosing. Examines various styles of scientific papers, including research articles, review articles, programmatic essays, ethnographies and popular media. Practices peer review techniques and critical analysis of complex texts. Verbal communication and synthesis of anthropological research in small group settings and an individual oral presentation. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Naval Warfare and Warships in Ancient Greece and Rome. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys topics such as Greek and Roman warships, naval warfare, naval strategy and tactics, drawing upon archaeological evidence, literary documentation and iconographic material. Covers the development of Mediterranean naval power from the Bronze Age (including Ancient Egypt and the mythical Trojan War) to the Imperial Roman Navy. Examines Greek naval dominance during the Persian and Peloponnesian Wars, the evolution of warships such as triremes, Roman naval organization and imperial fleets, and the technological, strategic and political dimensions of naval warfare. Students analyze ship construction, rigging, armament and naval technology within their historical and cultural context. TOPICS AND THEMES. Bronze Age Mediterranean warships; Egyptian naval warfare; Bronze Age naval battles; Athenian Navy; trireme; Greco-Persian Wars (499-449 B.C.); Peloponnesian Wars (431-404 B.C.); naval campaigns of Alexander the Great; Age of Titans; Greek war machines and weapons; Greek naval monuments; Phoenician Navy; Punic Navy; Roman naval organization; Roman Imperial Navy; Roman warships and tactics; Mare Nostrum; Punic Wars (264-146 B.C.); Roman Navy in the Eastern Mediterranean; naval campaigns of Julius Caesar; naval campaigns of Octavian; Roman fluvial warships; Roman naval shipwrecks; Roman war machines and tactics; ship construction; rigging; armament; naval technology; maritime strategy; naval logistics; naval archaeology; iconography; material culture; maritime military history; technological arms race at sea. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with CLAS 417.

Romans, Arabs, and Vikings--Seafaring in the Mediterranean during the early Christian Era. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of seafaring, maritime commerce, naval affairs, and shipbuilding in the Mediterranean from the late Roman Period until the fall of Constantinople in 1453. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Pirates, Privateers and Sea Raiders. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Provides an in-depth survey of the history and archaeology of piracy, privateering and sea raiding from ancient times in the eastern Mediterranean through the Viking Era in the Northern Atlantic and the rise of piracy in the New World and Caribbean during the 16th–18th centuries. Examines archaeological evidence of pirate ventures, the social organization of pirate and privateering communities and the economic, political and cultural effects of piracy on empires, trade networks and maritime law. Explores the sensationalism of pirate legend in literature, film and music, and introduces contemporary piracy in Africa, the Indian Ocean and Southeast Asia. Through lectures, readings, presentations and research assignments, students develop critical skills to evaluate primary and secondary sources, analyze cause-and-effect relationships and assess the broader impact of piracy across time and regions. TOPICS. May include: origins, causes and major periods of piracy, privateering and sea raiding; archaeological evidence of pirate activity in the Mediterranean, Northern Atlantic, Caribbean and Americas; Viking, European and New World piracy; raids, privateering and colonial interactions; social structure, codes of conduct and daily life of pirate communities; economic and political effects of piracy on trade, colonialism, slavery and national sovereignty; sensationalism of pirate legend in literature, film and music; cultural responses to piracy; female pirates and gender dynamics in seafaring communities; contemporary piracy in Africa, the Indian Ocean and Southeast Asia; case studies of shipwrecks, pirate lairs and maritime settlements; research methods and critical evaluation of primary and secondary sources. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

Advanced Museum Studies. (3-0). Credit 3. Advanced exploration of historical, political and cultural forces shaping contemporary museum practices and exhibition design, with emphasis on ethical and professional responsibilities in modern institutions. Focuses on the collaborative and interdisciplinary processes behind exhibition planning and production, with attention to visitor experience, inclusive design and object-based interpretation. Critically engages with contemporary challenges in the museum field, including representation, decolonization, repatriation, activism, censorship and institutional accountability. Highlights the museum’s role in public service, education, knowledge advancement and civic discourse. Includes field trips to campus and local museums, archives and historical or cultural institutions to support experiential learning and engagement with professional practices and careers. Fulfills core requirement for the Museum Studies Minor. Topics and themes may include: Historical and contemporary models of museum programming; research methodologies and scholarly use of collections; educational theory and practice in museum contexts; public outreach and community engagement; ethics of representation, access and inclusion; museums and democratic ideals, civic responsibility and public trust; professional standards and leadership in museum operations; critical evaluation of exhibitions and interpretive strategies; responsive programming tied to current events and emerging issues. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MUST 221, ANTH 221, ARCH 221 or MAST 220; junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with MUST 421.

Bioarchaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. Role of human skeletal studies in reconstructing the biological and cultural past of humans; evidence gleaned from human skeletal remains recovered from archaeological sites such as data regarding diet, health, genetics and migration.  Prerequisites:  ANTH 225; junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

Human Osteology. (2-3). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores human osteological analysis, which provides fundamental skills for fields such as bioarchaeology, paleontology, biomechanics, human anatomy and forensic anthropology. Investigates the concepts and methods anthropologists employ to identify, describe and analyze skeletal remains from archaeological and forensic contexts. Trains students in the proper use of anatomical terminology and the respectful handling of human remains. Intensive hands-on activities develop and apply essential skills in identifying and siding core skeletal elements and teeth. Focuses on how the human skeleton functions, grows and changes throughout the lifespan. Addresses the possibilities and limitations of anthropological skeletal analysis and the ethical concerns inherent in modern osteological study. TOPICS AND THEMES. Studies skeletal and dental biology, including gross and microscopic bone and tooth structure. Analyses effects of ontogeny, development and age on the skeletal system. Estimates parameters such as sex, age, ancestry, stature, anomalies and pathologies of human skeletal remains using standardized anthropological methods. Considers pathological analysis, dietary reconstruction and comparison with faunal remains. Examines cultural, occupational and postmortem modifications, including taphonomy. Reviews methods used in initial assessment, inventory and recovery of remains. Prerequisites: ANTH 225 and ANTH 226, or VIBS 305; junior or senior classification.

Dental Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the methods used to study teeth, a subdiscipline central to biological anthropology (the study of human evolution and variation), bioarchaeology (the study of human remains in archaeological contexts), anatomy, dentistry and palaeontology (the study of fossil life). Explores the essential questions regarding dental analysis: How are teeth studied, and what insights can dental research provide? Gains in-depth experience with the core concepts of dental anatomy, dental development, dental ecology and dental evolution. Develops confidence in identifying teeth in both human and non-human primates and their closest living relatives. Analyzes current literature concerning dental form, function and evolutionary patterns. Cultivates critical thinking abilities necessary for evaluating cutting-edge dental research and effectively presenting and writing about these findings. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers dental anatomy and introduces the tribosphenic molar as a key evolutionary feature. Analyzes the evolution of mammalian mastication and its implications for dietary adaptation. Explores evolutionary developmental biology as it relates to tooth formation and variation. Studies dental eruption patterns, life history traits and dentition patterns in primates. Investigates dental ecology and applies methods for reconstructing ancient diets. Examines dietary reconstruction techniques including macro- and microwear analysis, enamel thickness and dental topography. Reviews the dental-pulp complex, dental pathology and the role of dental form in understanding phylogenetic relationships among human and non-human primates. Prerequisites: ANTH 225 or approval of instructor.

Anthropology of Human Reproduction. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines human courtship, marriage, reproduction, family structure and parenting through the lens of evolutionary ecology. Explores how human reproductive and parenting patterns compare with those of other primates and how they vary across cultures. Evaluates different viewpoints on and approaches to the application of evolutionary logic to the study of these topics. Critically examines hypotheses explaining human behavior through biological, cultural and ecological lenses. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include evolutionary approaches to the study of human behavior, life histories, reproductive strategies, sexual selection, marriage, parental care, infidelity, divorce, as well as explorations of cross-cultural and cross-species variation in these areas. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

Medical Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces medical anthropology, the subfield exploring the biological and cultural dimensions of health, illness and healing across diverse societies. Defines and discusses key concepts, such as health, illness and disease, in relation to various social, environmental, political and evolutionary contexts. Analyzes the interconnections among micro- and macrobiological, cultural, social and political determinants to construct a holistic view of human health. Engages with contemporary and emerging issues in health and healthcare, emphasizing the comparative analysis of global medical systems. Compares and contrasts biomedicine with other ethnomedical systems to evaluate its role within diverse cultural contexts. Develops critical thinking, reading, writing and collaboration skills for engaging with multiple perspectives on health. Note that course content may include complex or sensitive topics designed to foster critical engagement. TOPICS AND THEMES. Surveys foundational theories and methodologies. Analyzes cultural beliefs and environmental influences on health, including ecological and evolutionary disease patterning. Explores health-related behaviors, mental health, medical systems and explanatory models across diverse cultural contexts. Examines environmental health challenges, globalization and infectious disease. Considers gender, race/racism, social inequality and health disparities. Discusses professional applications and emerging issues in the subdiscipline. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Ancient Egypt I - The Rise of Egypt. (3-0). Credit 3. Archaeology and history of ancient Egypt from earliest times to the end of the New Kingdom period. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with RELS 436.

Ethnobotany. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the dynamic relationships between people and plants through the interdisciplinary lens of ethnobotany. Introduces the field by examining how disciplines such as botany, anthropology, ethnopharmacology, ethnoecology and ethnomedicine contribute to understanding plant use across cultures. Engages critically with foundational concepts, including plant adaptations for defense, human strategies for utilizing those adaptations, diverse ways of knowing and the development of knowledge systems that codify plant use. Emphasizes analytical and methodological inquiry into how plant ecosystems and knowledge systems shape human-plant interactions. TOPICS AND THEMES. Studies plant structures, functions and identification using botanical methods; analyzes traditional ecological knowledge and cognitive ethnobotany through ethnographic and comparative approaches; considers ethnopharmacological practices including tinctures, infusions and salves with attention to preparation and efficacy; explores sensory and perceptual ecology using qualitative and observational techniques; examines ethnoecology and conservation strategies through field-based and participatory methods; investigates ethnomedicine, medical models and health conditions using cross-cultural and clinical perspectives; and evaluates ethical issues in research and practice through case studies and applied frameworks. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Ancient Egypt II - Egypt in Decline. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology and history of ancient Egypt from the end of the New Kingdom through the Graeco-Roman period, focusing on the years 1185–30 BCE. Examines the decline of pharaonic power, the rise of foreign influences and the resilience of Egyptian society under Libyan, Nubian, Persian and Ptolemaic rule. Reviews the interplay between political, social and cultural dynamics, exploring Egyptian adaptations to Hellenistic dominance, while tracing continuity and change in art, religion, literature and urban development. Through lectures, readings and analyses of primary and secondary sources, students gain a humanistic understanding of Egyptian civilization during its final dynastic phases and develop skills in interpreting archaeological, textual and iconographic evidence. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues pertaining to ancient Egypt. TOPICS AND THEMES. Decline of pharaonic authority; fragmentation of the Egyptian state; Libyan, Nubian and Persian interventions; internal political strife and social change; resilience of Egyptian cultural identity; Ptolemaic dynasty and Hellenistic influence; Cleopatra VII and the last Ptolemies; Alexandria as a cultural and economic center; Greco-Egyptian art, religion and literature; continuity and transformation of Egyptian traditions; interactions between foreign rulers and Egyptian elites; archaeological and textual methods for reconstructing late Egyptian history; humanistic approaches to interpreting material culture; synthesis of historical, artistic and archaeological evidence. Prerequisites: Completion of ANTH 436 or RELS 436 recommended but not required; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with RELS 438.

Studies in Africa and the African Diaspora. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the history of Africa and its global diasporas through the perspective of archaeology and related fields. Examines prehistoric African cultures, ancient civilizations and pre-Atlantic trade and exchange networks. Explores the nature of the transatlantic trade and the creation of the African Diaspora in the Americas and the Caribbean. Explores the cultural identities of African-descended communities in the Americas and other regions of the world. Applies interdisciplinary research methods that combine historical, archaeological and ethnographic case studies to challenge colonial narratives about Africa and its diasporas. Uses hands-on work with material culture and related evidence to highlight archaeology’s role in understanding the histories and cultures of Africa and its diasporas. TOPICS AND THEMES. African prehistory and civilizations, West Africa before Europe, Africa and its global diasporas, Atlantic Africa and the creation of the African diaspora, African cultural resilience, adaptation, and hybridity in the African diaspora, landscapes of power and resistance, material culture, memory, heritage and social justice. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

Lithic Artifact Analysis. (2-3). Credit 3. Laboratory-based course reviewing methods archaeologists use to analyze stone tools and debitage, including identification of tool-stone sources, reconstruction of technology, explanation of assemblage variability, and microscopic use-wear analysis. Prerequisite: ANTH 202 and approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

Quantitative Methods in Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Presents practical training in statistics applicable to anthropological and archaeological data. Provides anthropology students with the sophisticated statistical skills needed for an increasingly quantitative field. Discusses reasons why anthropological and archaeological data does not always meet the criteria set by many formal statistical models. Teaches the methods to analyze the chronological, geographic, morphometric, demographic, phylogenetic, genetic, linguistic, network/interaction and observational datasets (among others) that pose unique challenges for both analysis and interpretation. Conducts scientific statistical analyses of these datasets. Applies statistical concepts and techniques to real and hypothetical anthropological or archaeological problems during weekly lab sections. TOPICS AND THEMES. Quantitative analytical methods employed by anthropologists; includes statistical analyses, statistical software and sampling theory commonly used in anthropological research. Graphical techniques and statistics specific to anthropological datasets and research questions, including exploratory data analysis (e.g. principal components, canonical variates, factor analysis), and other multivariate methods (e.g. MANOVA). This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; STAT 302 or STAT 303.

The Archaeology and Anthropology of Foraging Societies. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the archaeology and anthropology of foraging (hunting and gathering) societies in time and space. Includes an overview of archaeology focused on foraging societies and current methodological and theoretical issues, especially the use of ethnographic and environmental data. Investigates ecologically oriented case studies of late Pleistocene and Holocene hunter-gatherers paired with the ethnographic record used to interpret these sites. Archaeological case studies will have an emphasis on land-use, site-structure and site formation analyses. Ethnographic case studies will focus on the diversity of hunting and gathering societies, change in these societies through time and discussion of forager economies, with specific attention to critiquing ethnohistoric accounts and the applicability of these case studies to the archaeological record. TOPICS AND THEMES. Forager (hunter-gatherer) variation in different environments; forager variation through time; forager social structures; forager mobility; forager subsistence; socio-political complexity in foraging societies; ethnographic critiques; archaeology of foraging societies; resource management; foragers in the modern world and change in forager societies in the recent past; archaeological site structure; lithic analysis; site formation processes; archaeological site survey; archaeological theory of foragers; site modeling and resource modeling. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisites: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 and approval of instructor.

Quantitative Ethnographic Methods. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces quantitative ethnographic field methods commonly used in anthropological research to formally test hypotheses. Explores the benefits and challenges of applying structured, quantitative techniques to the study of complex cultural phenomena within a field largely dominated by qualitative methods. Covers best practices for managing and analyzing anthropological datasets. Surveys common ethnographic methods designed to enhance comparability and analytical rigor of ethnographic research, including structured interviews, text analysis and network analysis. Through hands-on assignments, provides practical experience in developing and executing small-scale research projects. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include ethical considerations in field research, research design, data management, statistical analysis, structured interviews, online survey tools, standardized observation, network analysis, text analysis and cultural consensus analysis. Also includes student participation in all stages of the research process, including research design, data collection, data management and analysis, and write-up. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Environmental Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the paleoecological context in which past humans interacted with the natural environment encompassing plants, animals and landscape. Introduces students to theories and methods relevant to studying past human-environment interactions. Outlines types of environmental data that survive in the archaeological record (geological, botanical, faunal, chemical), recovery and analytical methods, absolute chronology and inferences made based on these data. Develops long-term, global perspective on human-environment interactions provided by the fields of archaeology and earth science. TOPICS AND THEMES. The use of archaeological sites as paleoenvironmental archives, human impacts on ancient environments, Quaternary extinctions, long-term landscape evolution, plant and animal domestication, the Anthropocene and cultural collapse and resilience. Prerequisites: ANTH 202, ANTH 204 or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

Method and Theory in the Peopling of the Americas. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Reviews current evidence from the fields of archaeology, genetics, biological anthropology and paleoecology for the dispersal of modern humans to the New World during the Pleistocene. Examines terminal Pleistocene cultures in Asia and the earliest sites in the Americas. Discusses various models proposed for this migration. Critically examines major archaeological sites and cultures. Stresses an interdisciplinary approach. Applies theory and method used to explain prehistoric human migration and colonization of empty lands. TOPICS AND THEMES. Pleistocene Americas; ancient DNA; paleoenvironments; radiocarbon dating; archaeological modeling; lithic analysis; ethnographic analogy; zooarchaeology and extinctions; archaeological site formation processes; critical analysis of fragmentary data; statistical analysis. This course will incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to the peopling of the Americas. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisites: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 and approval of instructor.

Cultural Heritage and Resource Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Evaluation of modern ideas about how and why archaeological, architectural, ethnographic, and natural resources should be preserved and presented to current and future societies; critical examination of the theories, methods, regulations, and ethics that guide efforts to preserve and protect cultural heritage within a context of past endeavors and future directions. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Ancient Biomolecules. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how biomolecules — DNA, proteins, lipids and metabolites — persist in plant and animal remains, artifacts and sediments for thousands to millions of years, preserving key insights into long-term ecological and human history. Determines how these molecules are preserved, identified and analyzed within archaeological contexts to address interdisciplinary questions about evolution, migration, diet, disease, culture, tool production, health and environmental change. Interpretation of biomolecular evidence will draw from archaeological, historical and scientific sources to reconstruct past lifeways within their own cultural and environmental settings. Develops the ability through lectures, discussions and data analysis to assess the suitability for different biomolecular methods for addressing specific research questions and critically evaluate current scientific literature in the field. Skills learned are directly applicable to making informed, evidence-based decisions, empowering students to navigate information-rich environments with discernment and confidence. Prior knowledge in either biology/biochemistry or archaeology is required, but not both. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analysis of the hereditary biomolecules DNA, proteins, lipids and metabolites; large-scale ‘omics’ approaches, including genomics, metagenomics, proteomics, metaproteomics, lipiomics and metabolomics used to investigate complex systems; instrumentation including PCR, Sanger sequencing, whole genome sequencing (NGS and WGS), chromatography and mass spectrometry; specialized applications such as environmental DNA, microbiomes and dental calculus genetics and proteomics; biomolecule preservation and degradation; ways biomolecular techniques are adapted for archaeological considerations; integration with other lines of archaeological, textual, historic and scientific evidence. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to archaeological biomolecules. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANTH 202 or BIOL 111, or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

Anthropology of Body Image. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Evaluates core psychological, medical, evolutionary and anthropological theories of body image, eating disorders, fat and cosmetic surgery. Surveys and critiques theories of body image from the lens of medical anthropology and global mental health. Develops expertise in articulating the major theoretical questions, strengths and limitations of different frameworks, particularly in relation to cross-cultural variation. Critically analyzes global case studies of body image-related illnesses. Applies anthropological theories to identifying biases in the body image literature and public health consequences. Formulates anthropological solutions to conversations and concerns in the body image literature surrounding emerging trends, cross-cultural value- and knowledge-systems, and the challenges of treatment. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analysis of anthropological theories of the body; critique of current theories of body image and eating disorders; assessment of psychological and anthropological approaches to fat talk; critique and synthesis of biomedical and social justice approaches to weight and weight stigma; evaluation of limitations of eating disorders research from a cross-cultural perspective; formulation of anthropological solutions to emerging discussions in body image among men, racial minorities and sexual minorities; evaluating the cross-cultural motivations and ethics of cosmetic surgery; critiquing current treatments for eating disorders and obesity from an anthropological lens. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

Anthropology Internship. Credit 0 to 3. Provides students with the opportunity to gain practical experience in a variety of settings, including local, state or federal agencies; museums; non-profit organizations; non-governmental organizations; private firms. May be taken four times for credit. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Directed Studies. Credit 0 to 9. For individual research in anthropology on subjects not included in established courses. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Junior or senior clasification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.
Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of anthropology. May be repeated for credit.

Research. Credit 0 to 3. Research conducted under the direction of a faculty member in Anthropology. May be taken four times for credit. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.

Biological Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. Survey of the field of biological anthropology covering the principles of evolution, human evolution, human adaptation, human variation, primate diversity and evolution, osteology and bioarchaeology.
Archaeological Methods and Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. Development of archaeology as a discipline; methods and theories used in archaeology for reconstructing cultural history and cultural process.

Seafaring Life and Maritime Communities.  (3-0). Credit 3. Employs primary and scholarly sources to examine the social organization, work routines, living conditions, and material culture of mariners between 1450 and 1950; broader trends in maritime communities and global seafaring are also investigated. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
Cultural Method and Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. Survey of the theoretical concepts used in anthropology and how to construct models used in cultural and social anthropology.

Conservation of Archaeological Resources I. (2-2). Credit 3. Fundamentals and applications of artifact conservation techniques in archaeology. Prerequisite: Knowledge of basic chemistry and physics recommended.
Conservation of Archaeological Resources II. (2-2). Credit 3. Comprehensive study of techniques used in the identification and conservation of metal and wooden artifacts. Prerequisite: ANTH 605.
Historical Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. Past and present theoretical positions and research strategies in historical archaeology. Prerequisites: ANTH 313 recommended.

Skills in Maritime Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. Themes and tools of maritime archaeology;  topics include remote sensing and mapping as wells as interpreting, recording and storing data used in maritime archaeological surveys. Prerequisites: Graduate classification; approval of instructor.

Outfitting and Sailing the Wooden Ship 1400-1900. (3-0). Credit 3. Archaeological and historical sources to exam the outfitting and sailing of wooden ships between 1400 and 1900, a period popularly known as the "Age of Sail"; emphasis on two aspects that are of particular interest to the nautical archaeologist. Prerequisites: Approval of instructor; graduate classification.

Nautical Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to the history and theoretical basis of nautical archeology as a discipline; fundamental concepts in nautical science relevant to the history of seafaring; key developments in the history of seafaring. Prerequisites: Approval of instructor and graduate classification.

Preclassical Seafaring. (3-0). Credit 3. Seafarers and watercraft of the ancient Near East and Mediterranean until ca. 700 B.C. Types of watercraft used, routes, cargoes, voyages of exploration and economics of maritime trade.

Classical Seafaring. (3-0). Credit 3. Culture history of Mediterranean seafarers between ca. 700 B.C. and end of Byzantine Empire; types of ships and boats, sea law, naval tactics, harbor-works, routes, cargoes and economics of trade.

History of Shipbuilding Technology. (3-0). Credit 3. Design and construction of preserved and excavated sailing ships, the expertise of their builders and technology involved in ancient and early shipbuilding. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Research and Reconstruction of Ships. (2-2). Credit 3. Techniques of recording and interpreting excavated ships; preservation of hulls; ship drafting, modeling, lofting, testing and other methods used in the research and/or reconstruction of ships. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Conservation III--Preservation of Organic Materials. (3-0). Credit 3. Advanced and experimental methods of organic artifact conservation; emphasis on composite artifacts, gamma radiation polymerization, scanning electron microscope evaluation of artifacts and preservation of traditionally difficult to conserve artifacts. Prerequisite: ANTH 605.

Medieval Seafaring in the Mediterranean. (3-0). Credit 3. Cultural history of seafaring in the Mediterranean region during medieval times; ship types and their uses, naval warfare, sea law, harborworks, routes and cargoes, and maritime economic institutions and practices. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Geoarchaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. An applied course on the contribution of earth sciences to the interpretation of archaeological contexts, this course consists of field, lab and lecture components. Reviews Quaternary geomorphology. Investigates site formation processes in different depositional environments and impacts on archaeological sites. Provides training in stratigraphic description and interpretation and archaeological dating methods and interpretations. Applies earth science fields and methodologies to archaeological problems. Field trips will be a required component of the course in order to complete field descriptions and sampling. TOPICS AND THEMES. The development of geoarchaeology; sediments and soils and their relevance to archaeological sites; stratigraphy; dating methods and archaeological applications; landscape reconstruction and geoarchaeological interpretations; depositional environments and site formation processes; remote sensing; geophysics. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to geoarchaeology. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Zooarchaeology. (3-3). Credit 4. Analysis of animal bones from archaeological sites; inference of how prehistoric peoples hunted, domesticated and used animals. Prerequisite: Basic knowledge of zoology and archaeology.

New World Seafaring. (3-0). Credit 3. Cultural history of seafaring in the Western Hemisphere from the fifteenth century to the present; ship types and their uses; harborworks, commerce, naval warfare, sailing routes, maritime practices. Prerequisites: ANTH 615 and ANTH 616 or approval of instructor.

Anthropology of Human Reproduction. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines human courtship, marriage, reproduction, family structure and parenting through the lens of evolutionary ecology. Explores how human reproductive and parenting patterns compare with those of other primates and how they vary across cultures. Evaluates different viewpoints on and approaches to the application of evolutionary logic to the study of these topics. Critically examines hypotheses explaining human behavior through biological, cultural and ecological lenses. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include evolutionary approaches to the study of human behavior, life histories, reproductive strategies, sexual selection, marriage, parental care, infidelity, divorce, as well as explorations of cross-cultural and cross-species variation in these areas. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Primate Behavioral Ecology. (3-0). Credit 3. Survey the behavioral ecology of the nonhuman primates exploring topics such as their hunting behavior; sexual coercion; language capabilities; culture; tool use; homosexuality; dominance; parental care, ethics of field study and their conservation. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Palynology. (3-3). Credit 4. Principles and techniques used in palynology, pollen morphology, ontogeny, biochemistry, dispersion and preservation; role of palynology as a research tool in plant taxonomy agriculture, medicine, paleobotany and anthropology.

Anthropological Ethics and Professionalism. (3-0). Credit 3. Codes of professional ethics applicable to excavation and preservation of archaeological sites; ethnographic fieldwork and professional relationships with colleagues and informants; professional protocols for publication and presentation of research results. Prerequisites: Graduate classification in anthropology and approval of instructor.
Research Design in Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. Research design used by anthropologists to develop sampling strategies, test hypotheses and compile quantitative data. Prerequisite: ANTH 602.

Lithic Artifact Analysis. (2-3). Credit 3. Laboratory-based course reviewing methods archaeologists use to analyze stone tools and debitage, including identification of tool-stone sources, reconstruction of technology, explanation of assemblage variability, and microscopic use-wear analysis. Prerequisite: Graduate classification and approval of instructor.
Ethnographic Field Methods. (3-0). Credit 3. Methods common to anthropology for the field collection of data on cultural behavior. Prerequisites: Graduate classification and approval of instructor.

First American Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. Survey of past frontiers in First American studies important to the peopling of the Americas: review of the archaeology, geology, and dating of early sites in North, Middle, and South America; human migration hypotheses; biological evidence; and late Quaternary environmental factors. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Ancient Foodways and Cooking Technology. (3-0). Credit 3. Study of ancient foodways and cooking technologies, particularly fire-based methods, especially in the context of human evolution, subsistence and settlement behavior, social organization, theoretical underpinnings, and archaeological manifestations thereof, with the focus on ancient hunter-gatherer populations, wild plants, terrestrial animals, and aquatic resources. Prerequisite: ANTH 602 or ANTH 604 or approval of Instructor.

Quantitative Ethnographic Methods. (3-0). Credit 3. Quantitative data collection and analytical methods employed by anthropologists including standardized observation, structured interviews, demography and network analysis; emphasizes hands-on assignments involving data collection among local community. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Field Archaeology.  Credit 1 to 12 each semester. Field instruction in the methods of archaeological excavations; recovery and cataloging of cultural, floral and faunal remains; and interpretation of these data. Locations of the field course will vary according to site. Field trips required. May be taken more than once but not to exceed 8 hours of credit toward an MA degree and not to exceed 12 hours of credit toward a PhD degree. Prerequisite: ANTH 602 or equivalent.

Analytical Methods in Archaeology and Conservation. (3-0). Credit 3. Conventional and advanced techniques used for artifact material analysis and artifact documentation; material analysis is the way that we study artifacts, both in structure and elemental composition; includes photography and artifact sketching, computer modeling, laser digitization, computer image photogrammetry, 3D printing and XRF elemental analysis.  Prerequisite: Graduate classification in anthropology or approval of instructor.

Medical Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces medical anthropology, the subfield exploring the biological and cultural dimensions of health, illness and healing across diverse societies. Defines and discusses key concepts, such as health, illness and disease, in relation to various social, environmental, political and evolutionary contexts. Analyzes the interconnections among micro- and macrobiological, cultural, social and political determinants to construct a holistic view of human health. Engages with contemporary and emerging issues in health and healthcare, emphasizing the comparative analysis of global medical systems. Compares and contrasts biomedicine with other ethnomedical systems to evaluate its role within diverse cultural contexts. Develops critical thinking, reading, writing and collaboration skills for engaging with multiple perspectives on health. Note that course content may include complex or sensitive topics designed to foster critical engagement. TOPICS AND THEMES. Surveys foundational theories and methodologies. Analyzes cultural beliefs and environmental influences on health, including ecological and evolutionary disease patterning. Explores health-related behaviors, mental health, medical systems and explanatory models across diverse cultural contexts. Examines environmental health challenges, globalization and infectious disease. Considers gender, race/racism, social inequality and health disparities. Discusses professional applications and emerging issues in the subdiscipline. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Teaching Anthropology. Credit 0. Introduction to course planning for future instructors of anthropology; includes course design, student motivation and engagement, assessment of design and implementation and technology use in education. Prerequisites: Graduate classification; admission to graduate program in the Department of Anthropology.

Seminar. Credit 0 to 1. Orientation to graduate degree requirements in the Anthropology Department at Texas A&M; systematic introduction to the department's faculty and bridging themes of their research. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Professional Internship. Credit 1 to 9. Opportunity to put anthropology learned in the classroom into practice; may be used to gain practical experience in a variety of settings including: local, state or federal agencies; museums; non-profit organizations; non-governmental organizations; and private firms. Prerequisites: ANTH 601, ANTH 602, and ANTH 604; approval of committee chair.
Directed Studies.  Credit 1 to 12 each semester. Directed individual study of selected problems in anthropology. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 12. Selected topics in an identified area of anthropology. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
Research.  Credit 1 or more. Research for thesis. Prerequisite: Approval of graduate advisor.
(ARAB 1411) Beginning Arabic I. (4-0). Credit 4. Introduction to Modern Standard Arabic in its written and spoken forms; emphasis on conversation, rudimentary vocabulary, simple grammar, and reading.

(ARAB 1412) Beginning Arabic II. (4-0). Credit 4. Introduction of more complex grammatical constructions; vocabulary building; emphasis on putting acquired vocabulary and grammar to conversational use. Prerequisite: ARAB 101 or equivalent.

COURSE_NARRATIVE: (ARAB 2312) Intermediate Arabic II. (3-0). Credit 3. Emphasis on comprehending printed material, perfecting pronunciation, and attending to more complex grammar; discussion of topics holding general and professional interest; knowledge of Arab culture and history. Prerequisite: ARAB 201 or equivalent.

Introduction to Modern Arab Culture. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of cultural, linguistic, religious, and ethnic diversity in the Arab world; investigation of the impact of tradition and modernity on modern Arab culture; relating diverse cultural practices and products to diverse perspectives in the Arab world; taught in English.

Introduction to Arabic Language and Society. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of critical linguistic issues in the Arab world from a sociolinguistic perspective, including language and religion; language and power; language and nationalism; and language and education. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

COURSE_NARRATIVE: Global Middle Eastern Cultures. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of the contemporary and historical cultures of the Middle East region; investigation of intercultural connections between the Middle East and the rest of the globe; emphasis on cultural traditions, religious communities, societal change, social movements, migration, and diaspora.

Directed Studies.  Credit 1 to 4. Individual supervision of readings or assigned projects in an Asian Language, selected for each student individually; written or oral reports. Prerequisite: Approval of Arabic and Asian Language Office Director.
Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of Arabic studies. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Reading and Composition. (3-0). Credit 3. Advanced Arabic grammar and readings of average difficulty and of different genres, including literary and journalistic texts and other culturally-enriched materials in order to develop awareness of cultural products, perspectives, and practices found in the Arab world. Prerequisites: ARAB 202 or ARAB 204, or equivalent; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Reading and Composition II. (3-0). Credit 3. Readings of average difficulty and of different genres, including literary and journalistic texts and other culturally-enriched materials; development of writing skills with emphasis on grammatical constructions; expansion of vocabulary and oral expression. Prerequisites: ARAB 301; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Business Arabic. (3-0). Credit 3. Business and financial terminologies useful in the Arab World; cultural etiquette for effective communication in Arabic business settings; oral and written business reports from a variety of authentic sources; language skills and communication strategies for traveling, shopping and conducting financial transactions in the Arab World. Prerequisites: ARAB 202 or ARAB 204, or equivalent; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Media Arabic. (3-0). Credit 3. Analysis of current events in the Arab World; use of print and electronic materials in Arabic from variety of media sources; discussion of different points of view in media representation/coverage; issues pertaining to business, politics, culture and entertainment in the Arab World. Prerequisites: ARAB 202 or ARAB 204, or equivalent; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Directed Studies.  Credit 1 to 4. Individual supervision of readings or assigned projects selected for each student individually; written or oral reports. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor and Director of AALO.
Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of Arabic studies. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Research. Credit 1 to 4. Research in Arabic studies conducted under the direction of faculty member approved by the Director of AALO. May be taken 2 times for credit. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.

Design and Visual Communications Foundations I. (2-10). Credit 5. Architectural design principles; development of skills in perception, thought and craft as they apply to the formation of two- and three-dimensional relationships; introduction to and practice of tools, methods, techniques available for graphic communication; graphic communication and the design process; observation and other forms of free-hand drawing and drawing systems that develop representational and descriptive capabilities. Prerequisites: BS in Architecture major.

Design and Visual Communication Foundations II. (2-10). Credit 5. Approaches to problem identification and problem solving emphasizing human, physical and cultural factors influencing architectural design; understanding of space, materiality and tectonics in a human body scale; development of drawing methods with emphasis on analytical drawing; reinforcement of visual and verbal communication as applied to design processes. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ARCH 105; major in BS in Architecture.

Visual Communication Foundations I. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to and practice of tools, methods, techniques available for graphic communication; graphic communication and the design process; observation and other forms of free-hand drawing and drawing systems that develop representational and descriptive capabilities.

Architecture Design I. (2-10). Credit 5. Issues and methods in designing environments for human habitation and well-being; projects addressing site, functional planning, spatial ordering, form generation through a recognition of the synthesis of space, structure, use and context; reinforcement of appropriate graphic and model building techniques. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ARCH 105 and ARCH 106.

Architecture Design II. (2-10). Credit 5. Fundamental issues of innovative design processes and creation explored through the creative use of past, present and future materials, tools, and technologies; with an emphasis upon the research of materials, methods, scale, craft and technique as instruments of design, fabrication, and production. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ARCH 205.

COURSE_NARRATIVE: Social and Behavioral Factors in Design. (3-0). Credit 3. Social and behavioral factors in the built and natural environment; environmental perception and spatial cognition; social-environmental processes such as privacy and crowding; setting-oriented discussion on residences, education, and the workplace; the psychology of nature and natural resource management; social design and social science contribution to architectural design.

Sustainable Architecture. (3-0). Credit 3. A comprehensive introduction to sustainability concepts, techniques and applications at all levels of the built environment, history of contemporary development of sustainable architecture from 1960 to the present; design strategies, environmental technologies and social factors for reducing building energy needs and carbon foot prints; global applications of sustainable approaches.

Computational Methods in Architecture. (2-2). Credit 3. Software and processes for computation design in architecture; image editing and creation, vector drawing, 3D modeling, parametric modeling, rendering techniques and simulation.

Foundations of Museum Studies. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. An introduction to the interdisciplinary field of museum studies, exploring how museums collect, preserve, interpret and exhibit material culture to convey cultural, historical and scientific knowledge. Emphasizes museums as dynamic institutions shaped by ethical, educational and civic responsibilities and fosters critical inquiry into questions such as: Who do museums serve? How do objects acquire meaning? What responsibilities do museums have to communities and history? Provides a foundation for further study in museum work while developing skills in civic engagement, applied learning, collaboration, inclusion and leadership. Engages museums as spaces for dialogue and lifelong learning, encouraging reflection on how they shape public understanding and express broader social values. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in museum studies. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include: history and development of museums; collecting practices from antiquity to the present; analysis of museum organization, leadership structures and varying types of institutions; consideration of professional standards, collections stewardship; evaluation of interpretation, educational programming and strategies for access and inclusion; ethical, educational and civic responsibilities of museums. Cross-listed with ANTH 221 and MUST 221.

Foundations of Historic Preservation. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration and evaluation of the cross-disciplinary work of historic preservation; emphasis on the significance of historic places to societal well-being and conservation alternatives for historic and cultural environments; review of preservation projects and treatments; guest presentations and case studies from practicing professionals and researchers in a variety of fields.
(ARCH 1301) Survey of World Architecture History I. (3-0). Credit 3. A survey of world architecture and the human-designed and built environment from prehistory to the 13th century.
