Welcoming seminar to the college of engineering to assist with transition to college; includes introduction to engineering majors, college and university resources; topics evolve as students advance through the engineering curriculum. Prerequisite: Must be enrolled in the College of Engineering; also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses.

Tools for Engineering Analysis. (2-2). Credit 3. Introduction to prominent categories of engineering quantitative analysis; pattern finding in data; optimization; prediction of future states; modeling of physical systems; laboratory exercises to use computational tools as means of implementing mathematical concepts. Prerequisites: CLEN 101; MATH 131, MATH 142, MATH 147, MATH 151, or MATH 171.

The Engineering Profession. (1-0). Credit 1. Introduction to interdisciplinary aspects of engineering careers; work engineers perform in their field; engineering practice within realistic constraints, e.g., economic, environmental, ethical, health and safety, and sustainability; engineering design process; effective communication in engineering settings. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisite: Enrollment in the college of engineering.
Special Topics In... Credit 0 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of engineering.
Special Topics in... Credit 1 to 4.  Selected topics in an identified area of engineering. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

STVSUBJ_DESC: CLVM - College of Vet Med & Bi

COURSE_NARRATIVE: (SPCH 1311) Introduction to Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces the field of communication as a broad and interdisciplinary area of study. Surveys major topics, research traditions and contexts of communicative practice across interpersonal, organizational, public and/or mediated settings. Examines verbal and nonverbal communication, media and technology, intercultural and health communication, strategic and religious communication, and leadership and conflict management. Considers how communication is studied from both humanities and social science perspectives, with attention to culture, ethics and methods of inquiry. Provides a foundation for understanding communication as both theory and practice in everyday life, civic engagement and/or professional contexts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds awareness of how communication functions across personal, academic, professional and/or civic settings. Develops foundational skills in analyzing, adapting and applying communication strategies to wide-ranging contexts. Enhances the ability to critically interpret messages in a world shaped by media convergence, cultural difference and/or global interconnectedness. Prepares for advanced coursework in communication and media fields, while also strengthening transferable skills valued across professions. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday assumptions about communication differ from scholarly perspectives developed in the field. Expands understanding of communication as both a practical skill and an area of research shaped by theory, culture and/or ethics. Examines ways of knowing that include humanistic, social scientific and/or critical approaches. Highlights how communication influences relationships, organizations and/or society, deepening appreciation for the complexity of interaction and meaning making. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include verbal and nonverbal communication; media and technology; intercultural communication; health communication; strategic communication; religious communication; leadership and conflict management; and/or academic research and methods of inquiry. Attention to contemporary issues and applications of communication theory may introduce perspectives that are unfamiliar and/or challenging, reflecting the broad relevance of communication to personal, professional and civic life.

(SPCH 1315) Public Speaking. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores principles, practice and criticism of public speaking. Emphasizes public speaking as more than performance, examining key skills, including audience analysis, research, organization, use of supporting materials and delivery techniques. Attention to ethical communication and sensitivity to diverse audiences across professional, political, religious, cultural and ideological contexts. Includes practice in informative, persuasive and group speaking, developing verbal and nonverbal communication strategies. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with skills essential for professional, academic and civic life. Builds competence in organizing ideas, supporting arguments, adapting them to varied audiences. Develops confidence in extemporaneous speaking, critical listening and communication across diverse contexts. Prepares students for leadership roles, workplace communication and active participation in public dialogue. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ideas about public speaking, such as viewing it only as performance or memorization, differ from research-based and practical perspectives. Develops understanding of speaking as a process involving invention, organization, style, delivery and audience adaptation, enhancing skills in extemporaneous speaking. Emphasizes that effective speaking requires ethical choices, critical thinking and sensitivity to diverse audiences as much as confidence in delivery. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of why public speaking matters in contemporary society; study of ethical principles in communication; development of confidence and listening skills; analysis of audiences and rhetorical situations; research and organization of supporting materials; crafting of effective introductions, bodies and conclusions; use of language and presentation aids; practice in informative, persuasive and ceremonial speaking; application of digital rhetoric and multimedia tools. Course speeches and examples may address diverse and sometimes controversial topics, reflecting perspectives represented in public life as well as subjects chosen by students; breadth of content emerges from student interests and experiences, and guidance from the instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

Public Speaking for Digital Platforms. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces principles, practice and criticism of public speaking adapted for online audiences and platforms. Emphasizes public speaking as more than performance, examining key skills, including audience analysis, research, organization, use of supporting materials and delivery techniques. Attention to ethical communication and sensitivity to diverse audiences across professional, political, religious, cultural and/or ideological contexts. Includes practice in informative, persuasive and ceremonial speaking, developing competence in composition, digital presentation and multimedia editing. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with skills essential for professional, academic and civic life. Builds competence in organizing ideas, supporting arguments, adapting them to varied online audiences. Develops confidence in digital delivery, critical listening and communication across diverse platforms. Prepares students for leadership roles, workplace communication and/or active participation in public dialogue through online media. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ideas about public speaking, such as viewing it only as performance or memorization, differ from research-based and practical perspectives. Develops understanding of speaking as a process involving invention, organization, style, delivery and audience adaptation across both in-person and digital contexts. Emphasizes that effective speaking requires ethical choices, critical thinking and sensitivity to diverse audiences, as well as confidence in both live and recorded delivery. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of why public speaking matters in digital society; study of ethical principles in communication; development of confidence and listening skills; analysis of digital audiences and rhetorical situations; research and organization of supporting materials; crafting of effective introductions, bodies and conclusions; use of language and presentation aids; practice in informative, persuasive and/or ceremonial speaking; training in composition, delivery, recording and editing of speeches for digital distribution; application of digital rhetoric and multimedia tools across video conferencing, online platforms and social media. Course speeches and examples may address diverse and sometimes controversial topics, reflecting perspectives represented in public life as well as subjects chosen by students; breadth of content emerges from student interests and experiences, and guidance from the instructor.

Communication for Technical Professions. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces principles, practice and criticism of public speaking adapted for technical fields. Focus on rhetorical invention and delivery for engineers, scientists and other technical professionals who must present complex information to general audiences, policymakers and interdisciplinary teams. Emphasizes public speaking as more than performance, examining key skills including audience analysis, research, organization, use of supporting materials and delivery techniques. Special attention to clarity, analogy and visualization as tools for translating technical knowledge. Includes practice in informative, persuasive and group speaking while integrating visual and graphic materials into their presentations. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with communication skills essential for technical professions. Builds competence in simplifying complex information, supporting arguments with evidence and adapting content for non-experts. Develops confidence in delivering technical presentations in professional, academic and civic settings. Prepares students for roles requiring leadership, interdisciplinary collaboration and the ability to explain technical processes to decision-makers and the public. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ways of describing technical work may not be effective outside specialized fields. Develops understanding of ways technical communication techniques—such as analogy, narrative and visualization—shape audience comprehension and trust. Emphasizes that effective technical communication requires ethical choices, critical thinking and sensitivity to diverse audiences as much as subject matter expertise. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of why communication matters in technical professions; study of ethical principles in technical communication; development of confidence and listening skills; analysis of general and specialized audiences; research and organization of technical content; crafting of effective introductions, bodies and conclusions; use of analogies, language and presentation aids to explain complex information; practice in informative, persuasive and group speaking; integration of visual and graphic materials into technical presentations. Course speeches and examples may address diverse and sometimes controversial topics, reflecting perspectives represented in public life as well as subjects chosen by students; breadth of content emerges from student interests and experiences, and guidance from the instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

(SPCH 2333) Group Communication and Discussion. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores principles, practice and research on small group communication. Focuses on definition, structure and functions of groups, including roles, norms, power and/or communication climate. Examines processes such as problem-solving, role-playing, decision-making, leadership, organization and/or conflict management. Attention to verbal and nonverbal codes, listening, relationships and/or cooperation as foundations for interaction and group productivity. Considers professional, political, religious, community and/or cultural contexts in which group communication occurs. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops both understanding and practical ability for effective participation and leadership in group settings with diverse participants across professional, academic and/or civic contexts. Builds competence in problem solving, decision-making and conflict management within teams. Strengthens ability to manage power dynamics, foster positive communication climates and/or adapt to cultural differences in group interaction. Enhances capacity for collaboration, organizational effectiveness and leadership in contexts where teamwork and collective decision-making are essential. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ideas about group work differ from research-based perspectives. Develops understanding of the ways roles, norms, leadership and/or power can shape group interaction. Emphasizes that effective group communication requires cooperation, critical thinking and constructive conflict management to improve decision-making and outcomes. Explores how divergent or unfamiliar perspectives and backgrounds shape group interaction, offering insight into effective collaboration in diverse teams. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of group definition, structure and functions; study of roles, norms and power in group dynamics; analysis of communication climate and culture; approaches to problem solving and decision-making; strategies for leadership, organization and conflict management; examination of verbal and nonverbal codes and listening skills; techniques for fostering cooperation and productivity in groups. Course discussions may also engage with diverse and sometimes unfamiliar perspectives, reflecting the variety of professional, political, religious, community and/or cultural contexts in which group communication occurs.

Interviewing - Principles and Practice. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of interviewing as a purposeful form of interpersonal communication. Focus on questioning strategies, listening and interaction between the interviewer and interviewee. Examines informative, persuasive, survey and/or employment interview contexts. Develops skills as both the interviewer and the interviewee. Emphasizes how structure, audience, goals and setting shape communication choices. Addresses the logical and psychological bases of interviewing. Class applications may involve exposure to perspectives and experiences across social, cultural and professional backgrounds. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds transferable skills essential to journalism, media, public communication and organizational practice. Involves questioning, listening, adaptation to audience and purpose and interaction across varied goals. Applies to situations that require navigating unfamiliar or sensitive territory with professionalism. Develops skill in effectively navigating differences in belief, identity, experience and disagreement within interview contexts. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how interviews function as purposeful conversations, showing how credibility, preparation and strategy shape outcomes. Encourages awareness of the interview as a structured exchange rather than spontaneous talk. Broadens understanding of how perspective and authority influence communication across roles and settings for both interviewer and interviewee. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of questioning techniques, listening practices, rapport-building, credibility assessment and ethical responsibility; examination of informative, persuasive, survey, research and/or employment interviews; consideration of how audience, purpose and context govern interview structure and performance. Course work may involve engagement with people from varied backgrounds and experiences. Interview practice may include topics connected to identity, culture, ethics, work and/or participants’ personal lives. Exposure to differing viewpoints and/or lived realities reflects the range of issues encountered in professional and public communication. May include resume writing skills in preparation for career interviews. Cross-listed with JOUR 215.

Communication Technology Skills. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines principles and practices of communication technology in the digital domain. Surveys the history and standards of television, radio, video gaming, streaming media, e-publishing and/or social networking industries and markets. Focuses on production skills such as composing, recording and editing digital content, as well as media literacy across platforms, including the ability to evaluate social, cultural and/or ethical implications of communication technologies. Emphasizes media-centric strategic foresight to postulate regarding the future of the communication and technological landscape. Class applications may also draw on popular culture and/or current events, connecting course concepts to contemporary media environments. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds technical competence and media literacy skills applicable across professional, academic and civic contexts. Develops the skills necessary to create digital media content, adapt communication strategies to emerging technologies, tell stories across multiple media platforms and evaluate the impact of communication technologies on audiences and industries. Strengthens preparation for careers in journalism, media production, marketing, communication design, public relations and related fields where technological fluency and critical analysis are essential. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Builds understanding of how communication technologies shape interaction, identity and/or culture beyond their technical functions. Highlights how tools such as streaming platforms, social media and/or virtual environments influence professional practice, everyday communication and public dialogue. Clarifies both opportunities and challenges presented by digital media, including questions of access, ethics and/or social impact. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of the development and application of communication technologies across industries; exploration of audio, video, web and interactive media tools; analysis of digital platforms and markets; consideration of issues such as media convergence, intellectual property, ethics and sociocultural impact. Course work may incorporate case studies from popular culture and/or current events to connect course concepts with real-world practices. The course may include discourses and perspectives that are unfamiliar or controversial, reflecting the diversity of discourses relating to digital technologies and practices. Prerequisites: Enrollment in communication or telecommunication media studies majors, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor. Cross-listed with JOUR 230.

Rhetorical Criticism. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces principles and practices for analyzing speeches and other forms of public discourse. Deploys rhetorical analysis to explain how symbols, images, language, performances and/or narratives shape meaning. Considers how communicative acts function in cultural, political, religious, institutional and/or historical contexts. Includes exposure to discourses and theories across a wide spectrum of political, cultural and/or ideological differences. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Demonstrates how public discourse shapes civic life. Provides tools for interpreting speeches, media and other forms of public discourse across various contexts. Builds skills in analysis, research and writing that transfer to fields including law, politics, media, public relations and education. Shows how studying rhetorical strategies can uncover arguments and explain how communication impacts civic decision-making, public controversy and cultural understanding. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Expands the understanding of rhetoric to be beyond speechmaking to include other forms of public discourse such as popular media, advertisements and digital content. Introduces frameworks scholars use to study how communication may be shaped by context, culture, ideology and/or power. Emphasizes understanding and evaluating these perspectives, building awareness of the range of approaches scholars bring to the study of public discourse. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include scholarly traditions of rhetorical analysis, including feminist, narrative, ideological, dramatistic and/or classical criticism. Material may draw from political speeches, media messages, entertainment media and social movements. Because rhetorical criticism examines communication across many areas of public life, the course may include discourses and perspectives that are unfamiliar or controversial, reflecting the diversity of ideas present in society.

(SPCH 2335) Argumentation and Debate. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores principles of argumentation and skills of debate, with emphasis on reasoning, evidence, refutation and briefing. Examines how arguments are constructed, supported, challenged, revised and delivered. Considers the standards of sound reasoning, common fallacies and tests of evidence and credibility. Attention to ethical and cultural considerations in arguments, including analysis of audiences and contexts. Explores the role of debate in decision-making. Includes exposure to debate topics across political, religious, ideological and/or cultural spectrums, reflecting the diversity of arguments found in society. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops skills in critical thinking, research and communication essential for professional, academic and/or civic life. Builds competence in evaluating arguments, analyzing evidence and presenting claims effectively to diverse audiences. Strengthens oral and written study of advocacy, responsive listening and adaptability in structured debate and informal discussion. Skills gained are directly relevant to law, politics, business, media, public policy and other areas where persuasive communication and sound reasoning are central. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday argument practices differ from structured approaches developed in debate and communication studies. Expands understanding of argument as more than personal opinion, showing how reasoning, evidence and ethical standards shape persuasion. Explores frameworks for evaluating arguments across different contexts, including individual decision-making, group deliberation, political campaigns and/or public debates. Highlights how cultural values and ideological perspectives influence the ways arguments are constructed and received. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include foundations of argument and debate; analysis of debate propositions; evaluation of evidence and proof; construction of affirmative and negative cases; cross-examination and refutation; ethical and cultural considerations in argument; listening and evaluation; debate as a form of public speaking; formats in academic, political and public debates. Course materials and debate topics may address diverse and sometimes controversial issues, reflecting the range of perspectives present in public discourse.

Difficult Dialogues on Power, Privilege and Difference. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the practice of difficult dialogues and the communication skills needed to engage productively across differences. Focus on active listening, perspective-taking, deliberation, collaborative decision making, teamwork and/or additional processes of collective problem solving. Examines how dialogic processes can be designed and organized to minimize destructive consequences of bias, prejudice, discrimination, power disparities and/or unexamined privilege across dimensions of difference, such as gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, social class, ability, nationality and/or religion. Considers the role of facilitation techniques in creating conditions for constructive conversations on complex and often polarizing issues. Includes exposure to perspectives that may be unfamiliar or challenging, reflecting the diversity of voices in contemporary public life. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops skills for navigating conversations on sensitive and complex issues in professional, academic, civic and personal contexts. Builds competence in listening across differences, managing conflict and fostering collaborative and intentional decision making. Strengthens the ability to engage constructively in contexts marked by diversity, disagreement or polarization. Skills gained apply to leadership, teamwork, organizational communication, relationships and community engagement across families, workplaces and/or public settings. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how different models of interaction, such as debate, dialogue, negotiation and/or everyday conversation, frame the goals and norms of communication, allowing for comparison, application or critique. Expands understanding of how communication shapes perceptions of power, privilege and/or difference in personal, organizational and/or civic contexts. Introduces frameworks for recognizing how bias, equity and/or cultural perspectives can influence interaction. Emphasizes awareness of diverse viewpoints, the productive value of disagreement and the role of constructive exchange in building community. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of dialogue as a communication practice distinct from debate or analysis of persuasion; exploration of active listening, perspective-taking and deliberation; skills in conflict management, collaborative decision making and team problem solving; consideration of communication in the context of bias, prejudice, discrimination, power, equity and/or privilege. Attention to how dialogue functions across interpersonal, organizational and civic settings. Course materials and discussions may address sensitive or controversial issues, reflecting a wide range of political, cultural and/or religious perspectives present in society.

Podcasting and Audio Storytelling. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores basic audio storytelling techniques required for podcast production within journalism and digital content creation, including principles of podcast development, scripting, interviewing, voice performance, audio recording and editing. May include instructions in microphone selection, sound environments and use of editing software. Covers branding elements such as titles, descriptions, cover art, music and metadata. Introduces strategies for publishing, promotion and audience growth across distribution platforms. Course content may include legal and ethical considerations related to privacy, attribution, licensing or defamation. Course content may reference real-world events or personal narratives for purposes of analysis and production rather than endorsement. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops production skills applicable to careers in journalism, strategic communication and digital content creation. Promotes skills in narrative design, research organization, technical proficiency and navigating teamwork in creative industry contexts. Supports academic preparation in media writing, audio reporting and multimedia storytelling. Enhances civic communication skills by training attention to voice, perspective and accountability in public messaging. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights differences between casual conversation and structured audio storytelling designed for listeners’ attention. Clarifies how tone, pacing, editing and sound design influence interpretation and credibility. Encourages recognition of ethical responsibility when representing others’ voices or lived experiences in recorded form. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of podcast formats and genres; interview preparation and questioning techniques; narrative scripting; ambient sound and music beds; recording equipment and vocal delivery; editing workflows and mixing practices; platform distribution and analytics; audience design and engagement. Course material may draw on real-world audio examples involving sensitive or emotional content, used for purposes of critical listening and professional development. Cross-listed with JOUR 248.

New Media and the Independent Voice. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the role of new and independent media in shaping cultural, political and social life. Surveys forms such as blogs, podcasts, video, digital storytelling and social media platforms. Considers how independent voices create, challenge and reshape narratives in communities and public discourse. Attention to the relationship between personal voice, creativity and professional practice, as well as to issues of credibility, trust, ethics and representation. Explores how traditional and independent media engage with topics including activism, identity, politics and/or popular culture, highlighting both opportunities and challenges for communication in digital environments as they are constantly evolving. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds media literacy and production skills relevant to journalism, communication, marketing and/or creative industries. Develops competence in analyzing the credibility, reach and influence of independent media. Strengthens preparation for roles requiring digital fluency, critical thinking and the ability to adapt messages across platforms. Provides tools for both professional communication and civic engagement in a media environment shaped by independent voices. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how independent media can be both a space of empowerment and a site of contestation. Highlights how digital platforms amplify personal, cultural and political voices, while also raising ethical and practical challenges. Highlights how identity, power and representation shape media production and reception. Develops understanding of the opportunities and limits of independent communication in contemporary society. Explores the opportunities and challenges presented by changes in the media landscape. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of blogs, podcasts, video and social media platforms; exploration of digital storytelling and creative expression; consideration of ethics, representation and credibility in independent media; analysis of activism, politics and identity as expressed through digital platforms; evaluation of how independent voices influence communities, industries and public life. Course applications may draw on popular culture, current events and emerging issues. Discussions may also engage with controversial or contested topics, reflecting the role of independent media in addressing subjects that shape public dialogue. Cross-listed with JOUR 250.

Media Literacy in the Digital Age. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores mass media as a form of communication across cultural, political and creative contexts. Examines how news media, podcasts, social media, video, television and advertising are used to inform, persuade, critique and/or tell stories. Analyzes source, audience, message design and the relationship between medium and purpose. Examines how information, misinformation and disinformation spreads, developing skills and techniques for assessing credibility and verifying sources. Includes engagement with real-world issues and diverse perspectives may arise through topics connected to politics, culture, ethics and/or lived experience. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices relevant to careers in media industries, strategic communication, journalism, political communication, public outreach, community outreach and digital content production. Involves skills relevant to designing messages, engaging audiences and producing or analyzing digital media across professional platforms. Prepares for advanced academic study in communication, media studies, journalism and related fields where digital fluency and critical media analysis are expected. Promotes awareness of how traditional media and independent media practices can contribute to civic discourse, cultural participation and emerging communication markets. Encourages media literacy in both communication careers and everyday life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how new media platforms differ from legacy communication systems in structure, purpose and power. Highlights the role of individual voice, audience interaction and platform design in shaping meaning and influence. Encourages recognition that public communication through digital media may challenge assumptions about authority, expertise and representation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis or creation of blogs, podcasts, social media campaigns, digital storytelling or multimedia commentary; exploration of how mass media engage politics, identity, culture and public issues; study of persuasion, narrative, audience engagement and message strategy in digital contexts. Assignments may involve analysis, production or both, depending on the instructor’s approach. Course materials may involve perspectives or content reflecting varied experiences, beliefs and interpretations encountered in contemporary media environments. Cross-listed with JOUR 255.

Introduction to Video Game Studies. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to the interdisciplinary study of video games as a cultural, technological, and artistic medium; key concepts in game studies including game mechanics, history, player engagement, narrative, and the social and cultural impact of video games; critical analysis, readings, and gameplay exploring the significance of video games in contemporary society. Cross-listed with FILM 256 and VIST 256.

Communication, Religion and the Arts. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of art and religion as forms of communication, with attention to how visual and artistic expression conveys meaning across cultures and traditions. Surveys artistic and media practices in religious and secular contexts, considering how aesthetics mediate religious experience and shape public understanding. Examines the role of art in supporting, questioning and/or challenging religious and social perspectives. Focus on interpretation and critique and dialogue of artifacts across diverse traditions, including attention to issues of pluralism, inequality, power, class and/or representation. Includes engagement with perspectives that may be unfamiliar or challenging, reflecting the diversity of voices in contemporary public life. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competence in interpreting and discussing art and religion across diverse cultural and historical contexts. Builds skills for engaging respectfully with differences in belief, practice and/or worldview. Strengthens intercultural awareness, critical thinking and creative communication skills, which can be applied to dialogue across divisions in civic, professional and interpersonal settings. Enhances understanding of how art and media shape public awareness of religion and contributes to broader conversations about meaning, identity and social conflict. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how the study of art and religion in communication differs from devotional or confessional approaches. Expands understanding of religion as a cultural and communicative practice shaped by history, power and interpretation. Highlights how art functions not only to express belief but also to question, challenge or reframe religious ideas. Introduces perspectives that encourage critical analysis of how religion and art intersect with broader cultural, social and/or political contexts. Emphasizes reflection on pluralism and contested meanings, deepening awareness of how religion and art shape, and are shaped by, the wider human experience. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication, art and religion as interrelated cultural practices; exploration of how visual and artistic forms convey meaning within Christianity, Buddhism, Islam, secular humanism and other traditions; consideration of iconoclasm, pluralism and the role of art in shaping or challenging belief and practices; attention to aesthetics, power, inequality and representation in religious and secular contexts. Course materials may also engage with the profane or the obscene when relevant to understanding how religion, art and communication define, resist and/or reframe cultural boundaries. Content may include perspectives that are unfamiliar, contested or controversial, reflecting the diversity of ways art and religion intersect in public life. Cross-listed with RELS 257.

Introduction to Communication and Sports. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how sports are communicated across media formats and within both interpersonal and intergroup contexts. Examines the production and circulation of sport communication through television, print, online platforms, podcasts, blogging and/or social media. Considers how teams, athletes, organizations and fans communicate within and about sport. Includes attention to how sports communication reflects and shapes cultural narratives involving community, gender, race, politics and/or national identity. Course material may draw on real-world events and perspectives that reflect diverse experiences within or about sport. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Supports workforce preparation by engaging practices central to sports media, journalism, broadcasting, public relations, digital content, interpersonal and organizational communication. Emphasizes applied skills such as writing, presenting, interviewing, photography, storytelling, analysis and audience engagement. Connects course work to professional settings in athletics, media industries, marketing, sports administration, journalism and strategic communication. Reinforces academic preparation for continued study in media, communication, sport culture or public discourse by linking applied practice to theoretical and analytical approaches within the discipline. Strengthens civic understanding by highlighting how communication in sports influences public dialogue, institutional decision-making and community identity. May include exploration of potential career pathways across the sports communication landscape. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how sports communication goes beyond entertainment or fandom to include cultural meaning, identity and/or power. Highlights the role of media and messaging in interpersonal, group and organizational dynamics that shape public perception of athletes, teams and sporting events. Considers how communication in sport settings can influence public dialogue around such contemporary issues as health and injury, gender, race, nationalism, economics and social belonging. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of sports media platforms; study of sportscasting, reporting and commentary; writing about sporting events; communication within teams and organizations; player–coach interaction; family communication about sport; fandom and fan culture; identity, gender, race and nationalism in sport; crisis and reputation management; sport as community and industry. Course content may address contemporary issues or public events that reflect differing perspectives or cultural debates connected to sport.

Voices of Democracy - United States. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines U.S. public discourse as a force in shaping citizenship and democratic life. Analyzes speeches, art, writing, popular media and/or digital communication representing different historical periods and perspectives. Examines how public arguments address questions of belonging, rights, governance and national purpose. Highlights voices from both dominant and marginalized groups, tracing the evolution and contestation of American and democratic ideals. Engages material that may involve differing interpretations, ideological conflict or historically situated controversy. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Connects historical and contemporary public communication to civic participation, political communication, social advocacy and/or leadership. Involves analysis relevant to media, law, public policy, education and public affairs. Supports academic preparation in rhetoric, communication, history, political science and related fields. Can highlight how public discourse informs public understanding, institutional change and national debate. Compares different historical periods and the rhetorical methods used to fight for democracy in each of these areas. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how democracy in America was originally established, is constructed, contested and reinterpreted through public communication over time. Highlights differences between popular, historical and scholarly understandings of rhetoric, citizenship and/or dissent. Encourages examination of competing claims to authority, rights and/or values in democratic discourse. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of foundational American speeches and writings in historical context; analysis of abolitionist, suffrage, civil rights, environmental, labor and other social movement’s rhetoric; examination of war, foreign policy and national myth making; exploration of presidential address, religious persuasion, judicial argument and grassroots organizing. Course content may involve speeches and perspectives that differ sharply in ideology, tone and/or historical impact, reflecting the diversity and conflict inherent in American public discourse.

Introduction to Social Media. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores social media as a communication environment shaped by technology, audience, participation and platform design. Surveys major platforms, concepts and theories used to understand how individuals, organizations and communities create, share and interpret digital content. Examines how social media intersects with journalism, marketing, activism, entertainment and/or everyday communication. Considers how digital communication practices reflect and influence public discourse, society and culture. Engagement with real-world examples may involve topics connected to politics, religion, identity, ethics and/or lived experiences. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices connected to media industries, strategic messaging, journalism, advertising, nonprofit work, politics and other forms of public communication. Involves skills relevant to content creation, audience analysis, audience engagement, platform analysis and communication strategy. Connects to professional and academic paths in media, communication, journalism, marketing, public affairs and digital culture. Supports academic preparation to analyze ways social media shapes institutional messaging, cultural participation, community formation and civic dialogue. Develops applied skill in using social media strategically within entrepreneurial, organizational or community campaign contexts. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how communication via social media platforms differs from legacy media in participation, access and influence. Explores communication theories and strategies underpinning social media communication. Highlights tensions involving credibility, persuasion, privacy, visibility and/or identity in digital environments. Builds understanding of how platforms shape perception, behavior and communication norms in ways that are not always immediately visible. Supports informed assessment of one’s own media usage patterns and communication practices as case material for analysis. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication theories, platform histories and digital ecosystems; analysis of messaging strategies and audience behavior; consideration of digital identity, participation and online communities; exploration of ethics, credibility, privacy, representation and influence in online environments; examination of how platforms shape visibility, participation and public discourse; study of consent, branding, advocacy, journalism and influencer practices; comparison of interactive and traditional media. Course materials may reflect varied perspectives and examples from professional, cross-cultural and/or global contexts. Cross-listed with JOUR 275.

Careers in Communication and Journalism. (1-0). Credit 1. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores fields and pathways in journalism, media and communication-related professions. Considers how professional interests, strengths and personality align with opportunities in media, public communication, journalism, strategic communication, digital platforms and related industries. Addresses foundational practices in networking, resume-writing, application material preparation, informational interviewing and digital presence. Includes exposure to campus resources and career planning tools. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds awareness of workforce expectations and industry pathways across communication-related professions. Introduces practical strategies for pursuing careers in media, advocacy, corporate communication, public affairs or related sectors. Assists in translation of classroom knowledge in securing internships, applied experience and long-term professional development opportunities. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how communication careers vary in purpose, setting and expectation. Highlights differences between common assumptions about media or communication work and the range of roles that exist across industries. Builds awareness of how skills, identity, professionalism and context shape access to and participation in communication fields. Provides support to students transferring into CMJR, promoting academic success and facilitating engagement with campus resources and communities. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include identification of career interests and strengths; exploration of communication professions and industries; development of application materials; digital portfolios and networking strategies; informational interviewing; engagement with professional resources and advising. Course activities may reference academic planning, campus involvement, workplace preparation and/or communications-specific career development. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Cross-listed with JOUR 280.

Directed Studies. Credit 1 to 3. Individual supervision of readings or assigned projects in communication. May be taken two times for credit. Prerequisites: Approval of instructor and department head.
Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of communication. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Research.  Credit 0 to 3. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in the department of communication. May be repeated 3 times for credit. Prerequisites: GPA 2.5 or higher; freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor and department head.

Rhetorical Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces major traditions of rhetorical theory from antiquity to the present, examining how thinkers have defined persuasion, argument and public influence across changing political and cultural contexts. Considers contributions from figures across historical and contemporary contexts and how they theorize the role of rhetoric to shape civic life, challenge authority and/or construct knowledge. Focuses on how rhetorical theories and practices emerge in moments of conflict, uncertainty and social change. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Provides grounding in the foundations of rhetorical theory, building academic preparation for advanced study in rhetoric, political communication, law, public affairs and media criticism. Builds familiarity with frameworks widely used in speechwriting, advocacy, leadership communication and public reasoning. Supports professional and civic participation by clarifying how arguments gain legitimacy, how authority is constructed and how persuasive strategies function across traditions and institutions. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how rhetoric is more than just “style” or manipulation by revealing its role in philosophy, religion, science and governance. Reveals how foundational ideas such as reason, justice, virtue and truth were articulated through rhetorical means. Highlights how rhetorical theory reflects its time and audience, prompting reflection on how present-day communication inherits past assumptions about credibility, character and civic participation. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics may include the study of classical Greek and Roman rhetoric, including persuasion, ethos and civic speech; consideration of Enlightenment and revolutionary rhetoric in the formation of democratic publics; examination of modern/contemporary rhetorical theories; exploration of rhetoric as epistemology — how discourse shapes truth, identity and/or power. Course material may include texts addressing religion, gender, sexuality, class, race, nationality and/or ideology, reflecting the diverse contexts of how rhetorical traditions have been developed and contested. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

The Mass Media and Politics. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how communication practices construct, circulate and contest political ideas and authority. Examines both how media influence political attitudes, participation and policy outcomes, and how political identity and conflict are shaped symbolically through news, entertainment, digital platforms and public rhetoric. Approaches may draw from social scientific models of media effects or rhetorical and critical analysis of political discourse. Emphasizes case-based evaluation of messages, sources and strategies across institutional, journalistic and citizen communication. Course content may include material involving political disagreement, conflict or graphic representation, examined for purposes of analysis rather than endorsement. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops literacy in how political messages are constructed, distributed and interpreted across media systems. Applies to careers in journalism, political communication, public affairs, advocacy, research, law and civic or governmental work. Supports informed participation in democratic life by strengthening abilities to evaluate claims, recognize framing and distinguish between reporting, persuasion and manipulation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how politics is communicated not only through speeches or news outlets, but also through satire, visuals, entertainment formats, algorithmic feeds and policy messaging. Demonstrates how political messaging often blends information, symbolism and emotion to shape interpretation. Highlights the ways messages are interpreted differently depending on audience history, identity and media environment. Clarifies how communication shapes what counts as “fact,” “controversy” or “consensus” in public life. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of political news coverage, campaign strategy, advertising, agenda-setting, framing, propaganda models, political entertainment, social media activism and theories of representation. Consideration of media regulation, government communication practices, the influence of media on policymaking and the production of ideology. Course material may draw on historical and contemporary cases from local, national or international contexts, including disputed elections and outcomes, political controversies and crises, disinformation and surveillance, and contested social movements.  Prerequisites: POLS 206 or approval of department head; junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with JOUR 302 and POLS 302.

Communication and Data Visualization. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores data as a form of communication and examines how information is interpreted, visualized and presented for different audiences and purposes. Emphasizes data storytelling as both an analytical and narrative practice, focusing on how visual choices shape understanding. Considers visualization designs that use data to inform, explain, persuade and/or support decision-making, using tools such as Excel and R. Addresses principles of visual perception, evidence-based messaging and interpretation of qualitative data and quantitative analyses, including descriptive and inferential statistics. Considers how visual choices, context and audience shape meaning in visual communication. Coursework may involve analysis, critique and/or development of data-driven messages in digital or visual formats. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds data visualization skills relevant to journalism, strategic messaging, marketing, public affairs, organizational communication, media production, research presentation and political advocacy. Builds capacity to interpret data, build visual explanations and representations and present insights in accessible formats. Supports effectiveness in academic and professional contexts where evidence, visualization and communication intersect. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how data gain meaning through interpretation, framing and visual design. Highlights the difference between raw information and communicative impact. Encourages attention to credibility, context and the persuasive or explanatory use of visualized evidence. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and critique of data visualizations; analysis of how charts, maps, dashboards, infographics or interactive visuals communicate meaning; consideration of audience adaptation, ethics, representation or narrative framing; exploration of digital storytelling strategies in data communication, including how sequencing, emphasis and interactivity guide interpretation; consideration of persuasive and informative uses of data in media, public communication, organizational settings or digital platforms. Course content may involve real-world issues or case studies that reflect diverse perspectives or public debate. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with JOUR 305.

Digital Communication Analytics and Metrics. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of digital communication, data and the use of analytics to generate insight, evaluate communication strategies and inform decision-making. Examines techniques for extracting and interpreting information from websites, social media platforms and/or digital campaigns. Examines how data are used to assess audience behavior, platform performance, search engine optimization, message reach, engagement and/or return on investment. Considers how digital tactics connect across marketing, digital media platforms and communication research. Draws attention to the role of data in strategic planning. Course concepts are illustrated with examples that may involve digital communication in organizational, commercial, journalistic, political and/or nonprofit contexts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Promotes workforce preparation for careers in strategic communication, public relations, advertising, journalism, marketing, audience research and digital media. Advances understanding and skills related to interpreting performance metrics, applying measurement models and using analytics to support campaigns, outreach, reporting and/or organizational decision-making. Supports academic and professional work in areas where communication effectiveness, audience insight and data-informed planning intersect. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies the role of analytics in shaping communication strategy, storytelling and/or organizational decision-making. Highlights the difference between data collection and meaningful interpretation. Builds recognition of how digital communication practices intersect with privacy expectations, ethical obligations and the constraints of data tracking and measurement. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of web traffic, audience demographics and user behavior; study of paid, earned and owned media metrics; consideration of measurement models, platform dashboards and optimization tactics; exploration of data-driven decision-making, campaign evaluation, content performance, randomized field experiment and competitive research. Course examples may involve sectors such as journalism, marketing, nonprofit advocacy, strategic communication and/or politics, reflecting the varied uses of digital analytics in public communication. Prerequisites: Grade of B or better in COMM 275, COMM 323, or JOUR 200; junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with JOUR 306.

Theories of Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores major theoretical approaches to human communication, focusing on how communication theory explains language and symbol use, rhetoric, interpersonal interaction, small group and organizational dynamics, persuasion and/or media/technological influence. Examines humanistic, social scientific and/or critical theoretical traditions in communication studies. Explores ways theories of communication help to explain what communication is, how it functions and why it matters in different settings. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in communication and related fields. Provides a foundation for understanding how theories inform research, professional communication strategies, media practices and organizational decision-making. Develops transferable skills in analytical reasoning, interpretation of communication processes and application of abstract concepts to real-world situations. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how theoretical perspectives may differ from everyday assumptions about communication. Demonstrates how concepts such as persuasion, meaning-making and media influence can be examined through different theoretical frameworks, offering distinct insights and applications. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of interpersonal communication theories; analysis of language and symbol use; examination of group and organizational interaction; consideration of persuasion and influence; exploration of media and technology’s role in communication; comparison of interpretive and scientific approaches to theory. Course content may reference diverse cultural, social and/or institutional contexts to illustrate how communication theories operate in practice. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

Communication Law and Policy. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the legal and ethical foundations of communication in journalism, media and public life. Considers First Amendment principles, constitutional protections and limits on free speech and free press. Surveys key areas of communication law, including libel, privacy, copyright, obscenity, advertising, broadcast regulation and/or digital communication. Considers ethical standards and professional responsibilities that shape communication practices across diverse contexts. Directs attention to the tensions between individual expression, institutional regulation and public accountability. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competence in understanding how legal frameworks and ethical codes guide communication decisions in professional, academic and/or civic life. Builds skills for identifying risks, evaluating responsibilities and applying standards to journalism, media and/or organizational settings. Provides preparation for careers requiring knowledge of communication law, professional ethics and public accountability. Strengthens civic awareness by highlighting the role of free expression in democracy and public debate. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday assumptions about “free speech” and “freedom of the press” differ from their legal and professional realities. Encourages awareness of the limits, protections and obligations that accompany communication rights. Expands understanding of how legal rules intersect with ethical reasoning, professional standards and social expectations. Promotes careful reflection on how controversies over speech, press and media practice reveal broader tensions in democratic societies. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of First Amendment foundations and constitutional principles; libel, privacy and copyright; obscenity, advertising and broadcast regulation; law and policy for digital and social media; ethical theories and professional codes; accountability, fairness, diversity and harm in communication practice. Course discussion may involve contemporary cases and controversial issues, addressed for purposes of legal and ethical analysis within an environment of respectful dialogue. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor; COMM-307 also taught at Galveston campus. Cross-listed with JOUR 301.

Research Methods in Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores major approaches to studying communication through empirical methods, with an emphasis on hands-on learning and research-by-doing. Focuses on how researchers formulate questions, select appropriate methods and collect and analyze data. Examines quantitative and qualitative approaches to studying messages, media, audiences and social interaction. Builds foundations in the application of specific research methods commonly used in the communication discipline such as surveys, experiments, content analysis, in-depth interviews, focus groups and rhetorical analysis. Incorporates consideration of research design, sampling, measurement, ethics, basic data analysis and interpretation across communication contexts. Emphasizes how different methods generate different types of insight and evidence. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Connects directly to fields that rely on evidence-based communication research, including media studies, public relations, organizational communication, health communication, audience analytics and strategic messaging. Involves practices used in academic research, market research, program evaluation and professional data analysis. Builds competencies valued in communication industries and graduate study, including research literacy, analytical reasoning, data interpretation and methodological decision-making. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how research in communication differs from everyday opinion, anecdote and assumptions. Considers how different research methods generate different kinds of evidence and how those differences shape interpretation and conclusion. Encourages reflection on the limits, possibilities and ethics of studying communication in human and mediated contexts. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of research questions and hypotheses; analysis of quantitative methods such as surveys, experiments or content analysis; consideration of qualitative and interpretive approaches such as interviews, focus groups or ethnography; exploration of sampling, measurement, validity, reliability, data collection and interpretation. Applications may draw from interpersonal, organizational, media, digital, political and/or critical/cultural communication contexts. Prerequisites: 6 hours of MATH 140, MATH 142, MATH 151, MATH 152, PHIL 240 or STAT 201.

Research Method Projects. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Focuses on the application of empirical research methods through the design and completion of a communication research project. Emphasizes experimental and survey-based approaches, with integration of qualitative components as appropriate to research design. Addresses each stage of the research process, including topic selection, research questions, hypothesis development, data collection, statistical analysis, interpretation and presentation of findings. Builds on concepts introduced in COMM 308 by moving from principles to practice in conducting communication research. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Connects research activity to fields such as communication science, health communication, media research, organizational studies and strategic messaging. Involves skills relevant to project-based inquiry, data collection, measurement strategy, statistical interpretation, evidence-based reporting and research presentation. Aligns with professional and academic settings where data-driven analysis, program evaluation and applied research inform communication decisions. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how knowledge is produced through systematic inquiry rather than assumption or anecdote. Reinforces literacy in the scientific method, including reliability, validity, interpretation of evidence and limits of generalization. Clarifies how empirical findings contribute to understanding communication behavior and outcomes. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include research design and project planning; formulation of research questions and hypotheses; development of measures and instruments; data collection through experimentation, survey methods or mixed approaches; statistical testing; interpretation of results; identification of limitations; written and oral presentation of findings. Course projects may address interpersonal, organizational, media, digital, health or political communication contexts. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in COMM 308; STAT 201 or 303; junior or senior classification.

Communication Intervention. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of communication interventions designed to create change at individual, interpersonal, organizational and/or community levels. Examines theories and models used to influence behavior, participation and decision-making in such contexts as voting, purchasing, membership, health campaigns and training. Focus on how communication strategies are designed, implemented and assessed using social science-based approaches. Addresses message design, needs assessment, change models, persuasion processes and evaluation of outcomes. Course work may involve application of theories to real and/or hypothetical cases. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops intervention skills relevant to professional practice in organizational communication, health communication, training and development, leadership, consulting, public relations, marketing and civic or community initiatives. Involves skills tied to planning campaigns, designing persuasive messaging, conducting needs assessments and evaluating effectiveness of communication-based interventions. Aligns with academic and applied fields that use communication to facilitate change within individuals, institutions, communities and public life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how communication functions not only as information delivery but as a strategic tool for intervention and influence. Highlights the role theory can play explaining how and why change occurs. Explores the complex factors to consider in designing effective communication interventions, as well as the need to ground strategies in research-based models rather than assumptions. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of intervention theories and models; analysis of change strategies across individual, group, organizational and community contexts; consideration of message design, persuasion and implementation; exploration of needs assessment, behavior change frameworks, action research, dialogic approaches, training design and evaluation models. Examples may draw from campaigns, organizations, communities, public initiatives and/or social or institutional problem-solving. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Interpersonal Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines key concepts and theories for understanding how people create, maintain and sometimes challenge relationships through communication. Considers person-to-person and online interaction, including perception, attraction, self-disclosure, listening and/or conflict management. Explores communication across interpersonal differences such as professional and social roles, class, age, ability, gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, nationality and religion. Examines practices for analyzing interpersonal communication through research and theory. Course materials may include consideration of diverse perspectives and examples of communication as both productive and destructive, in face-to-face and online contexts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds skills for effective interaction in personal, professional and civic settings. Develops tools for effective listening, conflict management and resolution and adapting to others from diverse backgrounds and perspectives. Supports understanding of how interpersonal communication influences health, well-being and quality of life. Builds academic preparation for advanced study and workforce preparation for careers requiring teamwork, leadership and strong relational and collaborative competence. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ideas about relationships and communication may differ from research-based perspectives. Considers ways that listening involves more than paying attention, that conflict can strengthen as well as weaken relationships and reasons disclosure and trust do not always follow predictable stages. Builds recognition of how identity, culture and context shape meaningful interactions, showing ways communication approaches that seem natural in one setting may be interpreted differently or counter-productively in another. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of perception, attraction, self-disclosure, listening and conflict management; study of interaction patterns and stages in relationship development; analysis of communication across interpersonal dimensions such as gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, social class, ability, nationality and religion; consideration of productive and destructive aspects of communication; application of interpersonal theory to face-to-face and online contexts, including social media. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Media Psychology. (3-0). Credit 3. An introduction to the field of media psychology and its impact on human behavior, emotions and thoughts. Topics focus on mass media and social media and how they are related to individual and societal functioning across a range of important psychological topics (e.g., personality, self-image, sexual behavior, mental health, violence). Prerequisites: PBSI 107. Cross-listed with PBSI 316.

Social Media Law. (3-0). Credit 3. Laws and regulations applied to social media, including communication law applied to enduring issues in the social media context; legal problems unique to social media; free speech, commercial speech and employment law as they affect individual users of social media as well as groups and organizations promoting points of view or products via social media, and employers.   Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with JOUR 317.

Organizational Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the study of communication within organizational contexts, with attention to how messages, relationships and structures constitute organizations and shape organizational life. Surveys foundational theories and contemporary perspectives on how communication influences organizing, including attention to practices associated with collective identity-building, leadership, decision-making, culture, power, technology use and/or change. Examines how communication enables coordination across teams and influences how people experience belonging, authority or conflict in organizational life. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds workforce preparation for professional contexts where collaboration, leadership and organizational activities depend on communication across roles, departments and demographic or cultural differences. Promotes effective practices relevant to management, consulting, training, human resources, organizational development, corporate and nonprofit communication. Strengthens communication foundations in coordination, adaptation and problem-solving that are relevant to effectiveness in civic, professional and community organizations. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Investigates how organizational structures are created, changed and sustained through communication. Considers ways assumptions about authority, participation or efficiency may be complicated through theoretical and analytical study. Encourages recognition of communication as both a tool and a site of influence, constraint and negotiation in organizational settings. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication systems and networks; analysis of organizational cultures and practices of socialization; consideration of power, leadership and decision-making; exploration of conflict, collaboration and change; examination of technology, identity and structure in organizational life; attention to communication challenges that emerge in diverse or multi-level organizations. Examples or case discussions may draw from corporate, governmental, nonprofit, academic and/or community contexts. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Strategic Communication Case Studies. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines strategic communication through the study of how organizations plan, design and implement communication campaigns. Examines how communication strategies are developed to align stakeholder needs with organizational goals within public environments. Considers planning models, message design, effective tactics, channel selection, evaluation, budgeting and collaboration with community or client partners. Emphasizes analysis, problem-solving and adaptation of communication practices across professional, nonprofit and/or civic contexts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Connects strategic communication to professional contexts, such as public relations, integrated marketing communication, nonprofit campaigns and initiatives, branding, media production and/or organizational communication. Develops skills and foundations relevant to situation, organization, and stakeholder analysis, campaign planning, message development, collaboration with stakeholders and applied research. Aligns with marketplace settings where communication is used to shape perception, coordinate action and address public needs or organizational challenges. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how strategic communication differs from general messaging, sales or promotion. Highlights the role of planning, research and ethics in shaping communication outcomes. Encourages reflection on how strategy must adjust to different audiences, purposes and constraints, rather than relying on a single model or platform. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include case analysis of campaigns; study of stakeholder identification, goals and messaging; application of communication research; media writing and visual communication; channel strategy; budgeting, collaboration with organizations; evaluation and adaptation of communication plans. Course projects or examples may involve nonprofit, corporate, governmental or community settings and may draw on diverse perspectives and public issues. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in COMM 323 and COMM 322; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Communication Tactics. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the strategic use of communication tactics in public and organizational contexts. Focuses on writing, planning and integrating traditional and digital media tools to support communication goals. Considers research, message and design development, media platforms and message evaluation. Examines how communication tactics are shaped by audiences, objectives, timing and professional standards. Includes analysis of how digital and legacy media operate in strategic communication campaigns across profit and nonprofit sectors. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Connects strategic communication to professional contexts, such as public relations, nonprofit campaigns, branding, integrated marketing communication, media production and organizational communication. Involves skills relevant to media writing, developing and designing content for campaigns, coordinating tactics across channels and adapting messages to audiences. Aligns with marketplace expectations in sectors that use communication to engage stakeholders, manage reputation or support organizational goals. Supports preparation for advanced study in communication, media strategy or related professional fields. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies that strategic communication involves planning, research and audience understanding; not just choosing platforms or sending messages. Highlights the relationship between communication tactics, planning, persuasion, credibility and ethics. Builds awareness of how media platforms influence message design and implementation, stakeholder response and public perception. Promotes critical thinking about communication choices and their consequences in real-world contexts. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of digital and traditional media tools; development of written and visual content; research for message planning; integration of communication tactics across platforms; evaluation of effectiveness; writing for news, Associated Press Style, features, public relations writing, social media and multimedia formats; audience targeting and message tailoring; portfolio-building; and collaboration with client, community or organizational partners. Content may incorporate diverse perspectives connected to stakeholder demographics, institutional needs and/or community contexts, as relevant to strategic communication work. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in COMM 323, junior or senior classification.

Strategic Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how strategic communication is used to shape policy, manage reputation and advance organizational goals across profit and nonprofit settings. Focuses on planning models, stakeholder analysis, campaign strategy and message design. Considers how communication tools are selected, adapted and evaluated in relation to audiences, goals and contexts. Examines ethical, legal and social dimensions of strategic practice. Includes study of branding, advocacy, media use and organizational communication across institutional, public and marketplace environments. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to fields such as public relations, public affairs, advocacy, corporate communication, nonprofit outreach, integrated marketing communication, branding and campaign management. Involves practices relevant to stakeholder engagement, message planning and strategic messaging across platforms. Supports preparation for professional roles that require designing, coordinating or evaluating communication strategies, as well as for advanced study in communication and related fields. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how strategic communication differs from general messaging or publicity. Highlights the role of research, planning, persuasion, ethics and stakeholder analysis in shaping outcomes. Encourages consideration of how communication strategy interacts with stakeholder behavior, power, policy and public opinion across institutional contexts. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of campaign planning, stakeholder identification, strategic messaging, branding, media selection, ethics, policy communication and/or public influence. Course content may draw on political, corporate, governmental, community, health and/or nonprofit case contexts. Examples and applications may involve public issues, institutional challenges or policy debates as relevant to strategic communication practice. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Communication Leadership and Conflict Management. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines leadership and conflict through a communication lens.
