Course content may include cases involving political conflict, privacy concerns or online controversy, examined for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Supports professional preparation in fields concerned with media policy, strategic communication, digital storytelling, user experience, ethics or advocacy. Strengthens civic literacy by analyzing how technological narratives influence public trust, participation and responsibility. Builds awareness of how institutions, governments and communities negotiate access, autonomy and accountability in digital environments. Clarifies how contemporary debates over technology shape journalism, marketing, policy development, design practice and workplace communication. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals ways technology is not always neutral but can be embedded within cultural expectations, economic systems and political values. Differentiates between everyday assumptions about innovation and scholarly approaches that analyze who benefits, who is excluded and how technological systems reinforce or redistribute power. Informs reflection on how personal devices, platforms and infrastructures can shape interaction, memory, identity and/or agency. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of technological determinism and cultural shaping of technology; utopian and dystopian narratives in media; infrastructures of communication throughout history; surveillance, data tracking and privacy; identity formation in digital communities; automation, labor and human-machine relations; digital inequality and access; governance of communication technologies in democratic and non-democratic contexts. Course materials may include historical case studies or contemporary examples involving censorship, exploitation and/or graphic or profane content as relevant to understanding communication and technology. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Communication and Video Games. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores video games as a field of communication study, examining their development as media industries, cultural practices and technological environments. Surveys scholarship on game studies history, video game production models, audience experiences and/or game design strategies. Investigates how gameplay involves storytelling, emotion, identity and interaction across different genres and mediums. Course material may include video games or related media that contain violence, mature content or controversial themes, examined for purposes of critical analysis and informed perspectives. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages skills applicable to media strategy, entertainment industries, marketing, game design, journalism and audience analysis. Builds familiarity with economic models, platform ecosystems and/or emerging markets surrounding digital entertainment. Supports academic preparation in communication, media studies, cultural studies and technology research. Enhances civic and cultural awareness by examining how interactive media shape norms, values and public debate. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how video games function not only as entertainment but also as sites of persuasion, identity performance, experimentation and cultural meaning. Examines distinctions between technological innovation and social consequences. Informs reflection on assumptions about players, genres, violence and/or interactivity by contrasting public debates with empirical and critical research. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of game history and platform evolution; analysis of development pipelines, publishing models and global industry structures; exploration of narrative design and emotional engagement; consideration of online communities, fandoms and participatory cultures; examination of regulation, monetization, labor, access and ethics. Course material may draw from games or case studies involving conflict, gender representation or political controversy as relevant to communication analysis. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Global Media. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how globalization and media are intertwined across national, transnational and diasporic circuits. Explores frameworks for understanding globalization through media ownership, migration, representation, content flow, technology, everyday life and/or political influence. Considers how news, entertainment, advertising and/or digital platforms travel across regions and are reshaped by local and transnational values, communities and regulations. Highlights both integration and inequality in global media landscapes. Course content may reference political or cultural controversies, including propaganda, censorship, immigration or conflict reporting, for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds awareness of how media industries function in global markets, supporting preparation for careers in journalism, strategic communication, public affairs, media production, policy analysis and international business. Supports adaptability within multicultural and internationally connected workplaces. Develops abilities to assess media influence across national and cultural boundaries, relevant skills in organizations operating in global or multicultural environments. Strengthens academic grounding for advanced study in communication, media studies, international relations or cultural analysis. Supports civic literacy by clarifying how global media shape public opinion, diplomacy and perception between nations. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals that media are not neutral carriers of information but products of political, economic, ideological and cultural systems. Highlights how similar content can carry different meanings depending on context, history, ideology and/or regulation. Encourages reflection on how local and/or personal media environments are shaped by assumptions and practices that may differ substantially across national and cultural boundaries, fostering greater awareness of perspective and context. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of transnational media ownership and conglomerates; global circulation of news, entertainment and advertising; audiences and consumers; comparative media systems in democratic, authoritarian and transitional societies; localization and cultural adaptation; media policy, censorship and regulatory control; streaming platforms, social media and telecommunications infrastructure; migration, diaspora, citizenship and identity across borders. Course material may reference real-world cases involving political or cultural controversy, such as extremism, disinformation or state propaganda, for purposes of analysis and critique within an environment of respectful dialogue. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with JOUR 458.

Communication and Contemporary Issues. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of how communication practices construct, contest, circulate and/or suppress contemporary issues. Focus may draw on rhetorical, critical, interpretive and/or empirical approaches to message design, media representation, public discourse and/or everyday interaction. Emphasizes analytical reading and case analysis grounded in scholarship. Course focus varies by instructor and term. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Uses the study of individual contemporary issues as a laboratory for understanding how communication shapes public problems across domains. Builds recognition of how messages influence perception, policy and action in government, health, technology, culture and/or everyday life. Develops skills relevant to professional roles involving analysis, advocacy, media interpretation, strategic messaging or organizational decision-making. Strengthens academic preparation by deepening proficiency in applying theory to real-world cases. Supports civic readiness by refining the ability to interpret competing claims, identify persuasive strategies and critically engage issues with clarity. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of how communication shapes issues related to health, environment, technology, labor, education, identity or public policy. May examine political rhetoric, media representation, scientific controversy, organizational messaging, global and transnational issues, colonialism and decoloniality and/or grassroots advocacy. Cases may draw from news, social media, institutional reports, cultural texts and/or lived experiences. Course material may include perspectives that conflict or critique one another, addressed for the purpose of understanding how issues are framed, debated and acted upon. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

Communication in Health Care Contexts. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how communication functions across health care settings, including interpersonal interactions, organizational systems and/or public messaging. Explores approaches to patient-provider dialogue, teamwork and/or institutional communication, alongside principles used in health campaigns and information dissemination. Addresses how communication practices influence access, understanding, decision-making and/or coordination. Course material may involve discussion of sensitive health topics, addressed for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices applicable to professional effectiveness in clinical, nonprofit, corporate and public-facing health roles. Develops analytical tools for evaluating message strategies, assessing interactional dynamics and interpreting communication within institutional structures. Supports preparation for advanced study in fields related to health, communication or organizational practice, as well as for participation in public discourse surrounding health issues. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how communication in health care involves more than information delivery, incorporating factors such as context, perception, institutional procedures and interpersonal dynamics. Informs understanding of how misunderstandings emerge and ways different approaches to communication may facilitate or impede clarity, coordination and trust. Considers communication as a process with measurable effects. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of physician-patient interaction; health literacy and information accessibility; teamwork and coordination in clinical settings; communication breakdowns and system-level challenges; message design and campaign strategy; risk communication; digital health platforms and telemedicine; confidentiality, regulation and public messaging. Course material may reference real-world health controversies or policy debates as useful for understanding communication processes. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

Media, Health and Medicine. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how health, illness and medical practice are represented across media environments, including news, social media, entertainment, advertising and/or public information campaigns. Analyzes how messages about bodies, risk, care, expertise and/or responsibility are constructed and circulated. Considers how media shape public expectations of patients, professionals and/or institutions. Course content may include real-world examples involving sensitive topics such as illness, disability, gender, sexuality, social class and/or race, examined for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to workforce settings in which effective communication about health is essential, including healthcare industries, public relations, nonprofit outreach, journalism and strategic communication. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in health communication, media studies and public health or policy. Strengthens civic media literacy by examining how health information and misinformation spread through media systems, institutional messaging and cultural narratives. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how portrayals of health are shaped not only by medical knowledge but also by narrative conventions, commercial pressures and/or cultural assumptions. Builds understanding of how media depictions of illness, caregiving and wellness can inform, inspire, mislead and/or stigmatize, depending on framing. Facilitates comparison between professional expertise and popular narratives to better understand how public perceptions of health are formed and challenged. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of medical dramas and documentaries; news coverage of disease outbreaks or medical innovation; health marketing and pharmaceutical advertising; public health campaigns and crisis communication; social media communities around wellness, disability or chronic illness; narratives of caregiving and recovery; depictions of healthcare providers and institutions. May include feminist and/or critical approaches to the intersections of health with topics like gender, race and sexuality. Course material may reference real-world historical and contemporary health controversies when useful for understanding communication processes. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Advanced Social Media. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the strategic use of social media in professional, organizational and/or public communication contexts. Analyzes how platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn and/or X structure their visibility, engagement and audience expectations. Explores how organizations and individuals craft identity, manage interaction and respond to feedback across different platform cultures. Includes both critical evaluation of existing accounts and hands-on creation of posts, visuals and/or campaigns for specific purposes. Course material may reference real-world social media campaigns related to political, cultural and/or commercial controversy, examined for purposes of communication analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies directly to careers in public relations, branding, journalism, advocacy, content strategy and digital marketing. Builds fluency in platform conventions, analytics, message design and audience targeting; skills applicable in both corporate and nonprofit communication roles. Supports academic growth in media analysis and prepares students for civic participation in increasingly networked communication environments. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how social media operates not only as a tool for promotion but as a space of negotiation between creators, institutions and publics. Highlights differences between personal posting, strategic messaging and algorithmic influence. Informs reflection on the challenges of authenticity, persuasion and accountability when communication is continuous, participatory and highly public. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of platform affordances and algorithmic logics; branding and identity construction; audience engagement strategies; visual and multimedia storytelling; analytics and performance metrics; influencer models and creator economies; platform policy, moderation and crisis response. Course examples may draw from corporate, political, entertainment, activist and/or nonprofit accounts. Content creation components may involve drafting posts, graphics, videos and/or campaign plans in response to simulated or real-world communication goals. Prerequisites: Grade of B or better in COMM 275 or JOUR 275; junior or senior classification.

Religious Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the role of religious communication in shaping public life through speeches, sermons, debates, campaigns and/or social movements. Considers how religious language, symbols and/or narratives influence cultural identity, moral reasoning and/or collective action. Surveys diverse approaches to studying religious communication, from historical traditions to contemporary debates, highlighting how meaning is constructed, contested and transformed in religious discourse. Considers interpretations of religious communication from multiple perspectives, fostering critical thinking. Explores a diverse range of scholarly frameworks, theories and methods employed in the academic study of religion and religious communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens transferable skills in critical thinking, interpretation and evaluation of persuasive messages in contexts ranging from personal dialogue to civic engagement. Enhances adaptability across diverse religious and cultural frameworks. Supports academic preparation for analyzing communication at the intersection of religion, culture and public life. Engages skills applicable to leadership, education, public study of advocacy and professional fields, when understanding religious perspectives and their influence is relevant. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how religious communication functions not only as a vehicle of belief but also as a force shaping history, politics and/or social change. Provides reflection on ways speeches, symbols and/or campaigns can both unite and divide, reinforcing traditions or sparking transformation. Provides frameworks for critical analysis of religious discourse from first-person and third-person perspectives. Highlights the interpretive challenges posed by pluralism, competing meanings and differing assumptions about authority, sacredness and public expression. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of religious speeches and sermons; debates over doctrine and belief; campaigns and movements shaped by religious rhetoric; analysis of religious symbolism and storytelling; exploration of the role of communication in sustaining or challenging religious traditions. Course materials may address diverse and sometimes controversial perspectives, reflecting the ways religious communication has influenced cultural identity, social conflict and civic life across history. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with RELS 480.
Health Communication Practicum. Credit 0 to 1. Directed individual health communication practicum. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.

Internship in Communication.  Credit 0 to 23. Directed internship in a public or private organization to provide students with on-the-job training and applied research experience; application of communication theory and practice in career settings; designed to enhance and clarify students' career objectives. May be repeated for credit. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisites: Cumulative GPR of 2.5 or higher for credits taken in residence; approval of department head.

Directed Studies.  Credit 0 to 3 each semester. Directed individual study of identified topics in communication; may include specific research, readings or other approved project in any area of communication; written report is required. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisites: Cumulative GPR of 2.5 or higher; approval of instructor and department head.

SCBCRSE_TITLE: COMM DIV SOC JUST CAPSTONE EXP
COURSE_TITLE: COMM DIV SOC JUST CAPSTONE EXP
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Communication, Diversity and Social Justice Capstone Experience. Credit 0 to 1. Directed individual communication, diversity, social justice capstone experience. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of capstone director.
Global Media Practicum. Credit 0 to 1. Directed global media experience. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.
Special Topics in... Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of communication. May be repeated for credit.

Research.  Credit 0 to 3. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in the department of communication. May be taken four times for credit. Prerequisites: GPA 2.5 or higher; junior or senior classification and approval of instructor and department head.

Independent Honors Studies.  Credit 0 to 3 each semester. Directed independent studies for upper division Honors students, regardless of academic major, in select aspects of communication. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification either as Honors student or with GPR of 3.25; letter of approval from head of student's department.

Foundations of Communication Inquiry. (3-0). Credit 3. Major approaches to data generation and theory building used in the communication discipline; survey of quantitative, interpretive, critical and bibliographic research methods. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

Foundations of Humanistic and Critical Inquiry in Communication Research. (3-0). Credit 3. Theoretical approaches for the interpretation of human motivations, collective actions, and textual artifacts; exploration of a variety of critical perspectives that constitute the tradition of the humanities from the classical to the modern period. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

SCBCRSE_TITLE: QUANT SOC SCI METH IN COMM
COURSE_TITLE: QUANT SOC SCI METH IN COMM
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Quantitative Social Science Methods in Communication Research. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of quantitative social science research methods in communication and media studies, including design, measurement and analysis for descriptive and experimental research; practice in evaluating and conducting research projects. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

Advanced Quantitative Methods in Communication Research. (3-0). Credit 3. In-depth exploration and application of quantitative research methods in communication and media research; examination of regression-based modeling and its extensions, including ordinary least squares, model selection, resampling methods, analysis of categorical dependent variables, data transformation, interactive effects, and regularization; introduction to time series models. Prerequisites: COMM 610; graduate classification.

Computational Methods in Communication Research. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to computational approaches to collecting, organizing, and analyzing data in communication research; examination of web-scraping techniques; interaction with API; a survey of supervised methods and unsupervised methods; introduction to neural networks; introduction to natural language processing. Prerequisites: COMM 610; graduate classification.

Interpretive and Critical Methods in Communication Research. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to interpretive, qualitative, textual, and critical methods in communication research; underlying epistemologies, design issues, and explanation of knowledge claims; methods including participant observation and interviewing. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Topics in Communication Methods. (3-0). Credit 3. Focused and in-depth examination on theory and practice of single method in communication research; includes surveys, interviewing, focus groups, ethnography, digital methods, rhetorical field methods, engage scholarship, historiography and experimental design. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Communication Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. The nature and role of communication theory; systems of ontology and epistemology in theory development; critical review of current theories concerning communication codes, functions and processes in various contexts. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

Cultural Studies and Critical Theory in Communication Research. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to the theoretical foundations of contemporary work in critical and cultural studies in Communication. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Power and Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. Patterns of language, the systems of media, and networks of influence that constitute and direct collective human action; study of how power is created, imposed, resisted, and changed through different communicative tactics and strategies. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Political Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. Interdisciplinary study of the intersection of politics and communication, especially the communications strategies of political elites; structure of media institutions and media technologies within democratic societies; effects of mediated communications on public opinion. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Propaganda and Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of the ethics in persuasion and the weaponized communication practices of propaganda; examination of the relationships among propaganda and demagoguery, democracy, democratic deliberation, media, and the public sphere. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Communication and Conflict. (3-0). Credit 3. Elements and central features of conflict theories and different approaches to communication in conflict management; analysis of communication research in interpersonal, family/marital, group, organizational, and public conflicts and the role of the media in social and international disputes. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Communicating Gender and Sexuality. (3-0). Credit 3. Gender as complex phenomena constituted through communication; topics include femininities, masculinities, language, power, nonverbal behavior, gender in media, organizations, interpersonal relationships, and social movements. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Communicating Race and Racism. (3-0). Credit 3. Critical and cultural studies approaches to understanding practices of communicating race and racism in various mediated and discursive contexts; examination of race, racism, and racialization; examination of intersections between race and other social identities like gender, sexuality, class, and religion. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Survey of Organizational Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. Theoretical and empirical literature on human communication and complex organizations; the study of messages, interaction, and meaning in the process of organizing; topics include superior-subordinate communication, communication networks, and technologies, language, message flow, symbols and organizational culture, negotiation and conflict, and power and politics. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Topics in Organizational Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. Investigation of a subject important to the understanding of organizational communication, such as communication and organizational decision-making, group communication within organizations, communication and organizational culture, and organizational rhetoric and issue management. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Rhetorical Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. Close reading of classical and contemporary systems of rhetoric; survey of principal applications to communication theory and research. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

Rhetorical and Textual Methods in Communication Research. (3-0). Credit 3. Comparative study of traditional and contemporary perspectives on the description, interpretation, and evaluation of public discourse, including textual analysis, neo-classical analysis, Burkean criticism, quantitative and qualitative approaches to content analysis, fantasy theme analysis, and semiotic analysis. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

Classical Rhetoric. (3-0). Credit 3. Origins of rhetoric in classical Greece and Rome; exploration of the relationship between philosophy, rhetoric and democratic political culture; the contemporary relevance of classical thought to contemporary problems. Cross-listed with ENGL 654.

Contemporary Theories of Rhetoric. (3-0). Credit 3. Investigation of the major figures in rhetorical theory in the 20th and 21st centuries; analysis of the relationship between rhetoric and power; identifying new challenges for rhetoric in global, multicultural, technological age. May be repeated for credit. Cross-listed with ENGL 655.

Communication and Culture. (3-0). Credit 3. Investigation of the ways that culture, religion, identity, gender, popular culture, community, history, and related ideas are shaped through communication in order to understand the development of social norms, political values, and the human experience. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Communication and Citizenship in the Public Sphere. (3-0). Credit 3. Theoretical examination of communication within democratic, republican, and liberal conceptions of citizenship; consideration of the ideal of the public sphere, and communication in global civil society; specific attention to the practices of American citizenship within the global civil society. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Media and Identity. (3-0). Credit 3. Representations of identity in media and popular culture; how media and technology use shape and are shaped by identity; media as sites for negotiation and construction of identities such as gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, social class, physical/mental ability, nationality and religion; impacts and effects of media stereotypes and counter-stereotypes; positive storytelling, counter-narratives and media initiatives that resist mainstream portrayals; media activism and social justice. May be repeated for credit.  Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Media Studies. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of research and theory in media studies; overview of the historical and theoretical orientation of media studies; exploration of approaches to analyzing media texts, technologies, audiences, reception processes, economics, and/or industries. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Topics in Media Studies. Credit 3. Intensive work on selected topics of research in media studies; may address work in the areas of audience studies, media effects, industries, policy, international issues, media and culture, media history or theory. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Media Processes and Effects. (3-0). Credit 3. Investigation of processes through which mediated messages influence our everyday lives; examination of social scientific approaches; understanding how viewers select, interpret and respond to mediated messages; includes media representations, mediated inter-group processes, news framing, political advertising, persuasive messages, entertainment media, popular culture, health campaigns, positive media psychology, new media technologies, pro-social media effects and critical media literacy. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Communication and Technology. (3-0). Credit 3. Examines the relationships between human communication and technology, investigating the social effects of communication technologies, the quality of messages, communicative practices, and rhetorical norms that typify effective communication in technological society. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Media and Health. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of theories, methods and research that characterize the use of media in health contexts; focus on mass media influence on public health and/or strategic use of mass media to promote health behaviors; engagement of social and behavioral science approaches to media effects and/or critical perspectives on the study of media as social institutions. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Health Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. Theories and research in health communication considering functions and outcomes of communication processes in various health contexts, ranging from interpersonal settings to public campaigns; emphasis on providing a framework for synthesizing and critically evaluating health communication research. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Topics in Health Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. Investigation of a subject important to the understanding of health communication, such as persuasion and public health campaigns, physician-patient communication, or communication in health care organizations. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Professional Seminar. Credit 0 to 1. Provides socialization to the profession of communication, focusing on graduate students' roles as scholars and teachers; provides instruction on teaching communication, conducting and writing publishable research, and fulfilling responsibilities to one's organization and profession. May be repeated up to three times. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Directed Studies.  Credit 1 to 6 each semester. Directed studies in specific problem areas in communication. Student may take up to two sections of directed studies in communication in the same semester, with a maximum of 6 credits. Prerequisite: Approval of department head.
Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4 each semester. Selected topics in an identified area of communication. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
Research.  Credit 1 or more each semester. Research for thesis.

Introduction to the Construction Industry. (3-0). Credit 3. Characteristics of the construction industry; types of construction companies; contracts; people involved in a project, their responsibilities and interrelationships; evolution of a project; interpreting working drawings; construction bonds; contract documents. Prerequisite: COSL majors only.

Construction Graphics Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. This course provides a foundational understanding of construction plans and specifications. Students will gain practical experience in interpreting construction drawings and architectural specifications, preparing them for further study and professional practice in the construction industry. Prerequisite: COSL majors.

Business Legal Practices for Construction Science. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to the U.S. legal system and its impact on business; includes general principles of law, the relationship of business and the U.S. Constitution, state and federal legal systems, the relationship between law and ethics, dispute resolution, contracts, sales, torts, agency law, intellectual property and business law. Prerequisites: Construction Science majors.

Introduction to Facilities Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Overview of facilities management principles; acquisition, operation, maintenance and disposition of the built environment; topics include construction documents, building systems (envelope, architectural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing), utility services, real estate and events and emergency management; owner’s interaction with occupants, architects, engineers and contractors.

COURSE_ATTRIBUTES: {"attribute":"Core Lang, Phil, Culture(KLPC)","attribute":"Univ Req-Cult Discourse (KUCD)","attribute":"NonTraditional Temp Exemption"}
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Cultural and Social Issues in the Construction Environment. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to cultural and social issues in the built environment; exploration of how individual and collective ideas, values and beliefs are expressed in the construction environment; how the field of construction internalizes and thinks about these values across cultures and how authority, majorities and privilege affect the creativity of the built environment; emphasizes civil discourse to help recognize positionality and work collaboratively in a multicultural society.

(ARCH 2312) Construction Materials and Methods I. (3-0). Credit 3. Overview of construction materials, methods, and sequences of the construction process; introduction to material specifications and construction drawings; focus of study includes wood, concrete, masonry, and steel.

Introduction to Construction Technologies. (3-0). Credit 3. Fundamentals of building information modeling (BIM) and virtual design and construction (VDC) for construction practice. Topics include building systems modeling for architectural, structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing and fire protection; linking and monitoring multi-discipline models; model coordination and clash detection; schedule simulation (4D); estimation and quantification through schedules and material takeoffs (5D); and exposure to industry collaboration and project information management platforms through guest presentations. Prerequisites: COSC 175; COSL majors.

Estimating I. (2-3). Credit 3. Systems approach to determining required quantities of construction materials; quantification of various types of foundation systems, structural systems and building envelope systems; excerpts of contract documents from a variety of different building projects. Prerequisite: COSC 253; concurrent enrollment in COSC 175.

Introduction to Applied Workplace Ethics, Etiquette and Communications. (1-0). Credit 1. Professional ethics, etiquette and communication for employment preparation with a construction or construction related company; various case studies emphasizing personal accountability, integrity and codes of conduct; etiquette and communication of all forms will be presented, applied and discussed in reflective writing assignments in order to prepare to meet the professional expectations of employers upon graduation. Prerequisite: COSL majors.
Directed Studies.  Credit 1 to 3. Special project in construction science. Project must be approved by the department. Prerequisite: Approval of department head.

Research.  Credit 1 to 4. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in construction science. May be repeated 2 times for credit. Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification; approval of instructor.

Construction Surveying. (1-3). Credit 2. Practical applications of surveying to the practice of construction project management; distance, grade and angular measurement; surveying equipment and its application to construction layout and control; surveying documentation and field work; introduction to other three dimensional measurement and positioning systems. Prerequisite: Admission to upper level in Construction Science.

High Performance Residential Building. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration into the concepts of homebuilding operations using green building methods, tools to reach consumers, organizational and operational theories and market driven green building solutions; alignment with ICC 700 National Green Building Standard; operations of publicly traded and private production homebuilders and best practices; application for the professional designation of Certified Green Professional (CGP) given by the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) upon completion. Prerequisite: Admission to upper level  in Construction Science.

SCBCRSE_TITLE: DESIGN AND CONSTR LEAD EDUC I
COURSE_TITLE: DESIGN AND CONSTR LEAD EDUC I
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Design and Construction Leadership Education I. (1-0). Credit 1. Promotion of personal leadership skills utilized within the design and construction professions; primary understanding and developing management skills with specific attention to developing personal attributes and skills necessary for achieving organizational goals. Prerequisite: CARC majors only pursuing the minor in leadership in the design & construction professions; junior or senior classification.

Immersion in Facilities Management. (3-0). Credit 3. In-depth exploration of tasks required for acquisition, operation, maintenance, and disposition of the built environment; includes commercial, healthcare, education, performance, athletic and high-rise residential buildings; site visits to relevant facilities. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in COSC 214.

Structural Systems I. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to the physical principles that govern classical statics and strengths of materials through the design of architectural structures. Prerequisite: Admission to upper level in Construction Science.

Construction Discourse Leadership. (3-0). Credit 3. Practicum on leadership skills; leading and managing difficult discussions in a professional setting; mentorship of new students; presentation of difficult discussion topics, demonstration of constructive critique methods.  Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in COSC 222.

Mechanical, Electrical and Plumbing Systems in Construction I. (3-0). Credit 3. Design, operation, materials and installation methods of mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems in construction. Prerequisite: Admission to upper level in construction science or minor in facility management.

Mechanical, Electrical and Plumbing Systems in Construction II. (3-0). Credit 3. Familiarization with more technical aspects of mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) system design, operations, materials and installation methods. Prerequisite: COSC 325.

Life Cycle Assessment in Building Construction. (3-0). Credit 3. Life Cycle Assessment from a coupled energy-carbon-water (ECW) nexus perspective; key LCA concepts; the LCA process; LCA standards; application of LCA approaches and software to assess the energy, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, water, and other environmental impacts of building construction industry at the material and whole building levels; study and analysis of factors relating to material and assembly choices, site logistics, on-site and off-site construction and/or fabrication processes, additive construction (large-scale 3D printing), and construction and demolition waste to reduce the energy use, GHG emissions, and water use; analysis and comparison of LCA results of process-based and macro-economic model-based Life Cycle Inventory (LCI). Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

Building Codes and Construction. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of the complex interrelationship of building codes and their influence on construction projects; emphasis on building code organization, construction types, and occupancy classifications; examines the role and responsibilities of the construction professional, the permitting process, and the inspection process. Prerequisites: Admission to upper level in Construction Science.

Principles of Roofing from Design to Installation and Beyond. (3-0). Credit 3. Study of roof construction, focusing on the nomenclature, building materials, estimating, safety, technology and the assembly of different roofing systems. Prerequisites: Upper-level Construction Science majors.

Construction Project Management. (3-0). Credit 3. An introduction to construction project management covering concepts of project selection, estimating bidding, scheduling, subcontracting practices, cost controls, project documentation, construction bonds, insurance, payments and the elements of close out; development of professional communication skills through prepared multi-media presentations. Prerequisite: Admission to upper level in Construction Science.

Construction Materials and Methods II. (3-0). Credit 3. Continuation of COSC 253; emphasis on advanced building methods for the assembly of building systems; focus of study includes concrete, masonry, and steel. Prerequisite: COSC 253.

Industrial Construction. (3-0). Credit 3. Industry specific knowledge such as concepts of developing construction management strategies of industrial projects, materials and methods, structural and mechanical components; preparation to effectively resolve challenges faced in the industrial construction sector. Prerequisites: Admission to upper level in construction science.

Estimating II. (2-3). Credit 3. Survey of cloud-based estimating technologies with hands-on use of advanced software to prepare lump-sum bid packages, including general conditions, through model quantification and inventory extraction. Prerequisites: Admission to upper level in Construction Science; COSC 275.

Professional Ethics in the Construction Industry. (1-0). Credit 1. Principles of ethical behavior in preparation for a professional internship with a construction or construction-related company; various construction company case studies emphasizing personal accountability, integrity, moral courage, individual, association and company codes of conduct; accepted business practices, decision making, company cultures, peer pressure, public opinion. Prerequisite: Admission to upper level in Construction Science.

SCBCRSE_TITLE: DESIGN AND CONSTR LEAD EDUC II
COURSE_TITLE: DESIGN AND CONSTR LEAD EDUC II
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Design and Construction Leadership Education II. (1-0). Credit 1. Development of competencies in various leadership and management practices that are useful in an array of situations; emphasis on organizational leadership and management development with specific attention to intragroup relationships and techniques for achieving group goals. Prerequisite: COSC 310, CARC majors only pursuing the minor in leadership in the design and construction professions; junior or senior classification.

Seminar in Design and Construction Executive Leadership. (1-0). Credit 1. Promotes an understanding of leadership and builds the capacity to understand and meet the challenges involved in developing and leading ethical and sustainable organizations in today’s economy; examination of theory, conceptualizing, reflection and application; share experiences in everyday life and learn to predict outcomes based on theoretical models. Prerequisite: COSC 410; CARC majors only pursuing the minor in leadership in the design and construction; junior or senior classification.

Contracted Services Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Overview of contracted services management for facilities design, construction, operations, and maintenance; topics include scope of work development, A/E and vendor selection and procurement, contract administration (insurance, payment, communication, scope execution, field oversight, closeout), and common tools, equipment, and material. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better COSC 214; Minor in Facilities Management; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Soils in Construction. (3-0). Credit 3. Physical properties of soils; including particle size analysis, plasticity and soil classification. Principles of soil compaction. Stresses in soils. Use of soil properties to estimate soil shear strength, settlement and consolidation, bearing capacity and lateral earth pressures. Prerequisite: COSC 321.

Project Execution and Administration - Constructionarium United Kingdom. (3-0). Credit 3. Development of project execution and management of a mock commercial construction project; includes aspects of estimating, bidding, schedule development, real time scheduling, job-site safety plans, project execution plans, material procurement, cost controls, construction management, owner, and architect presentations, close out, and post-construction requirements; includes multiple day field trip during the mock construction project. Prerequisites: Admission to upper level in Construction Science.

Preconstruction - the Art of the Project. (3-0). Credit 3. Instruction in the pre-construction processes that are necessary in construction project evolution; exploration of alternative project delivery options from the traditional design-bid-build linear approach; focus on engagement of Construction Professionals at earliest project phase; familiarization with the roles of professionals in all phases of construction including design, construction, and ownership. Prerequisites: Admission to upper level in Construction Science.

Interdisciplinary Capstone. (3-0). Credit 3. A senior capstone for students preparing to enter the designbuild sector of the construction industry; integration of the design and construction processes into a single, cohesive project delivery system, starting with project inception, and carrying through construction, operation and maintenance of various types of construction projects. Prerequisite: COSC 475; must be taken in graduating semester.

Residential Capstone. (3-0). Credit 3. A senior capstone course that prepares students for careers in residential construction through advanced training in project management and business planning, with emphasis on team collaboration and presentation skills. The curriculum includes market analytics, site analysis with attention to zoning and development codes, residential product selection aligned with building regulations, cost estimating, subcontracting, scheduling, site utilization, sales and marketing, financial planning and emerging trends in residential design and construction. Prerequisite: COSC 475; must be taken in graduating semester.

Commercial Capstone. (3-0). Credit 3. A senior capstone course for students preparing to enter the commercial construction sector; project management of commercial construction projects, including aspects of design, bidding/estimating; presentation, value engineering, contracts/negotiation, subcontractor relations, cost controls, management during construction, close out, and post-construction requirements. Prerequisite: COSC 475; must be taken in graduating semester.

Industrial Capstone. (3-0). Credit 3. A senior capstone course for students preparing to enter the industrial construction sector; project management of industrial construction projects including project acquisition, planning and staffing, engineering, procurement, construction, start-up, close out, operations and maintenance, and turn-arounds. Prerequisite: COSC 475; must be taken in graduating semester.

Specialty Capstone. (3-0). Credit 3. Senior capstone course for students preparing to enter the mechanical, electrical or other specialty construction company; project management of specialty contracts including project acquisition, schematic system design, estimating/bidding, scheduling, systems integration, value engineering, management during construction of crews and procurement, contract administration, business planning and current industry issues. Prerequisite: COSC 475; must be taken in graduating semester.

Building Information Modeling System. (3-0). Credit 3. Discovery and application of emerging technologies in construction automation including sensors, robotics, virtual/augmented reality and building information modeling (BIM); exploration of state-of-the-art information processing methods such as machine learning, computer vision and natural language processing; integration of hardware and software systems to facilitate the collection, analysis and use of construction information. Prerequisite: Admission to upper level in Construction Science.

Introduction to Construction Law. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to basic contract and tort issues and their application in the construction industry; delineation of the various types of contracts and remedies available to parties involved in a construction project; additional related topics including project procurement, delays, mechanics liens and bonds, site conditions; introduction to legal research and reasoning as used by professional constructors. Prerequisite: Admission to upper level in Construction Science.

Construction Safety. (3-0). Credit 3. Course curriculum content consists of 30 hour OSHA, Occupation Safety and Health Administration for construction, CPR/AED, industrial first aid, construction management certification, job hazard analysis and accident investigation of projects, ergonomic project analysis, quality assurance analysis and adult mental health and first aid certification. All topics in the course prepare the students for developing a site-specific safety plan for a project. Prerequisite: Admission to upper-level in construction science.

Advanced Topics in Construction Law. (3-0). Credit 3. Legal issues affecting construction, including the parties to construction work, contracting and the Uniform Commercial Code, responsibilities and risk, risk management, damages, handling of claims and disputes including warranties and statutes of limitation and repose, insurance, bankruptcy, labor and employment, and environmental laws as they relate to and impact the construction industry; litigation and alternative dispute resolution methods regularly used in the construction industry; emerging legal topics that impact construction. Prerequisites: COSC majors; COSC 463.

Risk Management in the Built Environment. (3-0). Credit 3. Decision-making and risk analysis concepts in the context of the built environment and construction projects; major categories and tools of risk management regularly used in the construction industry such as contracts, insurance and bonds. Prerequisites: Admission to upper level in construction science and COSC 463 or concurrent enrollment.

Built Environment in International Setting. (3-0). Credit 3. Survey of the built environment and how changing global societies have adapted in design, labor and materials used; exposure to to opinions and practices in the areas of politics, culture, gender and religion.   Prerequisite: Junior or Senior construction science majors or instructor approval.

Facilities Management Internship. (3-0). Credit 3. An internship (10 weeks, 400 hours) at the site of any facility type that exposes the student to the variety of tools, materials, equipment, systems, processes, peer service groups, contracted service partners and clients that are required to make the built environment safe, attractive, functional and efficient. Prerequisites: COSC 214 and approval of internship faculty coordinator; successful completion of an OSHA 10 for Construction training course.

Construction Project Planning. (2-3). Credit 3. Study of construction project planning and scheduling, emphasizing plan reading to identify required activities and sequencing. Students will develop work breakdown structures, define durations and logic relationships and create critical path schedules that span all project phases of a building project from pre-construction through close-out. Using industry-standard software, students will create baselines, update progress, evaluate schedule quality and prepare reporting tools, resulting in working project execution documents. Prerequisite: COSC 353; COSC 375.

Construction Project Controls. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to construction related financial documents including schedule of values, labor and operations cost reports, income statements, balance sheets and construction budgets; emphasis on the development of techniques required to effectively monitor the financial aspects of a construction project. Prerequisite: COSC 353 and COSC 494.
Seminar. (1-0). Credit 1. Seminar discussion of construction equipment selection, utilization maintenance and operating cost. Prerequisite: Admission to upper level in Construction Science.

Internship - 10 Week. Credit 3. An internship (10 weeks, 400 hours) with a construction or construction-related company that exposes the student to construction-related activities; daily logs, monthly reports, final report and completion letter required; distance education course with non-resident status; does not satisfy the College of Architecture semester away requirement unless taken while on Construction Science Spring Study Abroad. Prerequisites: COSC 284, COSC 353, and COSC 375; approval of internship faculty coordinator.
Directed Studies.  Credit 1 to 5 each semester. Special problems in building construction. Prerequisite: Admission to upper-level in Construction Science.
Special Topics in...   Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified field of construction science. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Admission to upper-level in Construction Science.

Research.  Credit 1 to 4. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in construction science. May be repeated 2 times for credit. Registration in multiple sections of this course is possible within a given semester provided that the per semester credit hour limit is not exceeded. Prerequisites: Admission to upper level in Construction Science and approval of instructor.

Internship. Credit 6 to 9. An internship (15 weeks, 600 hours) with a construction or construction-related company that exposes the student to construction-related activities, daily logs, monthly reports, final report and completion letter required; distance education course with non-resident status. No other Texas A&M Construction Science courses may be taken while enrolled in COSC 494. Prerequisites: COSC 284, COSC 353, and COSC 375; approval of internship faculty coordinator.

Advanced Construction Materials and Methods. (3-0). Credit 3. Study of construction materials and methods emphasizing interpretation of plans and specifications, including a research component requiring investigation of current and emerging materials, methods and practices. Prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.

Construction Cost Estimating. (3-0). Credit 3. Determination of quantities for various types of construction materials and works including earthwork, foundations, structural systems, mechanical and electrical systems, and building finishes; methods used for pricing of construction works including labor, materials, equipment, sub-contractors, overhead and profit; use of various types of cost data catalogs available in the industry. Prerequisite: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.

Construction Scheduling. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to commonly used techniques and computer applications for the planning, scheduling, monitoring, and controlling of construction projects; includes key scheduling techniques such as Gantt Chart, CPM, PERT, LSM, and EVM; practical scheduling practices such as tracking, controlling, and forecasting trends of schedules, cost control, and reporting. Prerequisite: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.

Mechanical and Electrical Construction. (3-0). Credit 3. Building environmental systems with a major emphasis on the design and control of the heating, ventilation and cooling systems, plumbing and drainage systems, electrical, fire and lightening protection, and lighting; design opportunities, calculations, equipment selection and economics as they relate to design and construction. Prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.

Structural Integrity and Failure Forensics. (3-0). Credit 3. Investigation of interrelationships between structural integrity, behavior and failure mechanisms in building systems. Through case studies and applied theory in construction structures, students explore real-world structural failures to understand how design, construction and maintenance decisions affect performance and safety. The course emphasizes professional responsibility, diagnostic reasoning and failure prevention in construction practice. Prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.

Construction Company Operations. (3-0). Credit 3. Running a construction company; strategic planning; business planning; organizational theory; competitor analysis; risk management; financial analysis; human resources; management information systems; leadership; codes of ethics; best practices. Prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.

Advanced Project Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Theoretical, practical, and strategic development in the management of contemporary construction projects; advanced techniques used in scheduling and evaluating progress in construction project control; exploration of state-of-the-art management principles and practices, and development of additional insights. Prerequisite: COSC 603 or COSC 475.

Construction Economics. (3-0). Credit 3. Foundation in Life Cycle Cost Analysis computation within the context of current issues in environmental sustainability and evidence-based thinking; lean construction as a strategy to overcome the hurdle of first cost. Prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.

Construction Accounting and Financial Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Fundamental theories and applied methods of construction accounting and construction financial management including cash flow analysis, financial planning, risk analysis, and project financing. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Construction Contracts and Risk Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Advanced construction law, contracts, and risk management applicable to construction management; identification of common disputes and construction risks among the owner, design professionals, and contractor; analysis of construction contracts with an emphasis on troublesome provisions and solutions; demonstration of tools of negotiation and dispute resolution; ethics in construction. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Advanced Productivity and Lean. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to lean history, concepts and methods; deduction of basic training modules in lean project delivery; application of lean management in construction projects. Prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.

Life Cycle Assessment in Building Construction. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to Life Cycle Assessment from a coupled energy-carbon-water (ECW) nexus perspective; Key LCA concepts; the LCA process; LCA standards; application of LCA approaches and software to assess the energy, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, water, and other environmental impacts of building construction industry at the material and whole building levels; study and analysis of factors relating to material and assembly choices, site logistics, on-site and off­ site construction and/or fabrication processes, additive construction (large-scale 3D printing), and construction and demolition waste to reduce the energy use, GHG emissions, and water use; analysis and comparison of LCA results of process-based and macro-economic model-based Life Cycle Inventory (LCI). Prerequisite: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.

Advanced Construction Systems. (3-0). Credit 3. Theoretical, practical, and strategic development in contemporary construction systems; exploration of state-of-the-art innovations in environmental control systems, structural principles and practices; integration of innovations with information technologies, and development of additional insights. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Data Science for the Built Environment. (3-0). Credit 3. Data science with a focus on built environment applications; overview of statistics, data collection, data visualization, data cleaning, and machine learning; focuses on tackling research problems in construction and built environment using machine learning. Prerequisite: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science or approval of instructor.

Sustainable Construction. (3-0). Credit 3. Contribution of materials and methods to meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs; overview of international, national and local programs promoting sustainable construction; characteristics of the components of successful sustainable construction projects; theories and practices through case studies. Prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.

Advanced Construction Safety and Health Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Evaluation of safety management practices and accident prevention techniques, including state and federal laws related to general and construction projects; theoretical concepts and industry practices used to model, evaluate, and improve construction worker safety through the design of the project features, construction operations, and site safety program elements; causes of construction site accidents, hazard recognition and comprehension, safety risk valuation and mitigation, and the true costs of injuries and fatalities; role of technology in enhancing safety and health management; fulfills the requirements for the ten-hour OSHA certification Prerequisites: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.

Facilities Asset Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Fundamentals of facility asset management and property management including concepts, theories, and principles of design, construction, accounting, finance, and management of the built environment; an overview of a project throughout its entire life cycle from various perspectives including the owner, users, designers, constructors and  facility management personnel. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.
Seminar. Credit 1 each semester. Discussion and review of degree requirements, career opportunities, and current research activities in construction management. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Professional Internship. Credit 3 to 6. Approximately 400-600 hours with a construction or construction-related company that exposes the student to construction-related activities; an initial report, monthly progress reports, a final report, and a final completion letter are required. Prerequisites: Graduate classification; approval of graduate coordinator; approval of internship coordinator.
Directed Studies.  Credit 1 to 6. Individual problems in the area of building construction involving the application of theory and practice. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified field of construction management. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Theory of Research in Construction Science. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to research, research tools, proposal writing and research reports; emphasis on research planning and design, conducting a comprehensive review of literature, quantitative and qualitative research methodologies, defining research problems in construction science, and the development of research proposals. Prerequisite: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.
Research.  Credit 1 or more each semester. Research for thesis. Prerequisites: COSC 690 or concurrent enrollment; approval of graduate coordinator.

Professional Study.  Credit 1 to 6. Approved professional study of project undertaken as terminal requirement for Master of Science, non-thesis option. Preparation of a record of study summarizing the rationale, procedure and results of the completed study. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: COSC 690 or concurrent enrollment; approval of graduate coordinator.
Counseling Theories for School Counselors. (3-0). Credit 3. Overview of various counseling theories and its application in a school setting. Prerequisites: CPSY 630.

Multicultural Counseling in Schools. (3-0). Credit 3. Intersecting role of ethnicity, cultural background, gender and sexual orientation and how they shape the psychosocial development of children and adolescents and impact their educational trajectories; development and appreciation of cultural and ethnic differences among individuals, groups and families to enhance school counseling service delivery. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Counseling Techniques for School Counselors. (3-0). Credit 3. Broad view of counseling techniques using a microskills approach; opportunities to observe and practice counseling techniques. Prerequisite: CPSY 630; graduate classification.
School Counseling Group Interventions. (3-0). Credit 3. Development of group counseling interventions for children and adolescents in school settings. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Career Counseling in Schools. (3-0). Credit 3. Understanding the culturally competent career counseling theory, assessment and skills as applied to the diverse populations in schools. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Planning and Organizing Comprehensive Guidance Programs. (3-0). Credit 3. Purposes and functions of a guidance program; components of a comprehensive guidance program; systems approach to implementing a comprehensive guidance program for elementary and secondary students and adults. Prerequisite: Graduation classification.

Psychopathology. (3-0). Credit 3. Causes, course, outcomes and treatment of abnormal and maladaptive behavior; degrees of variation possible from normal adaptive behavior; biological, developmental, social, cultural and psychological perspective on abnormal behavior. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Structured Personality Assessment in Counseling. (3-0). Credit 3. Personality evaluation using structured assessment instruments; variety of self-report personality inventories; the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory. Prerequisites: EPSY 622.
Foundations of School Counseling. (3-0). Credit 3. Philosophical, psychological, and sociological concepts fundamental to counseling in schools. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Techniques of Counseling. (3-0). Credit 3. Methods and procedures descriptive of the counseling process; dynamics of counselor-counselee relationship; interviewing techniques; use of test results in counseling. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Career Counseling. (3-0). Credit 3. Theories of career development; sources, classification and analysis of educational, occupational and social information including occupational trends, post-secondary programs and financial planning; use of occupational-educational information, appropriate psychological measures and computerized guidance systems. Prerequisite: CPSY 679.

Introduction to Group Process. (2-3). Credit 3. Principles, procedures and processes of group approaches to assisting individuals in their personal growth and development in education, public and mental health settings; participation as member of a personal growth required. Prerequisite: CPSY 630.

Social Counseling Psychology Interface. (3-0). Credit 3. Provides a foundation in theory and research at the interface of social and counseling psychology; fundamentals of social psychology theories, methodologies and perspectives; understanding the relevance to counseling psychology practice; focus on social and cognitive theories, concepts, and processes rather than specific psychological disorders. Prerequisite: Doctoral student in good standing in counseling, clinical, school or social psychology.

Psychological Consultation to Organizations. (3-0). Credit 3. Focuses on organizations as the target of analysis, intervention, and change; established social science concepts and principles; consideration of concepts, intervention strategies, and skills that extend beyond those used in counseling and psychotherapy; highlights consultation as a mode of change agency; considerable attention given to putting theory into practice. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Counseling Practicum I. (2-3). Credit 3. Supervised experience in individual counseling; cases engaged in the counseling laboratory on campus; off-campus counseling in schools and various public and mental health settings also assigned at supervisor's discretion. May be taken for credit 2 times as content varies. Prerequisites: CPSY 631 and CPSY 632; approval of instructor.

COURSE_TITLE: PROF ISSUES ETHICS IN COU PSY
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Professional Issues and Ethics in Counseling Psychology. (3-0). Credit 3. Legal, ethical, economic and practical issues that impact the training, credentialing, placement and marketing of counseling psychologists and their services. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Counseling Practicum II. (0-6). Credit 3. (1-6).Supervised experience in individual and group counseling requiring advanced technical skills; continuing counseling relationships with various, selected subjects. Prerequisite: CPSY 639.

Practicum in Counselor Supervision. (0-6). Credit 3. (1-6).Supervised experience in directing counseling and guidance activities of students involved in practicum and field experiences; intended for individuals preparing to become counselor educators or supervisors. Prerequisite: CPSY 664; approval of instructor.

Theories of Counseling and Psychotherapy. (3-0). Credit 3. Comprehensive and intensive study of major theoretical positions in counseling and psychotherapy; implications for research and practice in public and mental health settings. Prerequisite: CPSY 631.

Multicultural Counseling. (3-0). Credit 3. Effective communication skills in cross-cultural counseling or helping relationships in public and mental health settings; integration of theoretical knowledge with experiential learning; psychosocial factors and lifestyles of cultural groups; effect on counseling relationships. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Field Practicum. Credit 1 to 15. Supervised experience in professional public and mental health settings in counseling psychology; wide range of practical experiences and activities that are closely supervised by departmental faculty. May be taken up to 30 hours. Prerequisite: Graduate classification; approval of instructor.

Professional Internship. Credit 1 to 4. Credit 1 to 4 each semester. Limited to advanced doctoral students; faculty supervised experience in approved professional public and mental health employment settings; application for September assignments must be approved the previous October. May be repeated up to 9 hours. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisite: Completion of required coursework except CPSY 684 and CPSY 691; approval of instructor.
Directed Studies. Credit 1 to 4.   Credit 1 to 4 each semester. Directed individual study of selected problems. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
Research Proposal Development. (3-2). Credit 4. This seminar models the processes of developing and defending research proposals. Prerequisite: EPSY 640 and EPSY 641. Cross-listed with EPSY 688.
Special Topics in... Credit 1 to 4. Selected topic in an identified area of counseling psychology. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Theory of Counseling Psychology Research. (3-0). Credit 3. Theory and design of research problems and experiments in counseling psychology; communication of research proposals and results; evaluation of current research of faculty and students and review of current literature. May be repeated for credit. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.
Research. Credit 1 to 23.   Credit 1 or more each semester. Research for thesis or dissertation. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Programming I. (3-2). Credit 4. Basic concepts in using computation to enhance problem solving abilities; understanding how people communicate with computers, and how computing affects society; computational thinking; representation of data; analysis of program behavior; methods for identifying and fixing errors in programs; understanding abilities and limitation of programs; development and execution of programs.

Introduction to Computer Science Concepts and Programming. (3-2). Credit 4. Computation to enhance problem solving abilities; understanding how people communicate with computers, and how computing affects society; computational thinking; software design principles, including algorithm design, data representation, abstraction, modularity, structured and object oriented programming, documentation, testing, portability, and maintenance; understanding programs’ abilities and limitations; development and execution programs.

Program Design and Concepts. (3-1). Credit 3. Extension of prior programming knowledge and creation of computer programs that solve problems; application of computational thinking to enhance problem solving; analysis of, design of and implementation of computer programs; use of basic and aggregate data types; encapsulation and abstraction; development of software that uses dynamic memory and avoids memory leaks; study of error handling strategies to develop more secure and robust programs. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ENGR 102, CSCE 110, CSCE 111, CSCE 206 or PHYS 150.

Introduction to Program Design and Concepts. (3-2). Credit 4. Computation to enhance problem solving abilities; computational thinking; understanding how people communicate with computers, how computing affects society; design and implementation of algorithms; data types, program control, iteration, functions, classes, and exceptions; understanding abstraction, modularity, code reuse, debugging, maintenance, and other aspects of software development; development and execution of programs. Prerequisite: Programming course (high school or college); also taught at Galveston campus.

Introduction to Computing. (1-0). Credit 1. Introduction to the broad field of computing; presentations from industry and academia about how computer science concepts are used in research and end products; includes a major writing component.

Fundamentals of Cybersecurity. (3-0). Credit 3. Basic terminology, concepts, technology, and trends of cybersecurity; foundations of cybersecurity to include cryptography, public key infrastructure, standards and protocols, physical security, network fundamentals; workings of systems, networks, infrastructure; legal and ethical issues in cybersecurity. Cross-listed with CYBR 201.

(COSC 1420) Structured Programming in C. (3-2). Credit 4. Basic concepts, nomenclature and historical perspective of computers and computing; internal representation of data; software design principles and practice; structured and object-oriented programming in C; use of terminals, operation of editors and executions of student-written programs.

Data Structures and Algorithms. (3-2). Credit 4. Specification and implementation of basic abstract data types and their associated algorithms including stacks, queues, lists, sorting and selection, searching, graphs and hashing; performance tradeoffs of different implementations and asymptotic analysis of running time and memory usage. Prerequisites: Grade C or better in CSCE 120 or CSCE 121; grade of C or better in CSCE 222 or ECEN 222, or concurrent enrollment.

Discrete Structures for Computing. (3-0). Credit 3. Mathematical foundations from discrete mathematics for analyzing computer algorithms, for both correctness and performance; introduction to models of computation, including finite state machines and Turing machines. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MATH 142, MATH 147, MATH 151, or MATH 171.

Computing Ethics. (1-0). Credit 1. Introduction to legal, social and ethical issues in computing and software development; emphasizes ethical decision-making, professional responsibility and communication, with coverage of professional codes, organizational ethics, law and policy, intellectual property, open-source software and variety of contemporary topics. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221; also taught at Galveston campus.
Directed Studies. Credit 0 to 4. Special project in computer science; project must be approved by the department. Prerequisite: Approval of department head; also taught at Galveston campus.
Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of computer science. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Research. Credit 0 to 4. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in computer science. May be taken three times for credit. Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor.

Computational Data Science. (3-0). Credit 3. Computational practice of data science through a sequence of interactive modules that provides an integrated hands-on approach to its methods, tools, applications and supporting technologies including high performance and cloud computing platforms.
