COURSE_NARRATIVE: Contract Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Fundamentals of the contracting and procurement processes; exploration of the authority of government agents to contract; examination of remedies in government contracting, including the Government Accountability Office’s protest system and actions in federal courts; focuses on the federal level but applicable to state and local levels. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Local Economic Development. (3-0). Credit 3. Overview of the economic development policies and practices of states and localities within the United States from the theoretical and applied perspective; exploration of major rationales for undertaking economic development programs, commonly used tools in such efforts, and some of the major strategic issues confronting state and local public officials in their attempts to promote economic development within their jurisdictions. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of department head.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Professional Local Government Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Advanced instruction in local government management; emphasis on the role and responsibilities of appointed local government administrators in rural and urban communities; examination of challenges associated with jurisdictional overlap; discussion on the relationship between appointed and elected officials; topics include professional ethics, strategic planning, policy development, budgeting, project management, public safety, public engagement, and the variety of services provided by local government. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of department head.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Nonprofit Advocacy in the Policy Process. (3-0). Credit 3. Background in state and federal law related to lobbying in the tax exempt sector; focuses upon the range of strategies and tactics that are available to nongovernmental organizations; topics include advocating in the policy environment, offensive and defensive advocacy, ethics, and the forces that influence policy. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of department head.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Program Evaluation in Public and Nonprofit Organizations. (3-0). Credit 3. Organizations today are responding to increasing demands for accountability; demands come from an increasingly sophisticated public, clientele, and from funding sources including government, foundations, and corporations; designed to introduce theories, research, and practice for program evaluation and systems that support the organization's information needs. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Marketing for Nonprofit Organizations. (3-0). Credit 3. Provides overviews and examines the underlying fundamental principles, concepts, and methods of strategic marketing as it is associated with the nonprofit sector. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Fiscal Management for Nonprofits. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to the underlying fundamental principles, concepts and methods of managerial finance in nonprofit organizations; interpretation and evaluation of the financial reports to inform strategic decision-making in planning and budgeting. Prerequisites: Graduate classification; approval of MPSA director or PSAA department head.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Philanthropy: Fundraising in Nonprofit Organizations. (3-0). Credit 3. Examines the theory and practice of fundraising in nonprofit organizations; overview of fundraising strategies and techniques and how they relate to the achievement of organizational goals; focuses on ways of integrating various fundraising activities into an effective fundraising program. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Public Management. (3-0). Credit 3. This course examines the dynamics of public sector institutions. Balancing foundational theory with practical application, the course explores how formal structures, leadership styles, culture, incentives and external environments shape the functioning of government agencies. Students will critically analyze classic and contemporary approaches to organizational design and management, including bureaucracy and collaborative public management. Discussions will include the role of management in public service and incorporating public values to foster ethical and respectful workplaces. Through case studies and applied projects, participants will develop skills to diagnose organizational challenges, foster effective behavior and lead change in a variety of public sector contexts. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to assess organizational effectiveness and implement strategies that enhance performance, accountability and public value. Prerequisites: Graduate classification; approval of MPSA director or PSAA department head.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Social Welfare and Health Policy. (3-0). Credit 3. Explores the historical development and impact of US public welfare, child welfare, employment, and health social service programs; analyzes values and assumptions that formed the foundations of social welfare policy and explores the social, economic, political, and cultural context in which these policies developed and their potential future. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Grant and Project Management in the Public and Nonprofit Sectors. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of the use and provision of grants in the public and nonprofit sectors; exploration of the conceptual background of government and private grants; the management of grants and projects; application of skills and methods related to proposal writing needs statements, program budgets and evaluations. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Decision Making in Government and Public Service. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to the study and practice of judgment and decision making processes in government and administrative settings; content is firmly grounded in empirically-based theory and research with a practical slant designed to help develop and improve decision making skills. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Health Economics and Policy. (3-0). Credit 3. Examines health care and health care markets in U.S. and abroad; topics include production of and demand for health, moral hazard and adverse selection in insurance markets, information asymmetries in physician-patient relationships, regulation and payment systems for providers, Medicare, Medicaid and other programs, and comparisons to other countries. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Energy Policy and Security. (3-0). Credit 3. Policy and economic issues related to increasing global reliance on fossil fuels, including the resulting impact on security concerns and global warming; utilizes competitive and non-competitive market theories, non-renewable resource analysis, and cost-benefit analysis. Prerequisites: Graduate classification; BUSH 621; course experience in microeconomics and quantitative modeling.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Organization Behavior for the Public Sector. (3-0). Credit 3. Theories of bureaucracy and control, management, human relations, decision making and organizations and their environments; effects of organizations on individuals, the government and the policy formation process. Prerequisites: Graduate classification and approval of MPSA or MPIA director.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Ethics and Public Policy. (3-0). Credit 3. Theory and practice for analyzing and responding to the ethical responsibilities and dilemmas for professional conduct; ethical dimensions of analysis and decision making for policy makers and public administrators. Prerequisites: Graduate classification and approval of MPSA or MPIA director.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Foundations of the Nonprofit Sector. (3-0). Credit 3. This course provides an overview of the origins, size, scope and composition of the nonprofit and voluntary sector in American society today. It introduces the historical, political, economic, social and religious foundations of the sector and examines the theoretical and conceptual frameworks that explain its roles and functions. Students explore why nonprofits exist in societies and how these organizations intersect with government and business. The course addresses contemporary issues such as volunteerism, philanthropy, values and social movements. There is no doubt that nonprofit organizations (NPOs) are an important contributor to our society, economy and government operations. This course provides public and nonprofit leaders with an orientation to the essential and distinctive characteristics of the nonprofit sector. This course explores the roles that nonprofit organizations play in American society and the public policy issues confronting nonprofits, from historical, political, economic and sociological perspectives. We will also explore contemporary public policy developments that directly relate to nonprofit organizations, such as the continued privatization of public services, nonprofit lobbying and advocacy, civic participation and civil society, foundations and the role of nonprofits in shaping public policy. Although this course largely focuses on the theoretical foundations and policy implications of developments within the sector, nonprofit management implications will be highlighted as appropriate. Prerequisites: Graduate classification; approval of MPSA director or PSAA department head.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Management and Leadership of Nonprofit Organizations. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction and overview of nonprofit organizations and the environment they operate in; examination of the distinctiveness of these organizations and the special skills required for effective management of them; empirical and normative issues surrounding nonprofit management and leadership. Prerequisites: Graduate classification; approval of MPSA director or PSAA department head.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Performance Management in the Public and Nonprofit Sectors. (3-0). Credit 3. Drawing on readings, practical exercises and guest lectures; examine public sector performance management and measurement as tools for improving strategic planning, resource allocation, organizational learning, internal operational processes, and internal and external accountability; apply learning to the development of a particular organization's performance measurement system. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Volunteer and Human Resources in Nonprofit Organizations. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduces theories, research and practice for managing personnel and human resources for paid and volunteer staff in nonprofit settings; explores the behaviors and cognitions of participants in nonprofit organizations, the motivational and personnel programs required by the organization, and the managerial strategies for effective human resources management. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Social Innovation and Entrepreneurship in Nonprofit Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Nonprofit management practices and principles related to social entrepreneurship and innovation; research, theories, and practice examples utilized to teach principles of designing and implementing a social innovation which can be applied to domestic and international social problems. Prerequisites: Graduate classification, PSAA 634 or PSAA 644 or approval of instructor.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Homeland Security and Homeland Defense. (3-0). Credit 3. Comprehensive study of the strategy, laws, doctrine and policy governing the Department of Defense's (DOD) role in its Homeland Defense mission and also the Homeland Security mission; DOD's support to other federal departments and the states under federal law such as The Stafford Act and Defense Support of Civil Authorities. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Protection of the Nation's Critical Infrastructure. (3-0). Credit 3. Survey an overview of the Nation's strategies for Critical Infrastructure Protection and securing cyberspace and the definition of critical infrastructures as it exists today; master's level course intended for individuals preparing for professional careers in the conduct of international affairs.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Weapons of Mass Destruction. (3-0). Credit 3. Comprehensive study of weapons of mass destruction and their potential use by a terrorist group; considers both political and technological issues associated with WMD terrorism; focus will be on prevention, protection, response and recovery to WMD terrorism events; intended for individuals preparing for professional careers in the conduct of international affairs.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: U.S. Border Security: Policies, Strategies and Issues. (3-0). Credit 3. U.S. border security policies, strategies and issues; policies and strategies for homeland defense and security; Mexican and Canadian governments' border policies; southern U.S. border situation and issues; considerations when border land is privately versus federally owned; impact of criminal elements on border security; efforts to secure the U.S. coasts. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Domestic Intelligence Operations: Legalities, Policies, and Procedures. (3-0). Credit 3.  Examination of laws and national policies and operations surrounding domestic intelligence within the United States; departments and agencies with domestic intelligence responsibilities, their missions, operations and resources; selected readings, government documents and case studies. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Fundamentals of Homeland Security. (3-0). Credit 3. An introduction to the theory, practice, challenge and prospects for securing the "American Homeland" against terrorist attack, with special emphasis on how American policy makers are resolving this dilemma, and their prospects for the future; draws heavily on current events and emerging policy solutions as examples. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Terrorism in Today’s World. (3-0). Credit 3. Comprehensive survey of international terrorism from its origins to the present; emphasis on how the U.S. government has responded and how it has organized to counter the threat; all major terrorist groups studied; understanding the nature of the terrorist threat and the implications for the U.S. government. Prerequisite: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with INTA 657.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Disaster Recovery and Business Continuity. (3-0). Credit 3. Comprehensive overview of disaster recovery and business continuity management; guidelines for developing, implementing, maintaining and testing local, state and federal disaster recovery and business continuity plans; public and private roles and partnerships for emergency and crisis management; continuity of operations. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Domestic Terrorism: The Internal Threat to America. (3-0). Credit 3. Survey of domestic terrorism from the first manifestation of terror tactics in the United States to the anarchist movement of the 1880s to the present; study of domestic terrorist threats, the growing threats from weapons of mass destruction, and the implications WMDs have for all levels of government. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Natural Resource Economics. (3-0). Credit 3. Critical evaluation of policies and procedures in natural resource development and use; identification of problems in resource development, the political-economic decision-making processes and analytical tools which can contribute to economic decisions. Prerequisite: ECON 323. Cross-listed with AGEC 604.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Climate and Sustainability. (3-0). Credit 3. Foundational knowledge on climate change impact, mitigation, and adaptation; emphasis on climate change risk and preparing for its negative consequences; climate action at multiple scales from local to global and by diverse actors from government, businesses, nonprofits, and communities to individuals. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of department head.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: U.S. Law and Homeland Security. (3-0). Credit 3. Analyze the threat to the homeland as reflected in a number of pre and post 9/11 commission reports; master’s level course intended for individuals preparing for professional careers in the conduct of international affairs. Prerequisite: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with INTA 612.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Public Service and Administration Capstone Seminar. (3-0). Credit 3. Provides a capstone experience for students as they operate in teams to address an important policy and administrative issue; draws on the coursework and experiences of their Bush School education to develop specific recommendations for design, implementation and evaluation of this project task. Prerequisites: Graduate classification; approval of MPSA director or PSAA department head.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Public Service and Administration Capstone Seminar II. (3-0). Credit 3. Provides a capstone experience as they operate in teams to address an important policy and administrative issue; draws on the coursework and experiences of their Bush School education to develop specific recommendations for design, implementation and evaluation of this project task. Prerequisites: PSAA 675; graduate classification; approval of MPSA director or PSAA department head.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Professional Internship. Credit 1 to 6. Directed internship in a public or private organization to provide on-the-job training with professionals in organizational settings appropriate to the student's professional objectives. Prerequisites: Graduate classification and approval of MPSA or MPIA director.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Directed Studies.  Credit 1 to 4. Directed individual instruction in selected problems in government and public service. Prerequisites: Graduate classification and approval of MPSA or MPIA director.

COLL_DESC: Bush School of Gov & Pub Serv
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of government and public service. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisites: Graduate classification and approval of MPSA or MPIA director.

COURSE_NARRATIVE: Research.  Credit 1 or more each semester. Research for thesis or dissertation.

First Year Experience. (0-0). Credit 0. Development of self-efficacy, self-awareness and a sense of purpose; active engagement in the learning environment inside and outside of the classroom; social integration within the university community. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis.

Creating with Care. (3-0). Credit 3. Foundations of care and respect in art making and creative practices; strategies for fostering inclusive and equitable performance works and workspaces; safety and consent in staging intimacy and combat on stage and screen.

SCBCRSE_TITLE: INTRO TO AI IN THE ARTS
COURSE_TITLE: INTRO TO AI IN THE ARTS
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence in the Arts. (2-2). Credit 3. Investigation of how artificial intelligence (AI) can be integrated into the creative processes; understanding the basics of AI and how these technologies can enhance and transform their artistic practice; exploration of accessible AI tools, techniques, and methodologies across various artistic fields including visual arts, music, dance, theatre, and design; hands-on exercises and projects to learn how AI can collaborate with human creativity.

Introduction to Arts in Health. (3-0). Credit 3. This course introduces the interdisciplinary field of arts in health, tracing its development from ancient healing rituals to contemporary programs in hospitals, community centers, and public health initiatives. Students will examine philosophical foundations and cross-cultural histories of healing — music, movement, storytelling, visual symbolism and performance — as well as the methodological and epistemological shifts that have brought the arts into dialogue with modern healthcare. Drawing on perspectives from performance studies, anthropology, philosophy and the health sciences, the course explores how creative practices have been used to restore balance, foster resilience and generate meaning across time and cultures, and how these practices inform today’s evidence-based models and professional standards. Through lectures, case studies, guest speakers and participatory activities, students will engage with both the enduring questions of art’s relationship to well-being and the current best practices, ethical considerations and research methods shaping the field. As the entry point for advanced courses in Arts in Health programming, interactive design and practicum experiences, this course provides students with the critical vocabulary, historical perspective and conceptual frameworks needed to engage creatively and responsibly in the design and delivery of arts-based health initiatives.

Modern American History through Popular Culture. (3-0). Credit 3. CONTENT. Exploration of American history through the perspectives of popular culture, broadly conceived, such as dance, music, fashion, print media and screen culture including but not limited to tv, film and social media; examination of how popular culture mirrors and shapes society and identity, from the personal to the national; focus on the late 19th through 21st centuries through historical sources. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. History teaches evaluation and synthesis of evidence, development of persuasive arguments in written and oral form, expansion of understandings of historical contexts that have contributed to human complexity past and present, including but not limited to the formation of group and individual identities, social and political dynamics, and debates about values and rights. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Cross-listed with HIST 227.

Archiving and Documenting the Performing and Visual Arts. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to archiving and documenting artistic processes, performances, and materials; discussion of archival and preservation principles and practices; consideration of ethical, political, and social issues in archiving and documenting the arts; examination of examples of archives and repositories related to the performing and visual arts.

School of Performance, Visualization & Fine Art Study Abroad. Credit 0 to 18. For students in approved study abroad programs participating in reciprocal educational exchange programs. Artificial Intelligence, Ethics and Social Impact in the Arts. (3-0). Credit 3. Prerequisites: PVFA 201; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Performance in Virtual and Augmented Realities. (1-6). Credit 3. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or instructor approval.

Designing Arts in Health Programs. (3-0). Credit 3. Explores the principles, practices and design of arts-based programming for health and wellness. Create, adapt and evaluate arts experiences for diverse populations, including hospitalized children, older adults in assisted living, individuals with Parkinson’s disease, people with intellectual and developmental disabilities, mental health and those with limited mobility. Design arts interventions which support emotional health, enhance memory recall, encourage social connection and foster physical benefits such as coordination, range of motion and balance. Prerequisites: PVFA 202; PHLT 336, KINE 282, KINE 223, HHUM 107, ENGL 107 or PHIL 107.

Arts in Health Practicum. (2-2). Credit 3. This course provides students with experiential learning opportunities in applied arts-in-health settings. Students will partner with local hospitals, clinics, community organizations or wellness programs to observe, assist and implement arts-based initiatives that promote health and well-being. Through guided fieldwork, reflective writing and faculty mentorship, students will explore ethical practices, program design and the impact of the arts on diverse populations. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PVFA 370, or concurrent enrollment.

Artificial Intelligence in the Arts Capstone. (1-5). Credit 3. Culminating project that emphasizes an innovative and comprehensive solution for a complex problem in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and creative work; appropriate publication and exhibition venues; development of a detailed outline of the goal and completion schedule. Prerequisites: PVFA 201 and PVFA 301; junior or senior classification or instructor approval.

Interdisciplinary Arts Practicum. Credit 1 to 3. Faculty-supervised, project-based, collaborative art making experience with artist(s) in residence. May be taken four times for credit. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Directed Studies. Credit 1 to 6. Directed studies in identified areas of performance, visualization and fine arts. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; approval of assistant dean for international programs and initiatives.

Special Topics in... Credit 0 to 4. Selected topics in an identified field of performance, visualization and fine arts. May be taken up to 9 credit hours. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; approval of assistant dean for international programs and initiatives.

Research. Credit 1 to 4. Research conducted under the direction of a faculty member in performance, visualization and fine arts. May be taken two times for credit. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; approval of assistant dean.

School of Performance, Visualization & Fine Art Study Abroad. Credit 1-16. For Graduate students in approved study abroad programs participation in reciprocal educational exchange programs. This course acts a designated placeholder course for TAMU Graduate students studying away. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisites: Admission to approved program.

Writing for Publication in the Arts. (3-0). Credit 3. Investigation of how to write and publish scholarly articles, reviews, and essays in the arts; investigation of the requirements of journals in specialization areas of the arts; overview of how to write effectively in the arts; navigation of the publishing process with understanding of the different aspects of successful publications. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

The Arts in Higher Education. (3-0). Credit 3. Discussion of the theories and principles of teaching and learning in higher education as it relates to arts education; exploration of the unique challenges and opportunities of teaching arts courses in higher education, including issues of funding, faculty workload and research in the arts, accessibility and inclusion, ethics, student engagement, and technology as it relates to arts in higher education. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Understanding Communities in the Arts. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of aesthetic, sociocultural, political, and ecological issues in creating art that engages community and affects positive change; study of exemplary artworks and creation of proposals for new ones; emphasis on creative thinking, community involvement, collaborative enterprise, research, and the creation of art works honoring aesthetic and cultural values. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Research Methods in the Arts. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of the research processes and practices and initiates students' preparation for executing scholarly research and writing; critical examination of quantitative and qualitative research; overview of how to formulate research questions, research design, data collection, and analysis. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Analyzing Research in the Arts. (3-0). Credit 3. Overview of skills and knowledge to critically analyze and evaluate research in the arts; introduction to key concepts, methods, and ethical considerations involved in analyzing arts research; examination of the role of research in the creative process and how it contributes to production and innovation; research literacy in the context of the arts. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Interdisciplinary Arts Practicum. Credit 1 to 3. Faculty-supervised, project-based, collaborative art making experience with artist(s) in residence. May be taken four times for credit. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Directed Studies. Credit 1 to 6. Individual problems involving application of theory and practice in performance, visualization and fine arts in an international setting. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisites: Approval of instructor.

Research.  Credit 1 to 4. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in reading. May be repeated two times for credit. Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor.

Foundational Skills of Decoding for Elementary Students. (3-0). Credit 3. Foundational skills of decoding including print awareness, phonological and phonemic awareness, phonics and fluency. Prerequisite: Concurrent enrollment in RDNG 373.

Literature in the Middle Grades for all Children. (3-0). Credit 3. Focuses on interdisciplinary literature appropriate for middle grades students; implements and evaluates effective interdisciplinary instruction through selection, use and development of literature reflective of a pluralistic society situated in middle grades classrooms. Prerequisite: Junior classification.

Reading and Writing across the Middle Grades Curriculum. (3-0). Credit 3. Foundational skills of both reading and writing for middle grades; includes theoretical models of reading and writing; instructing middle grade students in teaching evidence-based strategies for vocabulary development, comprehension of literary text, comprehension of informational text, writing informational and persuasive essays, science lab reports, historical perspectives, and constructed responses. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

SCBCRSE_TITLE: FND SKILLS LANG COMP ELEM STUD
COURSE_TITLE: FND SKILLS LANG COMP ELEM STUD

Foundational skills of oral language development, vocabulary development, comprehension of literary text, comprehension of informational text, and beginning strategies and reading comprehension skills. Prerequisite: Concurrent enrollment in RDNG 351.

Reading in the Middle and Secondary Grades. (3-0). Credit 3. Reading needs of middle and secondary school students with emphasis upon curriculum organization for reading development and assessment of student progress in content area reading. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; SEED minor.

Reading and the Language Arts. (2-3). Credit 3. Essential Foundations of Language and Literacy for All Learners. (3-0). Credit 3. Relationship among literacy, language, dialect and linguistics; role of the child, community and school through stages of literacy and second language learning; literacy instructional procedures for all learners including dyslexia. Prerequisite: EDUC majors.

Reading/Language Arts Methods in Middle Grades Education. (2-0). Credit 3. Prerequisite: Senior classification; admission to teacher education; concurrent enrollment in MEFB 450, MEFB 452, and RDNG 490.

Assessment in Reading Instruction. (3-0). Credit 3. Evaluation and use of commonly used achievement tests, development of criterion referenced tests and interpretation and construction of informal measures for assessing reading skills. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in RDNG 351, RDNG 373, and RDNG 468.

Assessment in Reading Instruction in Middle Grades. (2-0). Credit 3. Evaluation of middle grades students reading performance; selection, understanding, and implementation of formal and informal evaluation procedures in classroom reading assessment, diagnosis, and instruction. Prerequisite: Concurrent enrollment and grade of C or better in MEFB 452; concurrent enrollment and grade of C or better in MEFB 450 and RDNG 470, or MEFB 460 and MEFB 470; admission to teacher education; senior classification.

Research.  Credit 1 to 4. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in reading. May be repeated 2 times for credit. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.

Teaching Reading in the Elementary Grades. (3-0). Credit 3. Methods and materials of reading instruction in the elementary grades; past, present and emerging programs; organization and administration of programs and classroom management; teaching reading to special groups; issues in reading.

SCBCRSE_TITLE: ADV LIT TCH LRN ACROSS DISC
COURSE_TITLE: ADV LIT TCH LRN ACROSS DISC
COURSE_NARRATIVE: Using Advanced Literacy to Teach and Learn Across Disciplines. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of pedagogies that use literacy to help students learn across disciplines and content areas; exploration of aspects of literacy practices including reading, writing, discussion, interpretive and critical activities for the comprehension and evaluation of new content; strategies for teaching new literacies skills associated with ICT, media and visual reading; examination of theoretically grounded and empirically supported instructional methods. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

Reading Diagnosis. (2-3). Credit 3. Appraisal and diagnosis of reading problems; practicum in administration and interpretation of individual reading inventories. Prerequisites: RDNG 602 or concurrent enrollment.

Practicum in Literacy Intervention. (1-6). Credit 3. Practicum in recognition, diagnosis, remediation and corrective procedures of reading-study problems; demonstration and laboratory analysis of physiological and psychological factors related to reading disabilities. Prerequisites: RDNG 604.

Foundations of Reading Instruction. (3-0). Credit 3. Psychological, linguistic and physical factors related to reading performance; implications for content and teaching methods; appraisal of current research and related reading for teachers, supervisors and reading specialists.

Children's Literature and Literacy. (3-0). Credit 3. Critical selection and evaluation of various children's literature genres; comparative studies of children's literature; development, implementation and evaluation of research in children's literature and literacy; integration of reading and response theory into the study of literature. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Children's Literacy and Literature for all Children. (3-0). Credit 3. Analysis and evaluation of a wide range of children's and adolescent literature; development, implementation, and evaluation of research in literature and literacy for meeting the needs of all students; analysis of issues influencing literature and literacy in a pluralistic society. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Organization and Supervision of Reading Programs. (3-0). Credit 3. Prerequisites: Doctoral classification; approval of instructor.

Literacy and Language. (3-0). Credit 3. Orthography of different languages and its relation to literacy acquisition and failure to acquire basic literacy skills. This is a seminar course in reading, language arts, bilingual education, psychology, linguistics, and related fields. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Writing: Development, Assessment and Instruction. (3-0). Credit 3. Examines the nature of writing development and how to assess both formally and informally; includes successful instructional techniques based on empirical evidence. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Reading Research and Trends. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of recent research in reading; identification of trends and patterns in research designs and findings; and generation of new hypotheses and guidelines for improving current practice. Prerequisites: Doctoral classification or approval of instructor.

Theories of the Reading Process. (3-0). Credit 3. Seminar in the study and critique of major theories of the reading process that have been influential in the fields of reading, language arts, educational psychology and related fields. Prerequisite: Doctoral classification or approval of instructor.

Holy War. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE_NARRATIVE: History of Christianity I - Origins to the Reformation. (3-0). Credit 3. CONTENT. History of Christianity from its inception until the beginnings of European colonial expansion in the first half of the 16th century. Themes include the teachings of Jesus and his disciples; the growth of Christianity as it spread throughout the Mediterranean basin into Mesopotamia, Africa, Northern Europe and central Asia; variations in doctrinal development and religious practice in diverse social, political and geographical situations. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. The presentation of course content fosters critical thinking in the context of scholarly consensus and debate, rather than instructors’ views, values or beliefs. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. History teaches evaluation and synthesis of evidence, development of persuasive arguments in written and oral form, expansion of understandings of historical contexts that have contributed to human complexity past and present, including but not limited to the formation of group and individual identities, social and political dynamics, and debates about values and rights. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Cross-listed with CLAS 220 and HIST 220.

History of Islam. (3-0). Credit 3. CONTENT. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Cross-listed with HIST 221.

COURSE_NARRATIVE: History of Christianity II - Reformation to Present. (3-0). Credit 3. CONTENT. History of Christian religion from the era of the Reformation (16th century) to the present, with emphasis on social, cultural, political and economic history in relation to Christian structures and theological movements. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. The presentation of course content fosters critical thinking in the context of scholarly consensus and debate, rather than instructors’ views, values or beliefs. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Cross-listed with HIST 222.

Classical Mythology. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to the most important myths of the Greeks and Romans; ancient and modern methods of interpreting myths; the role of myths in ancient literature; readings in English. Cross-listed with CLAS 251.

Communication, Religion and the Arts. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of art and religion as forms of communication, with attention to how visual and artistic expression conveys meaning across cultures and traditions. Surveys artistic and media practices in religious and secular contexts, considering how aesthetics mediate religious experience and shape public understanding. Examines the role of art in supporting, questioning and/or challenging religious and social perspectives. Focus on interpretation and critique and dialogue of artifacts across diverse traditions, including attention to issues of pluralism, inequality, power, class and/or representation. Includes engagement with perspectives that may be unfamiliar or challenging, reflecting the diversity of voices in contemporary public life. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competence in interpreting and discussing art and religion across diverse cultural and historical contexts. Builds skills for engaging respectfully with differences in belief, practice and/or worldview. Strengthens intercultural awareness, critical thinking and creative communication skills, which can be applied to dialogue across divisions in civic, professional and interpersonal settings. Enhances understanding of how art and media shape public awareness of religion and contributes to broader conversations about meaning, identity and social conflict. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how the study of art and religion in communication differs from devotional or confessional approaches. Expands understanding of religion as a cultural and communicative practice shaped by history, power and interpretation. Highlights how art functions not only to express belief but also to question, challenge or reframe religious ideas. Introduces perspectives that encourage critical analysis of how religion and art intersect with broader cultural, social and/or political contexts. Emphasizes reflection on pluralism and contested meanings, deepening awareness of how religion and art shape, and are shaped by, the wider human experience. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication, art and religion as interrelated cultural practices; exploration of how visual and artistic forms convey meaning within Christianity, Buddhism, Islam, secular humanism and other traditions; consideration of iconoclasm, pluralism and the role of art in shaping or challenging belief and practices; attention to aesthetics, power, inequality and representation in religious and secular contexts. Course materials may also engage with the profane or the obscene when relevant to understanding how religion, art and communication define, resist and/or reframe cultural boundaries. Content may include perspectives that are unfamiliar, contested or controversial, reflecting the diversity of ways art and religion intersect in public life. Cross-listed with COMM 257.

Directed Studies. Credit 0 to 3. Readings and/or assigned projects for specific needs of students minoring in religious studies; directed independent or individual study in an identified area of religious studies. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
Special Topics in... Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of religious studies. May be repeated for credit.
Research.  Credit 0 to 3. Research conducted under the direction of a faculty member in Liberal Arts. Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor.

Asian Religions. (3-0). Credit 3. Beliefs and practices of Hinduism, Jainism, Sikhism, Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism and Shinto with particular attention to their philosophical presuppositions. Cross-listed with HUMA 304.

Contemplation in the Modern World. (3-0). Credit 3. Interdisciplinary approach to examining contemplative practices: origins in philosophy and religious traditions, goals and techniques of contemplation, contemplation in relation to cultural and social problems or needs.

Introduction to Biblical Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces students to the archaeology and material culture of the Land of the Bible from the Epi-Paleolithic period through the first century A.D. The course examines the peoples, cities and societies of biblical times through material remains, integrating artifacts, iconography and texts to develop a holistic understanding of the ancient Near East. Students explore archaeological discoveries in relation to biblical narratives, including early agricultural communities, Canaanite city-states, Egyptian influence and Iron Age polities. The course also emphasizes the interpretation of archaeological evidence, historical context and the relationship of seafaring and trade to cultural development in the ancient biblical world. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in biblical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Epi-Paleolithic period; Neolithic period; first agriculturists; Chalcolithic period; Early Bronze Age; Early Bronze IV; Middle Bronze Age I-II; Late Bronze Age; Egyptian influence in Canaan; maritime trade and seafaring; Iron Age I; Sea Peoples; Philistines; United Monarchy (Saul, David, Solomon); Divided Monarchy; Persian period; archaeology of biblical texts; material culture; urbanism; Canaanite city-states; fortifications; religious architecture; iconography; ceramics; metallurgy; inscriptions; settlement patterns; excavation techniques; interpretation of artifacts; relationship between archaeology and biblical narrative; cultural geography and human-environment interaction. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with ANTH 317.

Political Islam. (3-0). Credit 3. Study of the interaction between Islamic movements and politics in various Middle Eastern countries; examination of the role of Islam as a tool for political and social mobilization. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor; INTA majors. Cross-listed with HUMA 321 and INTA 321.

Sociology of Religion. (3-0). Credit 3. Institution of religion and religious-related behavior; relationship between dynamic and structural religion and contemporary society. Prerequisite: SOCI 205. Cross-listed with SOCI 326.

Philosophy of Religion. (3-0). Credit 3. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students engage with philosophical problems of religion and religious belief, and explore such topics as rival conceptions of ultimate reality (e.g., naturalism vs. theism), arguments for and against the existence of God, the nature of God, the problem of evil, religious experience, miracles, the afterlife, divine providence and human free will, the relation of God and morality, and science and religion. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with PHIL 331.

Rise of Islam, 600-1258. (3-0). Credit 3. CONTENT. Late-Antiquity; Pre-Islamic Arabia; the rise of Islam and a historical survey of the development of the Islamicate civilizations from c. 600 to the Mongol Conquests c. 1258. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. The presentation of course content fosters critical thinking in the context of scholarly consensus and debate, rather than instructors’ views, values or beliefs. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. History teaches evaluation and synthesis of evidence, development of persuasive arguments in written and oral form, expansion of understandings of historical contexts that have contributed to human complexity past and present, including but not limited to the formation of group and individual identities, social and political dynamics, and debates about values and rights. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with HIST 347.

Religions, Utopias, and Happiness. (3-0). Credit 3. Thematic exploration of the science of happiness; exploration and critique of self-help culture; consideration of religious contributions to happiness; evaluation of individual and collective notions of happiness. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

Ritual and Expression in Ancient Religions. (3-0). Credit 3. Expressive practices such as rituals, re-enactments, processions and dance in ancient religious traditions. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

The Bible as Literature. (3-0). Credit 3. Narrative, structural and thematic study of the Hebrew and Christian Scriptures in English translation. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with ENGL 365.

Religion in Early America. (3-0). Credit 3. Religion in North America from colonial beginnings to eve of Civil War; relations between European Christianity, Native Americans and African Americans; religious pluralism, reform movements, social and political change. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with HIST 365.

Christianity and American Identity. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of interaction of religious ideas, especially Christian, with claims and conceptions of American identity and vice-versa; themes include American founding, civil religion and Americanization. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

Religion and the Secular. (3-0). Credit 3. Methods and approaches to inquiries in the study of religion; historical and contemporary topics and issues in the study of religion; analysis of artifacts, documents and primary sources; current scholarship in the study of religion. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Studies in Literature, Religion and Culture. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of literature treating significant religious topics in the context of cultural setting. Features topics such as writing as a spiritual practice, religious autobiography and memoir, poetry and rhetoric as a mode of religious inquiry. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken two times for credit. Prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above; junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with ENGL 392.

Anthropology of Religion. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Applies fundamental principles of cultural anthropology (the study of human variation and commonalities using a holistic mindset) to the analysis of religion. Examines the relationships connecting religion, culture, society and the individual through cross-cultural, theoretical analysis of religion as a cultural phenomenon. Investigates core questions regarding the existence and persistence of religion, analyzing how religious behavior manifests and connects with other cultural elements across diverse global settings. Develops skills to critically assess research findings, analyze differing viewpoints and perspectives and formulate hypothetical research agendas. Engages potentially charged topics in diverse settings, challenging students to explore their own assumptions and biases regarding their personal worldview. Fosters greater understanding of self-awareness and personal responsibility in society through exploration of the diversity of religious behaviors. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers theoretical approaches to the study of religion; analyzes religious features including symbolism, myth and ritual; studies religious specialists, magic, divination and witchcraft; explores altered states of consciousness; evaluates beliefs regarding gods, spirits, souls, ghosts and death; assesses religious change and searches for new meaning; examines religious violence and fundamentalism; and investigates vernacular religion, secularism, atheism and irreligion. Includes analysis of religious practices, beliefs and institutions from a variety of cultures. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus. Cross-listed with ANTH 403.

Intellectual History, 500 to 1600. (3-0). Credit 3. Political, social, cultural and religious histories of significant figures, groups, schools of thought and movements in western Afro-Eurasia from the rise of Islam to the Renaissance; developments in political theory, literature, sociology, arts, architecture, music, philosophy, law, sciences and education. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with HIST 419.

Nature, Sustainability and Religion. (3-0). Credit 3. Interaction between religion and the environment; examination of religious traditions and their concepts of the natural world; emphasis on cultural contexts and environmental sustainability. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

The Sacred and Profane in History. (3-0). Credit 3. Case studies of the sacred in varied times and regions; holy persons; holy places; holy objects; language and literature of the sacred; competing concepts of the holy within society; gender and the holy; institutions promoting holy people and places; the impact of social, political, cultural and intellectual developments on the relationship between the sacred and the profane. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with HIST 425.

African American Muslim Culture. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of popular culture and its impact on African American Muslims' intersectional identity formation and faith tradition through films, documentaries, readings, and lectures on and about Muslims emanating from enslaved narratives and the colonial period to the contemporary era. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with AFST 430.

Ancient Egypt I - The Rise of Egypt. (3-0). Credit 3. Archaeology and history of ancient Egypt from earliest times to the end of the New Kingdom period. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with ANTH 436.

Ancient Egypt II - Egypt in Decline. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology and history of ancient Egypt from the end of the New Kingdom through the Graeco-Roman period, focusing on the years 1185–30 BCE. Examines the decline of pharaonic power, the rise of foreign influences and the resilience of Egyptian society under Libyan, Nubian, Persian and Ptolemaic rule. Reviews the interplay between political, social and cultural dynamics, exploring Egyptian adaptations to Hellenistic dominance, while tracing continuity and change in art, religion, literature and urban development. Through lectures, readings and analyses of primary and secondary sources, students gain a humanistic understanding of Egyptian civilization during its final dynastic phases and develop skills in interpreting archaeological, textual and iconographic evidence. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues pertaining to ancient Egypt. TOPICS AND THEMES. Decline of pharaonic authority; fragmentation of the Egyptian state; Libyan, Nubian and Persian interventions; internal political strife and social change; resilience of Egyptian cultural identity; Ptolemaic dynasty and Hellenistic influence; Cleopatra VII and the last Ptolemies; Alexandria as a cultural and economic center; Greco-Egyptian art, religion and literature; continuity and transformation of Egyptian traditions; interactions between foreign rulers and Egyptian elites; archaeological and textual methods for reconstructing late Egyptian history; humanistic approaches to interpreting material culture; synthesis of historical, artistic and archaeological evidence. Prerequisites: Completion of ANTH 436 or RELS 436 recommended but not required; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with ANTH 438.

Civics After the Holocaust. (3-0). Credit 3. Analysis of the Holocaust as a challenge to previous theories of civics and civic engagement; investigation of theories developed in response to the Holocaust; exploration of comparisons of historical events following the Second World War to the Holocaust. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with JWST 465.

Religious Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the role of religious communication in shaping public life through speeches, sermons, debates, campaigns and/or social movements. Considers how religious language, symbols and/or narratives influence cultural identity, moral reasoning and/or collective action. Surveys diverse approaches to studying religious communication, from historical traditions to contemporary debates, highlighting how meaning is constructed, contested and transformed in religious discourse. Considers interpretations of religious communication from multiple perspectives, fostering critical thinking. Explores a diverse range of scholarly frameworks, theories and methods employed in the academic study of religion and religious communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens transferable skills in critical thinking, interpretation and evaluation of persuasive messages in contexts ranging from personal dialogue to civic engagement. Enhances adaptability across diverse religious and cultural frameworks. Supports academic preparation for analyzing communication at the intersection of religion, culture and public life. Engages skills applicable to leadership, education, public study of advocacy and professional fields, when understanding religious perspectives and their influence is relevant. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how religious communication functions not only as a vehicle of belief but also as a force shaping history, politics and/or social change. Provides reflection on ways speeches, symbols and/or campaigns can both unite and divide, reinforcing traditions or sparking transformation. Provides frameworks for critical analysis of religious discourse from first-person and third-person perspectives. Highlights the interpretive challenges posed by pluralism, competing meanings and differing assumptions about authority, sacredness and public expression. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of religious speeches and sermons; debates over doctrine and belief; campaigns and movements shaped by religious rhetoric; analysis of religious symbolism and storytelling; exploration of the role of communication in sustaining or challenging religious traditions. Course materials may address diverse and sometimes controversial perspectives, reflecting the ways religious communication has influenced cultural identity, social conflict and civic life across history. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with COMM 480.

Advanced Seminar in Religious Studies. (3-0). Credit 3. Intensive reading, study and discussion of topics in religious studies; interdisciplinary methods. May be taken four times for credit. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

Internship. Credit 0 to 4. Directed internship in a public or private organization to provide students with applied experience; opportunity to observe first hand issues and problems covered in religious studies courses; designed to enhance and clarify the student's career objectives. May be taken for credit up to six hours. Prerequisites: Approval of instructor.

Prerequisites: Enrollment in Professional Event Manager certificate; grade of C or better in HMGT 211 and HMGT 320; grade of C or better in RPTS 321 or concurrent enrollment.

Analytic Techniques in Recreation, Parks and Tourism. (3-0). Credit 3. Analysis of current research; instruments and analytic techniques used in the selection and formulation of research problems. Prerequisite: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with ALEC 672.

Youth Development Programs and Services. (3-0). Credit 3. Principles and practices of youth development supports, opportunities, programs and services; emphasis on the role of out-of-school time settings in youth development; programming considerations related to gender, disability and culture; introduction to evaluation and financing of youth development programs. Prerequisite: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with ALEC 670.

Practice and Development of Effective Skills for Youth Development. (3-0). Credit 3. Development of skills and competencies needed to successfully manage paid and volunteer staff, design youth programs, address safety and risk management issues; build community support of public, non-profit, and for profit or commercial youth programs and agencies; history and scope of youth serving organizations; programming and staffing strategies; managing, mentoring and training staff; diverse approaches to program curriculum and design; behavior management and recognition of youth participants; youth protection; relevant laws and legal mandates; safety, health and wellness; youth advocacy and engagement; working with parents and community partners; and issues and innovations in youth development. Prerequisite: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with ALEC 671.

COURSE_NARRATIVE: Grant Writing and Program Evaluation for Youth Development Organizations. (3-0). Credit 3.
