Exposure to scientists from a variety of biomedical disciplines through attendance at seminars followed by review and discussion of current scientific work in physiology and related subjects, and subsequent student seminar presentations. Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification; approval of instructor.

Directed Studies.  Credit 0 to 4. Course for freshman and sophomore students who desire additional laboratory work in physiology to supplement required courses. Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification; approval of department head.
Special Topics in... Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of veterinary physiology and pharmacology. May be repeated for credit.

Research.  Credit 0 to 4. Laboratory and/or field research supervised by a faculty member. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification; approval of instructor.

Physiology of Domestic Animals. (3-0). Credit 3. Physiology essential to the understanding of life processes; for animal science, wildlife, agriculture and related fields. Prerequisite: BIOL 111 or equivalent; junior or senior classification.

Biomedical Toxicology. (3-0). Credit 3. Understanding basic toxicologic concepts related to exposure, absorption and elimination of toxic compounds as well as mechanisms of action of toxicants and how they affect the body's organ systems; integration of toxicology with pharmacology and physiology to further understand how various toxicants impact on the body. Prerequisites: VIBS 222 or BIOL 319 or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

History of Human and Veterinary Medicine in Europe. (4-0). Credit 4. Addresses the major developments in human and veterinary medicine in Europe from the Middle Ages to the present; explores key events and figures in medical history and analyzes issues of current biomedical concern in a historical context; for example, animal rights, ethics of humane experimentation, euthanasia. Prerequisites: Admitted to major degree sequence in biomedical engineering; VTPP 434. Cross-listed with BMEN 400.

Food Toxicology and Safety. (3-0). Credit 3. Toxicity and safety of various foods and food additives, ingredients, and contaminants; occurrence, control and prevention of food transmitted diseases. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Systemic Veterinary Physiology. (3-0). Credit 3. Aspects of cellular physiology, physiology of excitable membranes, physiology of body fluids, neurophysiology, and the physiology of smooth, cardiac and skeletal muscle; basic understanding of mammalian physiology essential as a framework for advanced studies. Prerequisites: BIMS 320; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor; proper English composition and communication.

Applied Biomedical Physiology. (3-0). Credit 3. Physiological principles, review of cellular physiology, and development of understanding the nervous system and muscle, cardiovascular, and respiratory physiology; clinical applications related to organ systems. Prerequisites: BIOL 320; junior or senior classification.

Applied Pharmacology. (2-0). Credit 2. Modern themes about therapeutic drugs in animals and people including drug discovery and development, clinical use of drugs and drug regulation. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in BICH 410, BIOL 320, VTPP 423, VTPP 434, or approval of instructor.

Applied Biomedical Physiology I. (3-2). Credit 4. Human physiological principles, review of cellular physiology and development of an understanding of the nervous system and muscle, cardiovascular and renal physiology; clinical applications related to organ systems. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; VIBS 446, VIBS 402 or BIMS 402, or approval of instructor.

Biomedical Neuroendocrinology and Endocrine Disorders. (3-0). Credit 3. Neuroendocrine (hypothalamus-pituitary) control of puberty, menstruation, ovulation, pregnancy, labor, lactation, female reproductive cycles, male reproductive functions, thyroid and parathyroid, adrenal and kidney, diabetes, obesity, sleep, memory, learning and aging and their endocrine disorders; overview on biosynthesis, transport and signaling of peptide and neuropeptide hormones, steroids and prostaglandins. Prerequisites: Honors, junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with VIBS 424.

Pharmacology. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics; survey of major pharmaceutical classes; uses, mechanisms of action and adverse reactions of selected agents. Prerequisites: VTPP 423 or grade of C or better in BIOL 320; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Applied Biomedical Physiology II. (3-0). Credit 3. Human physiology focused on fluid balance and acid-base balance; development of an understanding of physiology as it applies to the cardiovascular, autonomic, renal, respiratory, gastrointestinal, endocrine, reproductive system; clinical applications related to organ systems. Prerequisites: VTPP 423 or grade of D or better in BIOL 320; junior or senior classification.

Physiology for Bioengineers I. (3-2). Credit 4. Engineering analysis of living systems; quantitative aspects of physiology and engineering applications to clinical medicine; body fluid balance, solute transport, endocrinology, reproduction physiology, neurophysiology, skeletal and smooth muscle physiology. Prerequisite: Biomedical engineering (BMEN) major or approval of instructor.

Physiology for Bioengineers II. (3-2). Credit 4. Engineering analysis of living systems; quantitative aspects of physiology and engineering applications to clinical medicine; vascular physiology, cardiac physiology, bone physiology, regenerative medicine, renal physiology, pathophysiology. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in VTPP 434 or approval of instructor.

Analysis of Genomic Signals. (2-2). Credit 3. Overview of current high throughput technology for data acquisition and analysis of genomic signals (e.g. mRNA or proteins); emphasis on the microarray technology, methods for analyzing microarray data, and approaches to model the underlying phenomena from the systems biology perspective. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; BIMS 320 or GENE 320 and BIOL 111, BIOL 112 or BIOL 213 or equivalent; STAT 302 or equivalent.

Practicum in Biomedical Research. Credit 3. Team or group development of sustainable collaborations that include biomedical research, high-impact educational practices and community service; emphasis on lifelong learning and the impact of research on biomedical issues and physiology; focus on connecting research experience to future career goals. Prerequisites: VTPP 223 and VTPP 224, or VTPP 234 and VTPP 235, or VTPP 232 and VTPP 233, or VTPP 207 and VTPP 208; junior or senior classification; instructor approval.

Fetal and Embryo Physiology. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of the physiologic processes driving embryonic development and pregnancy; focus on embryo implantation, establishment of the placenta, development of the fetal circulatory systems and the molecular processes governing embryo differentiation and development; special emphasis on the major organ systems affected by pediatric disease and on the actions of teratogens. Prerequisites: BICH 409, BICH 410, or equivalent; or approval of instructor.

Gamete and Embryo Physiology. (2-3). Credit 3. Physiology of gametes and preimplantation embryos in livestock and laboratory animals; oocyte growth and maturation in-vivo and in-vitro, fertilization in-vivo and in-vitro, embryo transfer, cryopreservation, nuclear transfer, chimera formation, gene transfer. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; grade of C or better in BIOL 319 or VTPP 413, or equivalent; or approval of instructor.

Seminar.  Credit 1 to 4. Exposure to scientists from a variety of biomedical disciplines through attendance at seminars followed by review and discussion of current scientific work in physiology and related subjects, and subsequent student seminar presentations. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; approval of instructor.

Directed Studies. Credit 0 to 4. Course for junior and senior students who desire additional laboratory work in physiology to supplement required courses. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of department head.

Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of physiology, pharmacology, endocrinology or toxicology. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
Research.  Credit 0 to 4. Laboratory and/or field research supervised by a faculty member. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; approval of instructor.

Systemic Physiology I. (3-0). Credit 3. Aspects of cellular physiology, physiology of excitable membranes, physiology of body fluids, neurophysiology, and the physiology of smooth, cardiac and skeletal muscle; provides a basic understanding of mammalian physiology essential as a framework for advanced graduate studies. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Physiology I. (1-0). Credit 1. Basic cellular physiology for continued exploration into human and animal physiology; excitatory membranes, regulation of homeostasis, body fluid maintenance. May be repeated four times for credit. Prerequisites: Graduate classification in the life sciences; approval of instructor.

Physiology II. (1-0). Credit 1. In depth study of mammalian physiology, covering the endocrine, reproductive and developmental systems; molecular, cellular and hormonal regulation of various body functions, including metabolism, reproduction and tissue regeneration. Topics include but are not limited to hypothalamic-pituitary axes, gametogenesis and the principles of regenerative medicine. This course is offered in multiple sections taught by different instructors; students enroll in one section of their choice. May be taken three times for credit. Prerequisites: VTPP 610; graduate classification in the life sciences; approval of instructor.

Food Toxicology II. (3-0). Credit 3. Public health implications of toxic factors in foods, their source, nature, occurrence and distributions; emphasis on mycotoxins including their isolation, detection, identification and toxicology; study of state-of-the-art food safety research techniques. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

Pharmacology. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics; survey of major pharmaceutical classes; uses, mechanisms of action and adverse reactions of selected agents. Prerequisites: Graduate classification; VTPP 423 or approval of instructor.

Analysis of Genomic Signals. (2-2). Credit 3. Overview of current high throughput technology for data acquisition and analysis of genomic signals (e.g., mRNA or proteins); emphasis on microarray technology, methods for analyzing microarray data, and approaches to model the underlying phenomena from the systems biology perspective. Prerequisites: BIOL 451 or GENE 320/BIMS 320 or equivalent; STAT 651 or equivalent; or approval of instructor.

Principles of Human Health Risk Assessment of Chemicals. (3-0). Credit 3. Principles of toxicology and environmental health with the basic concepts and approaches for conducting human health risk assessment of chemicals; use of different types of data and analysis approaches to conduct both qualitative and quantitative assessments of exposure, human health hazard, dose-response, and risk from chemicals in the environment; introduction to how risk assessment informs risk management decisions such as pollution regulations or hazardous waste cleanups. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

COURSE_TITLE: PRAC EVAL HUMAN HLTH RSKS CHEM
COURSE_NARRATIVE:
Practice of Evaluating Human Health Risks of Chemicals. (2-0). Credit 2. Basic principles of toxicology and environmental health with real-life examples of how diverse types of information are integrated for the purpose of judging what chemical exposures may pose a risk to human health.
Prerequisites: BICH 601, BICH 602, VTPP 625, or similar; VTPP 673, VTPP 670 or similar; and VIBS 641 or approval of instructor.

Fetal and Embryo Physiology. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to the physiologic processes driving embryonic development and pregnancy; focus on fertility, contraception and pregnancy loss; embryo implantation, establishment of the placenta, development of the fetal reproductive, neurological and circulatory systems; the molecular processes governing embryo differentiation and teratogenic outcomes; emphasis on the major organ systems affected by pediatric disease and birth defects. Prerequisites: Graduate classification in the life sciences.

Vascular Physiology. (4-0). Credit 4. Structure and function of blood vessels and vascular beds; molecular and cell biology of endothelium and vascular smooth muscle; microcirculation; capillary exchange; regulation of blood flow by local, neural and humoral signals. Prerequisite: MPHY 901 or approval of department head.

Gamete and Embryo Physiology. (2-3). Credit 3. Physiology of gametes and preimplantation embryos in livestock and laboratory animals; oocyte growth and maturation in-vivo and in-vitro, fertilization in-vivo and in-vitro, embryo transfer, cryopreservation, nuclear transfer, chimera formation, gene transfer. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

Advanced Toxicology. (3-0). Credit 3. Detailed overview of organ-specific effects of toxic substances, organ/tissue-oriented modules that will review basic anatomy and physiology, site-specific metabolism of xenobiotics, mechanisms of toxicity and experimental systems that are used to study toxic effects. Prerequisites: BICH 601, BICH 602, VTPP 625, or equivalent; VTPP 673 or equivalent; or approval of instructor.

Metabolic and Detoxication Mechanisms. (3-0). Credit 3. Fate of foreign compounds; their inhibitory and antagonistic action toward normal metabolic processes of the animal body. Prerequisites: BICH 603; approval of instructor and department head.

Genetic and Molecular Toxicology. (3-0). Credit 3. Mechanisms of toxicant-induced target organ toxicity with emphasis on molecular control of mammalian and cell growth differentiation. Prerequisite: Graduate course in cell biology and biochemistry.
Seminar. (1-0). Credit 1. Review and discussion of current scientific work in physiology and related subjects. Prerequisite: Approval of department head.

Professional Internship. Credit 1 to 4. A directed internship in an organization to provide students with on-the-job training with professionals in settings appropriate to the student's professional objectives. May be taken three times for credit. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisite: Graduate classification and approval of committee chair.
Directed Studies.  Credit 1 to 4 each semester. Problems in physiology, pharmacology or toxicology. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of veterinary physiology and pharmacology. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Research.  Credit 1 or more each semester. Original investigations in veterinary physiology, pharmacology or toxicology to be submitted by writing of thesis or dissertation as partial fulfillment for MS or PhD degree. Prerequisite: Approval of department head.

Physiology I. (5-2). Credit 6. Introduction to physiology: cell physiology, cell signaling, cell cycle, body fluids, translocation of materials, membrane potentials, neurophysiology, autonomic nervous system, thermoregulation, cardiovascular, and muscle physiology. Prerequisite: Enrollment in first year of professional curriculum.

Physiology II. (4-2). Credit 5. Respiration, renal physiology, acid-base physiology, reproductive physiology and gastrointestinal physiology. Prerequisites: Enrollment in the first year of professional DVM curriculum.

Professional & Clinical Skills I. (1-6). Credit 3.  Integration and reinforcement of foundational knowledge offered in concurrent courses through critical thinking exercises, professional skills application activities (ethics/contextual decision-making, leadership, skills for well-being, personal/practice financial literacy, core communication skills) and application of technical skills; opportunities for learning include didactic, hands-on and case-based interactions utilizing simulation, models, animals, actors and case scenarios; part I of a VI part series. Prerequisite:Enrollment in the first year of professional DVM curriculum.

Pharmacology. Credit 3 to 5. Drug disposition, pharmacodynamics, drug regulations, critical appraisal of evidence about use of drugs, drugs that affect respiratory, reproductive, gastrointestinal, endocrine, immune, urinary, integumentary, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, and nervous systems, and drugs for pain, anti-inflammatories, antineoplastics, antibiotics, and other antiinfectives in animals. Prerequisite: Enrollment in the second year of professional DVM curriculum.

Didactic Elective in Veterinary Physiology and Pharmacology.  Credit 1 to 12. Elective course in physiology and pharmacology for professional students who wish to supplement required curriculum. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Enrollment in the fourth year of professional curriculum.

Introduction to Women's and Gender Studies. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. This course explores the core concepts of the interdisciplinary field of women’s and gender studies, focusing on various perspectives, scholarship, theories and histories of sex, gender and sexuality; examines theories of intersectionality, analyzing the interplay among race/racism, class/classism, sex/sexism, disability/ableism, nation/nationalism, religion/religious bias among other factors in gendered experiences and systems; surveys feminist, queer, anti-racist, decolonial and/or global scholarship that examines how social institutions and control mechanisms enact power, privilege and bias; engages controversial material and historical and/or contemporary case studies that challenge and/or support conventional understandings of gender, sex, sexuality, identity and power as necessary to achieve course learning outcomes and proficiency in disciplinary concepts and ideas. TOPICS. Course may include and is not limited to discussions and descriptions of violence, sexual assault, homophobia, transphobia, femicide, genocide, familial/domestic abuse, forced sterilization and workplace harassment; investigations of political controversies centered on reproductive and gender healthcare, gender identity, policing and/or immigration; analysis of popular culture and creative expression, including but not limited to: performance, literature, drag, music, visual culture; examinations of primary texts from historical and/or contemporary social movements and activists across the United States and around the globe; investigations of contemporary and historical labor relations and globalization; analyses and descriptions of anatomy, physiology and psychology. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship, instructor expertise, and satisfy course learning objectives.

Introduction to Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Studies. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. This course is an interdisciplinary survey of the histories and theories regarding lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer (LGBTQ+) identities and communities. The course focuses on current scholarship addressing the social construction of sex, sexuality and gender; institutional ways in which homophobia, biphobia and transphobia are systematically deployed; histories and examples of LGBTQ+ activism; evolution of desire and subjectivity; and the contributions of queer scholarship in understanding society. TOPICS. Course may include but is not limited to discussions and readings that address queer approaches to institutions; intersections of sexual and gender identity with race, class, ability/disability and/or nationality; digital activism; gender violence; controversies related to LGBTQ+ issues and politics, among others. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship, instructor expertise, and satisfy course learning objectives. Cross-listed with SOCI 215.

Introduction to Gender and Society. (3-0). Credit 3. Explore the historical, cultural, social, economic and political dimensions of gender; define and distinguish gender roles and norms and identify sociological theories important to the study of gender; examine ideas and expectations about gender including historical and contemporary norms; understanding of scholarship on this topic increases intercultural competence and effective cross-cultural communication for participation in civic contexts and public life. In line with the American Sociological Association, sociology is the study of social life, social change and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations and societies and how people interact within these contexts. Since all human behavior is social, the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to global communities; from deviance to organized crime; from religious traditions to state institutions; and from the divisions of race, gender and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture. The specific topics and readings assigned may vary depending on the instructor’s areas of focus and research expertise. Cross-listed with SOCI 207.

Psychological Aspects of Human Sexuality. (3-0). Credit 3. Examine human sexuality through biological, psychological, social, relational and cultural lenses. Analyze reproductive anatomy, gender roles, sexual identity, sexual orientation and sexual behavior across the lifespan. Explore topics including love, attraction, sexual health, sexual victimization, diversity and sexuality as a commodity. Apply the bio-psycho-social-cultural model to understand how various factors shape sexual experiences and attitudes. Develop skills to assess sexual health, promote well-being and articulate what healthy sexuality means. Prerequisite: PBSI 107. Cross-listed with PBSI 210.

Gender and Health. (3-0). Credit 3. Examines the social and historical context of American health care and health professions and develops analytical and professional skills, especially for those seeking work in nursing, medicine and/or health care; analyzes peer-reviewed research on women’s health disparities; emphasizes professional communication of evidence in discussions and presentations, builds empirical and quantitative skills to analyze health datasets; considers ethical dimensions and community contexts while encouraging students to consider a range of perspectives and experiences while providing an understanding of how gender and health intertwine within a societal context. In line with the American Sociological Association, sociology is the study of social life, social change and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations and societies and how people interact within these contexts. Since all human behavior is social, the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to global communities; from deviance to organized crime; from religious traditions to state institutions; and from the divisions of race, gender and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture. The specific topics and readings assigned may vary depending on the instructor’s areas of focus and research expertise. Cross-listed with SOCI 213.

Feminist Approaches to Science, Technology, and Medicine. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to selected topics about gender and the history of science; focus on feminist critique of science, technology, and medicine; exploration of the connections between the biomedical sciences and the politics of gender and sexuality in a global context. Cross-listed with GLST 220.
Directed Studies.  Credit 0 to 3. Readings and/or research for specific needs of students majoring or minoring in women's and gender studies. Prerequisites: WGST 200 and approval of instructor.
Special Topics in...   Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of women's/gender studies. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of director.

Research. Credit 0 to 3. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in women's and gender studies. May be taken four times for credit. Prerequisites: WGST 200; freshman or sophomore classification; and approval of instructor.

Psychology of Women. (3-0). Credit 3. Examine the psychological experiences of women across the lifespan through feminist, developmental and intersectional frameworks. Analyze how social, cultural, biological and psychological factors shape women’s roles and identities in diverse contexts. Explore key topics including gender development, media representation, sexual and reproductive health, cognitive and emotional functioning, work-family dynamics and mental and physical health. Investigate how intersecting identities—such as race, class, and disability—impact access, opportunity and psychological well-being. Strengthen critical thinking and apply evidence-based insights to real-world issues affecting women. Prerequisite: PBSI 107. Cross-listed with PBSI 300.

Sociology of Marriage and Family. (3-0). Credit 3. Explore family life and contemporary family issues and debates, developing practical skills in critical analysis, communication and sociological evaluation that are used in related professional contexts, especially for fields such as counseling, law and law enforcement, public policy and health care; explore diverse family experiences, historical and contemporary norms, and public attitudes toward family structures; apply sociological approaches and research to analyze family forms, functions, processes related to inequality and the dynamics of interaction; evaluate sociological research methodologies and ethical considerations to assess evidence and policy debates; through the examination of themes like love, marriage and conflict, alongside the critical implications of family changes, develop an evidence-based understanding of the complexities and variation present in contemporary U.S. families. In line with the American Sociological Association, sociology is the study of social life, social change and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations and societies and how people interact within these contexts. Since all human behavior is social, the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to global communities; from deviance to organized crime; from religious traditions to state institutions; and from the divisions of race, gender and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture. The specific topics and readings assigned may vary depending on the instructor’s areas of focus and research expertise. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with SOCI 315.

Sociology of Gender. (3-0). Credit 3. An exploration of social construction of gender from a sociological lens, including understanding how social norms, social institutions and social processes are shaped by gendered meanings and contestations. Use empirical and theoretical research to investigate the roles of gender across social institutions such as family, state, law, marriage, nation and others. Also explores how gender intersects with other aspects of social identity such as race, class and citizenship. Students will learn to apply gender theories and empirical research to analyze current social issues and debates, both locally and globally. By the end of the course, students will be able to evaluate how gender shapes outcomes and how research explains change. In line with the American Sociological Association, sociology is the study of social life, social change and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations and societies and how people interact within these contexts. Since all human behavior is social, the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to global communities; from deviance to organized crime; from religious traditions to state institutions; and from the divisions of race, gender and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture. The specific topics and readings assigned may vary depending on the instructor’s areas of focus and research expertise. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with SOCI 316.

Work, Family and Public Policy. (3-0). Credit 3. Analysis of how work, family and public policy interact to shape labor market outcomes and inequality; theories and evidence on labor supply, human capital formation and earnings differences; effects of family structure, workplace flexibility and government policies on employment and wages; explanations and empirical measurement of discrimination; emphasizes the use of quantitative methods to evaluate costs and benefits of policies addressing inequality in the United States and abroad. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECON 323 or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with ECON 318.

Feminist Inquiry and Research Methods. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. This course is an interdisciplinary exploration of feminist research methods and inquiry in the humanities, social sciences and sciences. It explores ethical approaches to feminist research, feminist understandings of epistemology and feminist research design. TOPICS. Course may include but is not limited to discussions and readings about standpoint epistemology; poststructuralist, decolonial, feminist and queer approaches to research; and feminist science studies. Examples of feminist research discussed in class may focus on constructions of sex, gender, and sexuality, race/racism and other topics of contemporary relevance. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and instructor expertise and satisfy course learning objectives. Prerequisites: WGST 200.

Women in Ancient Greece and Rome. (3-0). Credit 3. Survey of women in classical Greece and Rome; emphases on female occupations and family relationships, legal and political status, traditional values, notorious women, how women were viewed and how they viewed themselves. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with CLAS 330 and HIST 330.

Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Literatures. (3-0). Credit 3. LGBTQ texts studied in their cross-cultural, historical, political contexts. Topics may include but are not limited to studies in camp, authorship, (mis)representations in popular culture, the closet and queer coding, queer visual and performance cultures; race, sex, empire. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with ENGL 333.

Women's Health. (3-0). Credit 3. A broad range of health issues that are either unique to women or of special importance to women; information for the health consumer; preparation as an advocate of healthy lifestyles; awareness of the role health plays in the life of all women. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with HLTH 334 and PHLT 360.

The Rhetoric of Gender and Health. (3-0). Credit 3. Study of field of rhetoric of health and medicine with specific attention to the study of gender, including issues in reproduction, expertise and illness; range of methods and methodological approaches within the field. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with ENGL 342.

Sex, Gender and Cinema. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of a significant topic at the intersection of women's/gender studies and film, such as cinema and sexuality studies, cinema and women, and cinema and masculinity; may include discussion of production, film content, and/or reception. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with FILM 343.

Women in Government in Comparative Perspective. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of women's representation in government based on comparison across multiple nation-states; focus on legislative and executive branches of democratic governments. Prerequisites: POLS 206; junior or senior classification or approval of department head. Cross-listed with POLS 367.

Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Queer Authorship. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of LGBTQ+ authorship through film and literary criticism and theories of performing the self in the act of authoring. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with ENGL 369.

COURSE_NARRATIVE: Women Writers. (3-0). Credit 3. Writings by women in English, with emphasis on issues pertaining to women’s experiences and on their literary contributions in a variety of genres. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; ENGL-374 also taught at Galveston campus. Cross-listed with ENGL 374.

Africana Women's History. (3-0). Credit 3. Black women’s history from the precolonial era to the present; emphasis on the cultural, political, legal, economic, sexual, social, and religious factors that shaped their experiences across the African Diaspora and the world. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with AFST 377 and HIST 377.

Gender and Genre. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration and analysis of the ways in which a single literary and/or film genre resonates with gendered perspectives and sexual subjectivity. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; WGST 200 or FILM 251 or ENGL 251.

Feminist Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. This course is an inquiry-based examination of feminist theory from various disciplinary perspectives, with application to past and current cultural and societal debates and controversies. Disciplinary approaches may include those from sociology, cultural anthropology, political science, rhetoric, philosophy, science studies, literary studies, legal studies, performance studies, history, visual culture and media studies, among others. TOPICS. Course may include discussions and readings related to intersectionality, traditions and genealogies of feminism, gender-based violence, performativity, domesticity, labor, Marxism, colonialism/postcolonialism/decolonialism, global capitalism, gender, sexuality and feminist and/or queer social movements, among others. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship, instructor expertise, and satisfy course learning objectives. Prerequisites: WGST 200 or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

Gender, Race and Media. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how gender, race, sexuality, ethnicity and related identities are produced, represented, negotiated, contested, consumed and/or performed in relation to media. Explores contributions of historically marginalized groups to media production, alongside analysis of how these groups have been portrayed as characters, audiences, communities and/or target markets. Focuses on media as a site of competing commercial, cultural, political, satirical and/or resistance narratives, rather than as a single, unified voice. Emphasizes critical interpretation of media texts and systems, while allowing space for multiple viewpoints and interpretations. Course material may include historical and contemporary examples that reflect both progress and controversy, analyzed for their cultural and communicative significance. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages issues central to media literacy, political economy, representation and audience awareness in contemporary communication industries. Builds recognition of the ways portrayals of gender and race shape perception, credibility and/or trust in journalism, entertainment, advertising, representatives, community and public communication. Supports careers in communication, media industries, public relations, education, nonprofit work and leadership roles where navigating diverse audiences is essential. Supports informed decision-making in professional and civic contexts by highlighting how media representations influence identity, inclusion and public dialogue. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies that studying media portrayals of gender and race is not limited to celebration or criticism but involves examining how representation functions within broader cultural, social, economic, political and/or institutional systems. Illustrates how media are grounded in economies of production, representation and consumption across platforms, products and pipelines. Considers ways media might be empowering, stereotypical, commercial and/or transformative, depending on context, audience and community. Promotes awareness that interpretations of media content may differ across social, cultural and/or generational perspectives and that disagreement over meaning is part of scholarly analysis rather than a flaw in the material. Normalizes engagement with sensitive or contested topics as a means of understanding how media both reflect and shape public life. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of media across film, television, news, advertising, music and digital platforms through production, representation and consumption; analysis of gender, race, ethnicity and intersectional identities in historical and contemporary contexts; consideration of media production practices, audience reception and the economic and institutional forces shaping representation; examination of stereotypes, invisibility, empowerment narratives and commercialized identity; discussion of how media both reinforce and challenge social norms related to power, privilege and belonging. Course material may include content that reflects real-world disparities or conflicting viewpoints. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with COMM 407.

Reproduction and Birth. (3-0). Credit 3. This course examines topics related to reproductive practices and experiences and of the meanings surrounding womanhood, motherhood and reproduction. CONTENT STATEMENT. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship in this field and satisfy course learning objectives. In line with the American Sociological Association, sociology is the study of social life, social change and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations and societies and how people interact within these contexts. Since all human behavior is social, the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to global communities; from deviance to organized crime; from religious traditions to state institutions; and from the divisions of race, gender and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture. The specific topics and readings assigned may vary depending on the instructor’s areas of focus and research expertise. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with SOCI 410.

Representations of Motherhood. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of motherhood as a cultural, social and communicative construct rather than a singular biological or personal identity. Examines how ideas about motherhood are created, reinforced or challenged through literature, film, popular media, digital media, political rhetoric, public policy, advertising, news, medical institutions and/or everyday discourse across different time periods and cultural contexts. Considers both idealized and marginalized portrayals, attending to such matters as gender, race, class, sexuality, ability and nation. Course material may include historical texts, contemporary examples, commentary and/or fictional representations. Content may include portrayals that are celebratory, critical or controversial, examined for purposes of interpretation. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds critical literacy for analyzing how cultural expectations shape perceptions of family, caregiving and social roles. Promotes awareness of how media narratives, cultural practices and public discourse influence policies, workplace norms, interpersonal expectations and public debates surrounding parenting, labor and care work. Supports workforce preparation in fields such as media, healthcare, public health, social work, policy development, education and public communication where sensitivity to diverse family structures and practices is essential. Enhances academic readiness for further study in rhetoric, gender studies, media studies and/or cultural studies. Encourages reflection on how public narratives about motherhood have evolved over time, affect social inclusion, policy decisions and public life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how ideas about motherhood vary across cultures, eras, socio-economic groups and/or ideological perspectives, challenging assumptions of universality. Encourages recognition of both biological and socially constructed dimensions of maternal identity. Clarifies the difference between personal belief and cultural representation, prompting reflection on how individuals internalize or resist public narratives about care, responsibility and motherhood and how it may modify behavior. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of motherhood in literature, film, television, music, news, advertising, music and digital media; historical shifts in maternal ideals; feminist and anti-feminist discourses; motherhood and labor; political uses of maternal identity; race, class and marginalized motherhoods; disability and motherhood; reproductive technology and infertility narratives; representation of motherhood in children's literature and films, childfree identities and resistance to maternal norms. Course material may involve emotional and sensitive content such as depictions of grief, trauma, marginalization or public controversy as relevant to understanding how motherhood is framed in culture. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with COMM 411.

Race, Gender, and the Environment. (3-0). Credit 3. Investigation of social inequalities related to environmental issues; focus on environmental justice and ecofeminism; exploration of the connections among racism, patriarchy, and the environment. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with GLST 413 and HISP 413.

Gender and Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of how gender shapes and is shaped by communication across interpersonal, organizational and public contexts. Examines how people express, interpret and negotiate gender in everyday interaction, media environments and/or institutional settings. Explores both stability and change in gendered expectations, roles and identities. Course content and discussions may touch on differing perspectives or points of disagreement for purposes of understanding communication dynamics surrounding gender. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Supports career pathways in media, public service, advocacy, education, law, nonprofit work and other community-facing professions by examining communication as grounded in diverse communities and lived experiences. Enhances preparation for careers involving interpersonal interaction, public communication, education, health, social work, policy development, human relations, consulting, advocacy or management. Builds recognition of how communication norms vary across individuals, cultures and contexts, which is an essential competency for workplace effectiveness, civic participation and collaborative problem-solving. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Explores how communication research addresses biological sex alongside cultural understandings of gender identity and gender roles and how each may influence interaction across different contexts. Highlights that everyday assumptions about gender and communication can vary across individuals, cultures and/or historical periods. Encourages examination of multiple scholarly perspectives on how gender-related patterns emerge, are perceived or are reinforced through communication, without prescribing a single interpretive lens. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of gendered language, voice and nonverbal expression; feminist and critical perspectives on communication and gender; communication across friendship, romantic, family and workplace relationships; leadership, authority and collaboration in professional settings; media portrayals of femininity, masculinity and gender diversity; intersections of gender with race, sexuality, class, nationality, religion and/or ability; communication surrounding health, body image, caregiving or identity disclosure; historical and cross-cultural perspectives on gender roles and expectations; analysis of humor, conflict, persuasion or storytelling through a gendered lens. Course material may reference real-world cases involving disagreement or controversy as relevant to understanding communication dynamics. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with COMM 420.

Employment Discrimination Law. (3-0). Credit 3. Legal issues surrounding employment discrimination, including disparate treatment and impact; intent; affirmative action; sexual harassment; pregnancy, sex, race, religious, salary, disability, age, and ethnic discrimination; policy issues and perspectives to aid human resource specialists and managers. Prerequisite: Admission to upper division in Mays Business School and senior classification. Cross-listed with MGMT 430.

Queer Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. This course examines the field of queer theory as it emerged in the U.S. academy in the 1990s and grew and developed within and beyond U.S. borders in the early 21st century. The course includes scholarship on gender and sexual diversity and its overlaps with and divergences from feminist theories, while also highlighting the ways it functions as a critical practice that extends far beyond questions of gender and sexuality. Drawing on philosophy, literature, cultural studies and political theory, the course examines how “queer” operates as a challenge to systems of normalization — of identity, desire, embodiment and knowledge itself. The course considers foundational and contemporary texts in the field. TOPICS. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. Prerequisites: 6 hours in Women's and Gender Studies; senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with SOCI 455.

Gender in Asia. (3-0). Credit 3. Gender dynamics in Asia; changes in gender roles; women's movements; women and the economy; women and politics; men's and women's private lives. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with ASIA 463 and SOCI 463.

Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Queer Cinemas. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of cinema by and about LGBTQ individuals or communities; discussion of production, film content and reception. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in WGST 200, FILM 215, FILM 251, ENGL 251, or FILM 299, and junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

Women in America Since 1877. (3-0). Credit 3. CONTENT. History of women in the U.S. from the late 19th century to the present; role of intersectionality in defining the experience of modern womanhood; women as activists, workers, consumers, mothers and feminists; experiences, lives and influence of women of color; examination of contemporary social, political and economic histories. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. The presentation of course content fosters critical thinking in the context of scholarly consensus and debate, rather than instructors’ views, values or beliefs. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. History teaches evaluation and synthesis of evidence, development of persuasive arguments in written and oral form, expansion of understandings of historical contexts that have contributed to human complexity past and present, including but not limited to the formation of group and individual identities, social and political dynamics, and debates about values and rights. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; HIST-473 also taught at Galveston campus. Cross-listed with HIST 473.

Studies in Women Writers. (3-0). Credit 3. This course is organized thematically around the expansive category of women’s writing. Topics vary by instructor design. Students will engage in advanced critical analysis of texts and hone interpretive skill in discussion and assignments. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken two times for credit. Prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at the 300-level; junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with ENGL 474.

Sex and Sexuality in History. (3-0). Credit 3. CONTENT. Changing ideas about sex and sexuality over time; includes their interaction with ideas about gender, race, class, religion, science, technology, medicine, politics and popular culture; historical and cultural processes creating modern concerns about sex and sexuality. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. The presentation of course content fosters critical thinking in the context of scholarly consensus and debate, rather than instructors’ views, values or beliefs. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. History teaches evaluation and synthesis of evidence, development of persuasive arguments in written and oral form, expansion of understandings of historical contexts that have contributed to human complexity past and present, including but not limited to the formation of group and individual identities, social and political dynamics, and debates about values and rights. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with HIST 476.

COURSE_NARRATIVE: Women and Gender in Modern European History. (3-0). Credit 3. CONTENT. History of women in Europe from the 18th century to the present: women's contributions to their societies; realities of their daily lives and their responses; perceptions of women; role of institutions in defining women's roles; significance for women of industrialization, revolution, warfare, scientific discoveries. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. The presentation of course content fosters critical thinking in the context of scholarly consensus and debate, rather than instructors’ views, values or beliefs. Instructors may assign different readings and/or topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. BENEFITS. History teaches evaluation and synthesis of evidence, development of persuasive arguments in written and oral form, expansion of understandings of historical contexts that have contributed to human complexity past and present, including but not limited to the formation of group and individual identities, social and political dynamics, and debates about values and rights. Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with HIST 477.

Senior Seminar. Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. This capstone course for majors is an inquiry-based study of topics in women’s and gender studies. The course uses theories, analytic approaches and feminist and other methods in women’s and gender studies to investigate a topic of social and cultural significance. TOPICS. Topics will vary depending on the expertise of the instructor. The course includes development of research and writing skills such as forming research questions, practicing research methods and drafting and revising research-based writing. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship, instructor expertise, and satisfy course learning objectives. Prerequisites: WGST 200 and junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

Internship in Women's and Gender Studies. Credit 0 to 4. Directed internship in a public or private organization to provide students with on-the-job training and applied research experience; opportunity to observe first hand issues and problems covered in women's and gender studies courses; designed to enhance and clarify the student's career objectives. Prerequisites: WGST 200, junior or senior classification, and approval of instructor.
Directed Studies. Credit 0 to 4. Readings and/or research for specific needs of students majoring or minoring in women's and gender studies. Prerequisites: WGST 200 and approval of instructor.
Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of women's and gender studies. May be repeated for credit.

Research. Credit 0 to 3. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in women's and gender studies. May be taken four times for credit. Prerequisites: WGST 200; junior or senior classification; and approval of instructor.

Feminist Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. Inquiry-based examination of contemporary feminist theory from an interdisciplinary perspective; topics may include intersectionality, LGBTQ+ issues, reproductive health and rights, sexuality and identity, economics and labor, legal and political issues facing women and LGBTQ+ communities, debates about priorities for feminist theory and activism, popular feminism, and feminism and ethics. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

Reproduction, Birth, and Power. (3-0). Credit 3. An examination of topics related to reproductive practices, experiences, and ideologies and of the constructed and contested meanings surrounding womanhood, motherhood, sexuality, reproductive freedom, and eugenics. Prerequisites: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with SOCI 610.

Readings in Gender and Sexuality in History. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of how gender and sexuality operate both as categories of identity and as analytical tools; how scholars have employed them to understand historical processes; how languages shape power relationships; how other vectors of identity (class, race and nation) intertwine with gender and sexuality. May be taken three times for credit. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with HIST 618.

Research Seminar in Gender and Sexuality in History. (3-0). Credit 3. Research and writing seminar focused on topics relevant to gender and sexuality in history. May be taken three times for credit. Prerequisites: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with HIST 619.

Sex, Gender and Cinema. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of a significant topic at the intersection of women's and gender studies and film, such as cinema and sexuality studies, cinema and women, and cinema and masculinity; may include discussion of production, film content, and reception. Prerequisites: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with FILM 643.

Queer Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of the origins of theories of gender and sexual diversity and their intersections with feminist theories; study of foundational and contemporary texts that address queer theory with a particular emphasis on how its utilizations within performance studies. Prerequisite: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with PERF 645.

Sociology of Gender. (3-0). Credit 3. Overview of the Sociology of Gender; historical development, primary concepts, contemporary issues, theory, methods, and applications. Prerequisite: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with SOCI 661.

Theories of Gender. (3-0). Credit 3. Theories of gender, sexualities, feminism, embodiment, and difference with particular focus on their relationship to literary and cultural studies; emphasis on contemporary theoretical positions, discourses, and debates. May be taken two times for credit. Cross-listed with ENGL 680.

Seminar in Women's and Gender Studies. Credit 3. Intensive investigation on selected research areas in Women’s and Gender Studies; exploration of the intersection of gender, queer and feminist scholarship in various disciplines and areas of study. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.
Directed Studies.  Credit 1 to 4. Directed individual study of selected problems in the field of women's and gender studies. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
Special Topics in... Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of women's and gender studies. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Research. Credit 1 or more each semester. Research toward thesis or dissertation. May be repeated for credit. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisite: Approval of Instructor.

Gender and Genre. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration and analysis of the ways in which a single literary and/or film genre resonates with gendered perspectives and sexual subjectivity. May be taken two times for credit. Prerequisite: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with FILM 694.

Contemporary Issues in Water Resources. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of contemporary issues in water resource systems including water quantity, water quality, ecosystem sustainability and water supply; focus on economic, legal, political and social considerations, and alternatives in water resource systems. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Geochemistry of Natural Fresh Waters. (3-0). Credit 3. Chemistry of aqueous solutions; weathering/redox reactions and controls on fresh waters; natural and anthropogenic factors affecting major, minor, and trace elements in fresh waters; evaluation of fresh water composition; application of water-quality measurements to quantitative hydrology. Cross-listed with GEOL 640.

Seminar. (1-0). Credit 1. Presentations on important developments and current research in hydrological sciences and water management; seminars presented by faculty, graduate students, visiting scholars and water professionals. May be repeated 3 times for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Professional Internship. Credit 0 to 1. An on-the-job supervised experience program, conducted on an individual basis in the area of the student's specialization in water management and hydrological science. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

Directed Studies.  Credit 1 to 4 each semester. Special topics in water not within scope of thesis research and not covered by other formal courses. Prerequisite: Graduate classification and approval of instructor.
Special topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of water management or hydrological science. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
Research.  Credit 1 or more each semester. Research toward thesis or dissertation.
Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of zoology. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

Research.  Credit 1 to 4. Active research of basic nature under the supervision of a Department of Biology faculty member. Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor.
Special Topics in...  Credit 1 to 4. Selected topics in an identified area of zoology. May be repeated once for credit.
Research.  Credit 1 to 4. Active research of basic nature under the supervision of a Department of Biology faculty member. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.
